The Fifth Treatise: Of Children

Children Showing Respect for Parents

The Fifth Treatise: Of Children · §§. 1–10

§. 1. Of the general heads of children’s duties.

Eph 6.

1. Children, obey your+ parents in the Lord, for this is right. 2. Honor your father and mother (which is the first commandment with a promise), 3. that it may go well with you, and that you may live long on the earth.

The second couple in a family are parents and children.

In laying down their duties, the apostle begins with children. His direction and urging to them is laid down in the first three verses of the sixth chapter. In these verses:

  1. He declares their duty.
  2. He adds reasons to enforce it.

In laying down their duty he notes three points.

  1. In what it consists (obey, honor).
  2. To whom it is to be performed (your+ parents).
  3. In what manner it is to be done (in the Lord).

The reasons the apostle uses are four.

  1. The place of parents (in the Lord).
  2. The justice of the thing (this is right).
  3. The charge of God (honor your father, etc.)
  4. The reward promised (that it may go well, etc.)

Under this word (obey), which the apostle uses, and that word (honor), which the law uses, are included all the duties that are enjoined on children anywhere throughout the whole of Scripture.

We will therefore set them down in some order, and handle them separately, one after another.

  1. The fountain of children’s duties must be searched out.
  2. The streams that flow from it must be observed.

The fountain is an inward disposition of the heart, compounded of love and fear.

The streams issuing from it extend to parents both while they are living and also when they are dead.

The duties children are to perform to their parents while they live concern their

  • Authority.
  • Necessity.

The authority of parents requires of children

  • Reverence.
  • Obedience.

Their necessity requires recompense.

The duties children owe to their deceased parents concern their

  • Body.
  • Reputation.

Their body must be buried with decency.

Their reputation must be maintained with honor.

§. 2. Of children’s love for their parents.

I make the fountain of children’s duties a mixed and compound disposition, because of the authority and affection that are mixed together in parents. The authority of parents requires fear in children, and their affection, love. So entire and so ardent is parents’ affection toward their children that it would make children too bold and insolent if there were no authority mixed with it to produce fear. And so supreme and absolute is their authority over them that it would make children dread their parents like slaves, if a fatherly affection were not tempered with it to breed love. But both of these joined together make a very good mixture: love, like sugar, sweetens fear, and fear, like salt, seasons love. And so, to join them both together, it is a loving fear, or a fearing love, that is the ground of children’s duties.

Where Christ forbids an excessive love in children for1 their parents, he implies that parents are a fit object for children to love (so long as their love is well moderated). Indeed, he implies that love for their parents is a feeling grafted into children even by nature. Joseph is commended to children as a worthy pattern in loving his father, and that from his youth until his father’s death. As evidence of this, in his younger years he brought his father “a bad report” about his2 brothers, by which he incurred their envy and hatred; he would never have done this if he had not loved his father. And having been long absent from his father, when by God’s providence an occasion was offered for him to meet his brothers, one of his first questions to them was about their father;3 and hearing that he was alive, he did not think it enough to send him food for his need, but must also see his face4 and have him live with him. And while his father was on the way, he went out to meet him, and at first sight fell on his neck5 and wept a good while (a token of great affection).

The love that parents naturally bear their children6 ought in justice to breed in children a love for their parents. For love deserves love, and those who cannot love in return are most unworthy to be loved. The love of parents, above all others, must be answered with love on the children’s part to the utmost of their power, because it is free, great and constant.

Besides, love in children toward their parents is a necessity,7 for without it their subjection (which of all others ought to be most free) would turn into slavish servitude.

Children ought to labor after this all the more, because by nature they are nowhere near as prone to love their parents as their parents are to love them. Love is weighty, and like weighty things it descends. Children therefore, out of conscience of their duty, must labor to make up this defect, and help nature by grace. I do not deny that there is naturally in children a greater love for their parents than for others; yet compared with the heat of their parents’ love for them, their love for their parents is cold. Therefore, just as the heat of the sun, shining much and long on a stone wall, draws a reflection of heat from that wall, so the hot beams of parents’ love, cast on children with fervency and constancy, ought to provoke and stir up children to send back a reflection of love on their parents.

Two extremes are contrary to this love.

One is lack of natural affection, a vice most odious8 and abominable in all, but most of all in children. The apostle counts this among the most heinous vices there are.

The other is hatred and spite toward parents, a vice more than monstrous and against nature. From it come the mocking and cursing of parents, of which we will hear later.

§. 3. Of a child’s fear of his parent.

To the duty of love named above must be added fear, which is a child’s awe-filled respect for his parent.

This awe-filled respect arises from an honorable esteem that a child has of his parent in his judgment and opinion, as he is his parent. From it proceeds, on the one side, a desire and endeavor to please the parent in all things, and, on the other side, a reluctance to offend him.

In this respect the fear of a child is set against the fear of a slave. For a child’s fear, being mixed with love, looks to the offense a parent may take; but a slave’s fear, which is ordinarily mixed with hatred, looks to nothing but the punishment his master may inflict on him. The fear named above belongs so distinctively to children that the awe-filled respect the saints bear to God is called a9 filial or childlike fear.

This fear in a child is a special branch of that honor10 which the law requires of children toward their parents, and it is in11 express terms enjoined on children by the law. The words God uses of Miriam12 (“If her father had but spit in her face, would she not have been ashamed for seven days?”) show that there ought to be such a fear of the parent in a child’s heart as would work shame in it when the parent is offended.

We have a worthy pattern of this in Jacob,13 who was loath to gain the blessing by offending his father.

This fear keeps love within bounds, and restrains a child14 from too much sauciness and impudence.

And it is a cause of a child’s reverent and dutiful conduct15 toward his parent. For as the heart is disposed, so the conduct will be ordered.

Contrary to this is that slight esteem of parents, or (what is more abominable)16 that base and vile esteem of them, which is in the hearts of many children, especially if their parents are poor, of low degree, unlearned, ignorant, or subject to any weaknesses. Ham17 must have had too slight an esteem of his father, if not a base one, when he mocked him. A true filial fear would have restrained him from that extreme.

Therefore, to breed and cherish this fear, and to prevent18 or remedy the contrary extreme, let children inform themselves well of their parents’ place and authority: how they are in God’s place, and a means under God of their children’s being. Children have received their very substance from the substance of their parents. In this respect, though parents should seem contemptible to others, yet they must not seem so to their children.

So much for a child’s inward disposition toward his parent. It must be shown by his outward conduct, and that in two things, reverence and obedience, both of which concern a parent’s authority.

§. 4. Of a child’s reverence in refraining from speech before his parent, and in listening to his parent.

The outward reverence that children owe to their parents consists partly in their speech, partly in their conduct.

Their speech both to and about their parents must savor of reverence: to their parents in their presence, about their parents in their absence.

In their presence, by refraining from speech and by framing it well.

For refraining from speech two virtues are needed:

  • Silence.
  • Patience.

Silence, in refraining from speaking and in breaking off speech.19

Patience, in listening to their parents.

The two branches of silence, refraining from speaking (especially when parents are speaking, or until parents give their children leave to speak), and breaking off speech when parents come into the place where children are speaking, are tokens of great reverence. In this way children testify that someone is present whom they greatly respect and honor. Job sets out in this way the respect that princes and others bore him in his prosperity: “The princes” (he says) “refrained20 from speaking and covered their mouths with their hands. The voices of the nobles were hushed,” etc. That is, while he was present, or while he spoke. The same may be said of children’s patience in enduring21 their parents’ speech, which Job also notes in these words: “Men listened to me with expectation, waiting silently.” Though parents may seem long and tedious in their speech, yet children must endure it.

And it is very needful that patience be added to silence, because many parents, out of tender love for their children and earnest desire for their good, think they can never say enough in instructing and admonishing them. The many exhortations22 given to children in Scripture to hear, listen, give ear, pay attention, mark and observe the words of their parents imply the silence and patience named above. For those who23 ought to be “quick to listen” must be “slow to speak.” I do not deny that much more is intended by those phrases, namely obedience; yet these must also be presupposed. For he who will not listen patiently and in silence to his parents while they speak will much less obey what they say.

Contrary to silence is sauciness (as we say) and too much24 boldness in children, when, without due respect for their parents’ presence, they will be chattering about this thing or that, so much so that if strangers came into the room where such children are, they would not think the children’s parents were present; or if they knew it, they might well think that such children bear little respect for their parents.

Contrary to patience in hearing is fretting and grumbling25 against parents (at least if their speech is at all long), and flouncing off or slinking away before they have finished. These faults are all the greater if children, by their talkativeness or impatience, hinder or interrupt their parents’ speech when they are giving any admonition or instruction. For in this way they show both too slight a respect for their parents and too little regard for the means of their own good.

§. 5. Of a child’s reverent framing of his speech to his parent.

A child’s reverence in framing his speech well to his parents26 may be shown in many ways, as

1. By giving them reverent and honorable titles. No title can be more honorable than the one that most properly belongs to them and is most usual: father for the one parent, and mother for the other. God takes the title father27 to himself, as a title of great dignity.

Objection. This title belongs so exclusively to God that28 we are to call no one on earth Father.

Answer. This is not to be taken absolutely of the title itself, but of the mind of the one who gives that title or covets it.

If it is coveted or given so as to obscure God’s Fatherhood, or to make a man a father of himself, without dependence on God or reference to him, who is properly the Father of all, it is an impious and sacrilegious title. But otherwise it is lawful and warrantable.

In Scripture the title father is given to every degree of dignity among men: to kings,29 captains,30 and other chief governors; to priests,31 prophets,32 apostles,33 and other ministers.34 In the fifth commandment all superiors are included under it; therefore father is a title of great honor. And by the rule of relation, mother is a title of equally great honor for the female sex. Religious and dutiful children have always been accustomed to give those titles to their parents. “My father,” says Isaac35 to Abraham, and Jacob36 to Isaac. “My mother,”37 says Solomon to Bathsheba. I also find the title sir38 or lord used: a title39 of honor.

2. By using few words before their parents, and those few40 not without just occasion: when they are first spoken to by their parents, or have leave from them, or are making some needful matter known to them; at least not so against their parents’ liking that their parents would be offended by it. And if they observe that their parents are unwilling to hear them speak any more of such and such a matter, then they ought to lay their hands on their mouths, as Isaac (Gen 22:7) and Jacob (Gen 27:12) did. This is a token of great respect.

3. By meek and humble speech. Such was the speech of41 Jonathan,42 Saul’s natural son, and of David,43 his son-in-law, with which Saul was much pleased and his wrath pacified.

4. By watching for a fit opportunity: as when parents are not44 seriously busy, or in company, or angry. When Saul45 was not angry, how well he accepted Jonathan’s defense of David! But46 in his anger, how badly he took it! This wise watching for a fit opportunity shows great reverence.

5. By a prompt, ready, willing and pleasing answer when they are spoken to by47 their parents. Eli was like a father to Samuel; therefore when Samuel48 thought that Eli called him, he answered at once and readily, “Here I am.” And when Eli pressed to know what the Lord had said to him, “Samuel told him everything and did not hide a thing from him.”4950 The younger son (noted in the parable) showed a son’s reverence in giving his father a willing and ready answer, though he failed in his obedience by not doing what he promised.

§. 6. Of the vices in children contrary to the aforesaid reverence in speech.

Contrary to those branches of reverence in speech are these:51

1. Pride: when children scorn to give their parents the title of father or mother. This is the attitude of many who have gained more wealth or honor than their parents ever had. In public especially such children most refuse to give those titles. Solomon was not of that mind. Though he was a great king, sitting on his throne in the sight and hearing of all his people who were around him, he called Bathsheba mother.52

If children had the regard for their parents’ honor that they should, then, being themselves in places of honor and dignity, they would all the more openly call their parents father and mother, so that their parents might be known to be the father and mother of so eminent a person.

2. Talkativeness, and too much insistence, or rather impudence53 in speech: when children, in dealing with their parents, can never have done (as we say), but must press matters to the very utmost. Many parents are often greatly provoked by this. It does not matter that the child is in the right, especially in a matter of no great consequence. For reverence’s sake the child must hold back, at least for a time. And if the matter in dispute is weighty, as in points of religion, the child must either take some other opportunity of better informing his parent, or else get some other wise friend to do it.

3. Defiance, when children answer their parents as if they54 were their equals, giving word for word. It is as unbecoming for children to answer back as for servants (whom the apostle has expressly forbidden to do it, Titus 2:9). Both law and nature forbid children to be provoked to this by anything their parents say or do. How great, then, is the fault of those who give scornful and defiant words to their parents when they are not provoked at all, as the elder son noted in the parable did, and the elder brother of the prodigal son!

4. Indiscretion, when children, in speaking to their parents, have no regard for their parents’ time, business or mood, and55 so greatly provoke them. It is laid down as a caution to parents that they must not provoke their children to wrath. How much more must children observe that caution?

5. Stubbornness, when children pout, scowl, sulk and give56 their parents no answer at all. This is too common a fault in children, and many parents are much offended and grieved by it. We heard57 before of a childlike silence that was very commendable and a token of great reverence; but this is worthy of much blame, a token of great undutifulness, and is to be avoided as carefully as that is to be practiced.

§. 7. Of children’s reverent speech about their parents.

The reverent respect that children bear their parents ought to be so true and entire that their speech, not only to them before their faces but also about them behind their backs, must be so framed in both matter and manner, whenever they have occasion to talk about their parents, that all who hear them may note that they bear a reverent respect for their parents.58

As a general direction for performing this duty better, let children say nothing about their parents that they would be unwilling to have come to their parents’ ears. More particularly, let them speak of the things that most tend to their parents’ praise, so that (as Christ said of his Father59) they may honor their parents. Let other things be buried in silence, as far as they can. And if others speak of matters disgraceful to their parents, let them put the better construction on things doubtful, and, as far as they may, lessen things evident, and sharply rebuke those who slander their parents. This is the blessing that children owe to their parents. For neglecting it the wise man reproaches children, saying, “There is a generation that … does not bless its60 mother.”

Contrary to that kind of blessing is exposing parents’61 infirmities, noted in cursed Ham;62 and spreading untruths about them, noted in impious Absalom;63 and mocking and cursing them,64 which is expressly condemned. The reward of this by65 God’s law is death; indeed, a shameful and ignominious death, for “the ravens of the valley will pluck out his eye, and young vultures will devour it.”6667 This phrase sets out the end of a notorious criminal who is hanged.

§. 8. Of a child’s reverent conduct toward his parent.

As their speech, so the conduct of children toward their parents must be seasoned with reverence, because:

  1. This is a fruit and proof of filial fear as well as that.
  2. Of the two, this is the surer evidence, for actions are better signs of the disposition of the heart than words.
  3. Fair words joined with contrary deeds cannot be counted anything but mere show and hypocrisy.
  4. Where words and deeds contradict each other, the one will be a witness against the other, and that man’s condemnation the greater.68

Therefore let all reverence be shown in children’s behavior toward their parents, and that in these and similar instances.

1. If a parent is coming to a child, and the child notices it, let him hurry to meet his parent. So Joseph69 did to his father, and70 Solomon to his mother. These two examples are all the more to be noted because both were in eminent places: one a great governor, the other a king.

2. Let such childlike gestures of respect be performed as befit71 the child’s age and sex, whether in going to a parent, remaining before him, or going from him: such as uncovering the head, bending the knee, bowing the body, standing up, and the like. The two eminent persons named above, Joseph72 and Solomon,73 bowed, the one to his father, the other to his mother.

3. Let the expression and bearing of the body be so soberly74 and modestly ordered in the parent’s presence as to show due respect.

4. Let the upper place and precedence be given to parents; and75 if on occasion a child is above his parent, let him come below him. For that is a clear token of inferiority and subjection. What makes men strive for precedence, but that they want to be counted better than those with whom they strive? But that ought not to be the mind of children toward their parents.

Question. What if children are wealthier or more honorable in their condition than their parents? Are they still to give them precedence?

Answer. No honor is comparable to the dignity of fatherhood. It gives the parent a greater eminence over his child than any other honor can give the child over his parent. I grant that a child may be so advanced above his father by some office and outward dignity that other men may honor and reverence the child more, and give the upper place to him; and for order’s sake the child may and ought to take it in company. But when they are alone, the child must rather reverence the father.

5. According to the custom of the time and place in which76 they live, let children ask their parents’ blessing.

§. 9. Of children’s asking their parents’ blessing, whether it is lawful or not.

Some doubt is raised about this duty, both with respect to the thing itself and also to the gesture of kneeling used in performing it. I will therefore prove both separately.

As for the thing itself, it is noted of Jacob that he brought savory food to his father so that his father might bless him;77 and of Joseph, that he went to his father and took his two sons with him,78 so that his father might bless both him and them. For this end the twelve sons of Jacob gathered to their father.79

Objection. These were extraordinary examples. The patriarchs were endowed with the spirit of prophecy, by which they revealed to their children what their condition would be in the times to come; and their children came to them to know this.

1. Answer. Their blessings were more than predictions of things to come. They were confirmations and assurances to the80 children that God would indeed perform the blessing their parents had pronounced. For they bore a double role: the role of a prophet and that of a father. As prophets they foretold things to come; as fathers they obtained the blessings pronounced,81 and an assurance of them for their children, and that by faith and prayer.

2. Answer. Though not every parent can, with such an extraordinary spirit, assure his children of any distinct and particular blessing, yet the faithful prayer of parents is a special and ordinary means of obtaining a blessing from God on their children; and that because of God’s promise, which extends82 not only to faithful parents but also to their descendants. Therefore, as the children of the patriarchs came to their fathers to be assured of some extraordinary blessing, so other children may go to their parents as a means of obtaining an ordinary blessing. It is noted of Elijah83 that by an extraordinary spirit in prayer he obtained extraordinary things; yet the apostle sets out that example to all Christians as a motive to stir them up to pray in faith for ordinary blessings. But to clear this point further, note the phrase84 used in the fifth commandment as a reason to move children to honor their parents. Word for word it is this: “that they may prolong your days,” etc. How can parents prolong their children’s days, except by begging that blessing from God?85 The prayers of parents, then, are a great blessing to children, and children ought to seek this blessing from their parents.

Objection. If parents are wicked, their prayer is an abomination. What blessing, then, can children look for from wicked parents?

Answer. Though God does not hear wicked parents out of love and goodness toward themselves, yet for the good of their children he may and will hear them, and that all the more to maintain a reverent respect for parents in their children’s hearts. For asking a blessing is an acknowledgment of superiority and authority, according to the apostle’s words, “the lesser is blessed86 by the greater.”

As for the gesture of kneeling, it corresponds to the87 gesture that God’s people used of old in a similar case. Of Joseph it is said that “he bowed facedown.”

Objection. Kneeling is a gesture belonging only to the worship of God.

Answer. It does not belong to it so exclusively that it cannot be used in secular matters. Otherwise Christ would have reproved the young man for kneeling before him as well as for calling him good;88 for he took Christ to be only a man, and the worship he gave him was only social honor.

It is not the gesture alone, but the occasion of the gesture, the mind of the one who performs it, and the end for which he performs it, that make it divine or social. Cornelius fell down before Peter with the notion of some divine excellence in him, and was not allowed to do so; his manner of worship was divine. The jailer fell down before Paul and Silas in acknowledgment of some outward eminence in them, and was not reproved; his manner of worship was merely social. The same gesture may be performed to different persons with a different regard. A child may kneel to his parent and to the king, yet it does not follow that he makes his parent a king. Neither will it follow that by kneeling to his parent he makes him a God, because men kneel to God.

§. 10. Of the vices contrary to children’s reverent bearing toward their parents.

Contrary to the branches of reverent bearing named above are these:89

1. Rudeness and bad manners, when children do not know how to make a difference between their parents and strangers, but can90 let their parents come to them while they stay in their place and do not stir to meet them.

2. Disdainful haughtiness, when they resent having to stand91 bareheaded for any length of time in their parents’ presence. It often happens that when parents and children are together before their betters, the parents will show more reverence than the children. For the father will stand bareheaded while the son sits down and puts on his hat, on the notion that his father shows more reverence than is fitting. But even if that were so, the son should stoop somewhat lower for his father’s sake.

3. Frivolity and boldness, when children are overfamiliar92 with their parents, fooling about and giggling on every slight occasion. This kind of conduct cannot help but tend greatly to the disgrace and dishonor of their parents. For what can those who see it think, but that such children have been too much pampered and badly nurtured?

4. Ambition, when children are so ambitiously eager for place,93 especially in company, that rather than be below some whom they suppose to be at least their equals, they will be above their parents. This often happens when parents, being of a lowly mind, give place to those whom their children, being of a lofty mind, think lower than themselves. Then, rather than be under their inferiors (as they suppose), they will be above their parents: a point of great insolence. The respect of a child for his parent ought to be such that he would rather lower himself below those who are his inferiors than exalt himself above his parent. As with other men a man must, for peace’s sake, give up his right in many cases, so he must do so especially with his parent in a matter of superiority. Would not everyone who knows what honor a child owes a father condemn the ambition of a child who would so insist on place and precedence as to take them from his parent?

5. The overscrupulous and erroneous opinion of those who think it94 unfitting for any child to ask his parents’ blessing. Their own opinion sways them more than the continual, approved practice of God’s people in all ages. They are not unlike the man whom Solomon calls “wiser in his own eyes than seven men who answer95 discreetly.” Others, though they do not disallow this duty so generally, yet think it fitting only for young children, not considering of what years, stature and standing Joseph was when he performed it.

As for those who do not think it unlawful, yet carelessly neglect it, they little consider the benefit of a parent’s blessing. Profane Esau96 will one day rise up in judgment against them. He begged and begged, again and again, and that with a loud cry and salt tears, for a blessing from his father.

So much for children’s reverence. Their obedience follows.

Children Getting Parents’ Permission

The Fifth Treatise: Of Children · §§. 11–26

§. 11. Of children’s obedience.

The obedience of children most proves the authority of parents, and is the surest evidence of the honor a child gives his parent. That is why it is97 expressly named in the text, and all the other duties are included under it. Reverence without obedience is a mere mockery, not at all acceptable. Of the two, a child would do better to fail in the former, as the98 parable of the two sons shows. Reverence, compared with obedience, is only an outward honor of courtesy. Obedience is a true, real honor, the surest test of a dutiful child. Obedience is a duty so much children’s own that the apostle applies it to them as their own attribute, saying, “As obedient children, do not conform,”99 etc. The example of Christ is set before us in this as a pattern: of his parents it is said that he “was obedient to them.”100 Solomon counts the neglect of it a despising101 of a parent.

Contrary to it are disobedience and rebellion, the greatest blow102 to parents’ authority there can be. For to what end is authority over those who resist it and rebel against it? The103 apostle counts disobedient children among the most wicked people there are, and he describes their disobedience by104 a metaphor taken from untamed, headstrong beasts that will not be brought under the yoke. So the word is not unfitly translated unruly. And it corresponds in some measure to a105 Hebrew phrase given to disobedient children, namely sons of Belial. By its derivation this means sons without profit; or, as some will have it, sons without yoke: that is, children who, refusing to be in subjection to their parents, are of no profit in any way, but do much harm and cause great grief. The106 punishment that God’s law appointed for disobedient and rebellious children was a public, shameful death.

§. 12. Of children’s forbearing to do things without their parents’ consent.

So that children may know their duty in this respect the better,107 I will set out distinctly both the parts and the extent of a child’s obedience:

  1. What it consists in.
  2. How far it extends.

The general parts it consists in are two:

1. A forbearance from doing things without their parents’ consent.108

2. A performance of such things as their parents want done.

The former of these is a duty children are most bound to while they are under their parents’ government. For during that time their parents’ consent is not only fitting but necessary,109 and that for these reasons.

1. Children are like their parents’ goods, wholly in their power, to be ordered and disposed of by them. On this ground Satan, having all that Job had put into his hand, took liberty over110 his children as well as over his goods and possessions.

2. Children, while they are under government (even the eldest, who are heirs), are no different from servants.111

3. By God’s law given to the Jews, parents had power to sell112 their children.

4. Parents had power to annul what their children had done. Take for example the case of a vow made to God,113 which was one of the most inviolable things a person could do.

Contrary to this is the opinion and practice of many, who hold that parents’ consent is at most a fitting thing: that it is good, if children are willing, to have their parents’ consent; if they do not have it, it is no great matter; their contracts, or the other things they do, are as firm and good without their parents’ consent as with it. If this were so, how would the authority of a parent be any more than that of a wise, experienced friend? It is fitting and good to have such a person’s consent.

But so that the power of parents and the duty of children in this point may be seen the better, I will illustrate it in five particular cases: 1. Entering into a calling. 2. Making a marriage. 3. Disposing of goods. 4. Ordering clothing. 5. Making vows.

§. 13. Of parents’ consent to children’s entering into a calling.

I. That children ought to have their parents’ consent in choosing their calling, and not place themselves as they please, is evident from the approved practice of the saints recorded in God’s word. Jacob114 was sent by his parents to Laban to be brought up under him. David115 was appointed by his father to keep sheep; when Saul wanted to have David attend him, he sent to Jesse, David’s father, for him. Since Jesse116 was so concerned to send provisions to his three eldest sons, who followed Saul to the war, we may well think that they went to the war with his consent. It is noted of Jonadab117 that he appointed his sons to live in tents, that they did so accordingly, and that they are commended and rewarded for this obedience of theirs. Both118 ancient and119 later divines gather that our Lord Jesus Christ120 in his younger years, before he began to exercise his public ministry, occupied himself in his father’s trade, and that this was the way in which he showed his subjection to his parents. This conclusion is drawn by comparing Luke 2:51 (where his subjection is noted) with Mark 6:3 and Matt 13:55, where he is called121 “the carpenter” and “the carpenter’s son.”

Justice requires that parents should have a hand in placing their children, because they brought them into the world, and brought them up with much care, pains and expense while they were young, until they were fit for a calling.

Besides, God has laid it as a charge on parents that they should see their children well trained up. There is great reason, therefore,122 that the parents’ consent be obtained in setting children out in a calling.123

§. 14. Of the unlawfulness of children’s entering religious orders without their parents’ consent.

Contrary to this is the opinion of the papists, who say that children may124 enter religious orders not only without the consent, but even against the mind and approval, of their parents. By this they not only defend open disobedience in children, against the express word of God, but also disable children from helping their parents in case of need. For both of these Christ rebuked the scribes and Pharisees in a similar case.

Objection. The papists grant that if parents are in such need125 that they cannot live without their children’s help, their children must not forsake their parents by entering any religious order. For they are bound by the law of God to help their parents.

Answer. 1. This caveat has been wrung from them by the evidence of arguments taken from God’s word and pressed on them by their opponents.

2. It does not touch the principal argument, taken from God’s precept, which they make of no effect by this tradition of theirs.

3. Though parents are not in such extreme need at the time when their children first enter their religious order, yet they may be afterward. But once children have entered, the papists hold it utterly unlawful for them to attend on their parents to help them, whatever the parents’ need.

Objection. Children who have entered religious orders may126 help their parents as befits religious persons: by their prayers to God.

Answer. 1. This is exactly the Pharisees’ Corban, which Christ mentions in Mark 7:11, and by which he plainly exposes the hypocrisy of the Pharisees, who made a show of religion into a hindrance to the obedience God required of children.

2. To pray for something a man does not try to do, when he is able to do it, is a plain mocking of God.

The arguments they bring to confirm their erroneous opinion are taken from extraordinary examples or from mystical resemblances, such as

  1. Abraham’s leaving his father’s house.127
  2. Levi’s speech about his father and mother, when he said, “I do not consider them.”
  3. The advice given to the royal queen, “Forget … your father’s128 house.”
  4. The test of our love for Christ, by loving him more129 than father or mother.
  5. Christ’s forbidding one who followed him to go and130 bury his father.

Answer. 1. As for Abraham’s example: 1. It cannot be proved that he left his father’s house without his father’s consent. 2. He was then married, and so of another house. 3. He had131 an express, particular charge from God to leave his father’s house, just as he had to sacrifice his son. Unless a like charge can be shown, his example proves nothing to the purpose.

2. As for Levi’s speech: 1. Moses noted it in connection132 with a particular zealous deed of the Levites in carrying out the vengeance of the Lord, and so it is to be counted among those extraordinary things that are not set as examples. 2. What moved the Levites to make no difference between their parents and others was the Lord’s cause. Their parents and relatives, as well as others, had notoriously sinned against God, and in that respect the Levites took no notice of them. But the parents the papists teach children to forsake are not such parents, but any parents. Now what kind of inference is this: some children have been God’s ministers in carrying out just punishment on their wicked parents; therefore children may enter such places as will exempt them from helping any parents, however well deserving? 3. The Levites had an express charge133 for what they did; but what the papists infer from their example makes the commandment of God of no effect.134

3. As for the135 advice to the queen: 1. It is to be taken mystically. 2. If it were taken literally, it is to be taken as given to her after marriage, when she was out of her parents’ government. 3. It concerns the136 law of marriage, and implies not an outright forsaking of parents, but a preferring of a husband before them.

4. As for loving father and mother more than Christ: 1. It does not necessarily imply a forsaking of our parents, for we may love Christ more than them and still perform our duty to them. 2. If they are forsaken, it must be in opposition to Christ, when either Christ or they must be forsaken, because if we hold fast to them they will draw us away from Christ.

5. As for Christ’s forbidding one who followed him to go and bury his father: 1. It was because of an extraordinary calling which that man had. 2. It is set down as a pattern for ministers, to show that they should especially attend to their own office, and leave other worldly matters to be done by those who can do them well enough. To apply it to children’s forsaking of their parents is to pervert its sense.

So we see how little to the purpose the arguments named above are brought to prove that erroneous opinion, that children may enter religious orders without their parents’ consent. I might further show how irreligious their so-called religious orders are, and so how unlawful it is to enter them even with the parents’ consent; but that is nothing to the point in hand.

§. 15. Of the unlawfulness of children’s traveling, and binding themselves as apprentices, without their parents’ consent.

Contrary also to the part of children’s obedience named above is the practice of those children who travel and seek their fortunes (as they say) without their parents’ consent, like the prodigal child,137 if not worse. For it is likely that he forced a general consent from his father, since he obtained his portion of goods from him. Such children usually bring great grief to their parents, and often make them fear more than there is cause, as old Jacob feared when he did not know what had become of138 his son.

Among these failings may be counted a custom in this land, more common than lawful, for children to bind themselves as apprentices without their parents’ consent. Those who take indentures from such children, or otherwise make agreements with them without knowing that their parents consent, make themselves accessories to this fault.139

§. 16. Of parents’ consent to the marriage of their children.

II. That children ought to have their parents’ consent to their marriage is clear beyond all question. For

1. God himself has given us a pattern in this. He first brought the woman to the man (Gen 2:22). By this he would show that he who gave the woman her being had a right to give her in marriage; and parents now have that right, for from them, under God, children receive their being. In this case parents stand in God’s place, and are, as it were, God’s hand to join their children in marriage.

2. God has given express laws on this point. I pass over that general moral law, “Honor your father and mother” (which, as it is the ground of all the other duties belonging to children, is the ground of this one too). The authority and charge which God by his law (Deut 7:3) has laid on parents, to give their daughters to husbands and to take wives for their sons, has the force of a law binding children from taking wives or husbands without or against their parents’ consent. This law did not belong to the Jews only; as a branch of the moral law it is pressed on Christians, 1 Cor 7:36, 37.

To this may be added the judicial law (if it is to be counted merely judicial) of a parent’s power to give his daughter in marriage, or to refuse to give her, to the man who had deflowered her, Exod 22:17.

3. The practice of God’s saints, recorded and approved in Scripture, has been in keeping with the law. Isaac married the wife his father provided (Gen 24:67). Jacob both obeyed his father in going to Laban’s house for a wife (Gen 28:2) and also, when he came to Laban, asked him for his daughter (Gen 29:18 etc.).

Though Samson saw a daughter of the Philistines who140 pleased him well, yet he would not marry her before he had his parents’ consent, Judg 14:2.

4. These words of Tamar (2 Sam 13:13), “Speak to the king” (who was her father), “for he will not withhold me from you,” show that children were not accustomed to be married without their parents’ consent. This is further confirmed by this oath of the Israelites: “Not one of us will give his daughter141 in marriage to a Benjamite,” Judg 21:1.

5. The142 ancient fathers of the church have taught children this duty in their ages, and pronounced marriages of children without their parents’ consent to be unlawful.

6. The very143 heathen have observed the justice of this. Though Shechem loved Dinah, and had deflowered her, yet he would not marry her without the consent of his father and hers, Gen 34:3 etc. Ishmael had learned as much, either from the instruction he had received in Abraham’s house or else by the light of nature; for he kept to the choice his mother made for him, Gen 21:21.

7. Though144 the papists in other cases make the authority of parents of no effect, yet in this case they count it utterly unlawful for children to marry without or against their parents’ consent, and have made canons against it on that ground.

8. The145 law of nature and of nations, the civil and canon law, the common and statute law of our land: every kind of law agrees with God’s law in this point.

9. It146 has been a custom in all Christian churches throughout all ages for the parent, or someone in the parent’s147 place, to give the bride to the bridegroom at the time of the marriage; and by this the parents’ consent is openly shown.

10. Many148 divines of good note and name have judged marriages made wholly without, or directly against, the parents’ consent (especially if the parents have just cause of objection to those marriages) to be of no force until the parent is brought to ratify them; and in many churches, after due examination of the matter, they usually count them as no marriages. Experience has shown the boldness of many children in making light of their parents’ consent in those places where marriages, once completed, are ratified149 and made indissoluble, though they were made wholly without or directly against the parents’ consent. Many children think that though it is done unlawfully, yet once it is done it will stand. So if they fear they will not have their parents’ consent, they will contrive to get their marriage completed in such a way that their parents do not know of it in time to hinder it before it is done; and after it is done, they brazenly resolve to ride out, as well as they can, the storm of their parents’ displeasure. To prevent such contempt of the power of parents, and to establish the authority God has given them over their children, marriages made without or against the parents’ consent, as described above, are made void in many churches.

§. 17. Of the justice of the point, and reasons why children should have their parents’ consent to their marriage.

1. By marriage children are separated from their parents, for150 “a man will leave his father and mother and be united to his wife.”151 Is it not great reason, then, that those from whom children had their being, and by whom they have been maintained and brought up until the time of their marriage, should be told of that kind of leaving them, and give their consent to it?

2. By the marriage of his child, a parent’s power passes over to the husband or wife of the child. And should such a power be taken away without the parent’s consent?

3. Children, for the most part, are headstrong and rash for lack of experience, and seek more to satisfy their present carnal desire than to provide themselves a good and lasting helper. But parents, by the instinct of nature, love their children as well as children love themselves; by much experience they have a better understanding of a fitting helper; and they are better able to use their gift of discernment in this case, because it is not their own case, and yet it is the case of one whom they love as themselves, and to whom they wish as much good as to themselves. Is it not fitting, then, even for the child’s good, that in a matter of such weight as marriage the parent should have a say?

§. 18. Of a child’s conduct in case a parent provides an unfit mate or none at all.

Question. What if parents urge their children to marry someone152 they cannot feel affection for and love: must children yield obedience in this, against their mind and liking?

Answer. If there is no just objection to the person recommended, they ought to strive with the utmost of their power153 to bend their affection to their parents’ will. As a help to this, let them be persuaded that their parents are as concerned for their good as they themselves are, and wiser than they are. Indeed, above all they ought to pray earnestly to God (in whose hand man’s heart is, to turn it154 wherever he will) that he would be pleased to change the course of their affection and to settle it on the person their parent has chosen for them; if, at least, they see no just cause to the contrary. But if, despite all the means they can use, they still find their heart wholly averse, they may in a reverent manner entreat their parent to stop pressing that match, and to think of some other.

2. Question. What if the parent is negligent, and does not provide a fit match in due time: may the child not provide one for himself?

Answer. A parent’s negligence is not a sufficient pretext for a child to cast off the subjection he owes his parent. Yet I do not deny that a child who knows where a fit match is to be had may make it known to his parent (as Samson did)155 and ask for both his consent and his help in it. And if his parent gives no ear to his humble request, he may use the mediation of his relatives or other friends. Indeed, if necessity requires that the child be married, and his parent adds willfulness to negligence and will not be moved at all, either by the humble request of his child or by the earnest pleading of any friends, an appeal may be made to the magistrate (who is in God’s place over the parent as well as over156 the child, and ought to give relief to the child); and what the magistrate does in that case is as good a warrant to the child as if the parent had done it.

The same means may be used if a parent is an idolater, a heretic or an atheist, and will not allow his child to be married to anyone but one of his own persuasion and disposition.

§. 19. Of the sin of children in marrying without their parents’ consent.

Contrary to this is the mind and practice of those children who, thinking too lightly of their parents’ power, take matches of their own choice: sometimes secretly, without giving their parents any notice at all; and sometimes most rebelliously, against their parents’ mind and charge. They are not much unlike those in the old world who are condemned because “they took as wives whomever157 they chose” (which was one branch of the wickedness for which the world was drowned); or rather they are like Esau,158 who took such wives as turned out to be a grief to his parents. What blessing can be expected to fall on such marriages? Or rather, what curse may we not fear will follow them? God’s law is transgressed by them. His image in parents is despised. What is more the parents’ own than any goods is taken from them, either by fraud or by violence. Their souls are grieved by it, and they are159 often provoked to cast off their children and curse their marriages. Now God’s curse often follows the just curse of a parent.

§. 20. Of objections in favor of children’s marrying without their parents’ consent, answered.

1. Objection. Though Jacob married one wife according to his parents’ direction, yet he married three others (at least the two maidservants) without their consent.

1. Answer. Jacob’s example in marrying more wives than one is not to be justified.

2. Answer. Jacob had a general consent from his parents to160 take a wife from the daughters of Laban. If, therefore, his marrying two wives had been lawful, neither the one daughter nor the other would have been taken wholly without his parents’ consent. As for the two maidservants by whom he had children, neither of them was his wife: for long after they had children they are called his “maidservants,”161 and distinguished from his wives.

2. Objection. Servants may marry without their masters’ consent: why then may children not marry without their parents’?

1. Answer.162 It is not lawful for servants to do so while the term of their covenant lasts.

2. Answer. Though the servitude of a servant is greater than that of a child, yet a parent has in many respects a greater power over his child than a master over his servant. The power a master has comes by a mutual covenant between him and his servant, and by the servant’s voluntary subjection to his master. But the power of a parent comes by the bond of nature, since a child has his being from his parents. Besides, this subjection of a child to his parents in the matter of marriage is not for servitude but163 for the good of the child.

3. Objection. Children marry for themselves and not for their parents: why then should parents’ consent be insisted on so much?

1. Answer. Though they do not marry for their parents, yet they marry164 from their parents: by marriage they are freed from their parents’ power.

2. Answer. Children are not their own. They are “a heritage from the Lord”: the Lord has given them to parents as a heritage. A child, therefore, has no more right to marry for himself without his parents’ consent than to give away his parents’ goods for himself.

§. 21. Of stealing children from their parents for the sake of marriage.

Those who by fraud lure children away, or by violence carry them off, to marry them otherwise than their parents would wish, make themselves accessories to the165 sin named above, and to its vengeance. This is a worse kind of felony than stealing a man’s goods. For children are much more truly a man’s own than his goods, and dearer to him than any goods can be; indeed, they are to be valued so much more highly, as rational creatures are to be preferred before senseless and merely sentient things. Our166 statute law expressly condemns this, and imposes a severe punishment on those who offend in it. And such offenders justly deserve to be severely punished, both because of the heinousness of the sin and because of the many167 harms that follow from it, such as alienation of parents’ affection from their children, disinheriting of heirs, enmity between the relatives of each party so married, lawsuits, ruin of families, and (if the persons whose children are married without their parents’ consent are great and noble) disturbance of whole towns, cities and nations. Take for example the destruction of the Shechemites, Gen 34.168 This is said to have been the cause of the ten years’ war between the Greeks and the Trojans, and of the ruin of Troy.

§. 22. Of ministers’ sin in marrying children without their parents’ consent.

Those ministers also who, through carelessness, not taking due account of the parties they marry, whether they have their parents’ consent or not, or through bribery, being hired by a reward, marry such children as they know do not have their parents’ consent, make themselves accessories in a high degree to the169 sin named above. Their deed is as bad as the deed of the principals themselves. Their solemnizing of such marriages emboldens both the parties so married and all the persons present at it. They greatly dishonor God’s holy ordinance, because, acting in God’s person, they say of those whom God has forbidden to be so joined together, “Those whom God has joined together, let no man separate.” If ministers did not have a hand in such unlawful marriages, they could not be made, for our church ratifies no marriage except one made by a minister. So some minister or other is guilty of this foul sin whenever any child is married without his parents’ consent. Our church therefore does well (to prevent this sin) to forbid ministers expressly to marry anyone without their parents’ consent, and to inflict a severe censure on those who offend in it.

§. 23. Of children’s forbearing to dispose of any of their parents’ goods without consent.

A third branch of the subjection of children, in forbearing to do anything without their parents’ consent, concerns their parents’ goods.

That children, though living in their parents’ house, ought not to dispose of their parents’ goods without their consent is evident from the extent of their obedience: in everything.

Since Isaac was pleased to send Jacob to Paddan-aram without any great provision, it seems that Jacob made it a matter of conscience not to take anything secretly, and went as his father sent him, with only his staff.170 And the171 defense he made to Laban, his father-in-law, concerning things taken away shows that he held it unlawful for children secretly to carry off their parents’ goods: “What is my trespass? What is my sin?” (he says). “Have you found anything that belongs to you?”

Does he not imply by this that if Laban’s daughters had taken away any of their father’s goods, it would have been a trespass and a sin?

The apostle says of the heir (who of all the children may172 seem to have the greatest right) that “as long as he is a child” (that is, under the government of his parents), “he is no different from a servant,173 although he is the owner of everything.” If he is no different from a servant, what right can he have to dispose of his parents’ goods at his pleasure? Does a servant have any such right?

It is very needful that children should be bound to their parents’ consent in this, both for the good of the parents and for the good of the children themselves.

For the parents, so that they may know what they have174 or do not have, and order their expenses accordingly. How can parents tell what they have, if children secretly, without their knowledge, steal and dispose of their goods?

For the children, so that their spendthrift disposition may by this means175 be restrained (for youth is very prone to spend beyond moderation, if it has the means), and so that their parents may be the better able to “lay up” for them.176

§. 24. Of the sin of children in stealing and squandering their parents’ goods.

Contrary to this are both the opinion and the practice of many177 children.

As for opinion, many think and say that whatever is their178 parents’ is theirs too. And so, when the watchful eye and provident care of their parents restrain them from overlavish spending, or from laying out anything with their own hands, they grumble against that restraint.

Knowing and being persuaded of their subjection in this matter would be a good means to suppress that discontented disposition.

As for practice,179

1. Some secretly take away and steal whatever goods, money, wares or anything else of their parents’ they can come by. The Holy Spirit counts this plain theft: for when Rachel had secretly taken away her father’s idols, the Scripture says that she “stole” them.

Those who counsel and encourage children to do so make themselves accessories to this: as many busybodies and deceitful persons advise daughters, when God has taken away their mothers, to take linen and other such household goods away from their father, claiming that their father may marry another wife, who will carry everything away. And on a like pretext they also persuade sons, when their fathers die, to carry off what they can from their mother. But such pretexts are no sufficient warrant for children to deceive their parents. It would be better for children to be deprived of their parents’ goods than to enjoy them by such deceit, for they will be like that bread which “is sweet to a man, but later his180 mouth is full of gravel.”

2. Others spend their portion in wild living, like the prodigal181 child, and run into debt, and so force their parents either to pay it or to leave them to the law. Many scholars at the universities, gentlemen at the Inns of Court, and such children as are brought up somewhat liberally in their parents’ or other relatives’ houses, offend greatly in this. This excess and wild living differs little from the kind of theft named above, and ordinarily it brings as many harms as that does.

3. Some also are so graceless and ungrateful that, when they182 have come of age and their parents have grown old, they seek to cheat their parents out of all they have, and to bring their parents under them, to be ordered by them. They labor to get possession of everything before their parents are dead, or before the parents are willing to resign any such right to their children. Such were183 Absalom and Adonijah. How highly displeasing such practices are to God is shown by the vengeance that fell on the heads of184 those two brothers in evil, traitorous and disloyal children.

All such children as seek after the means named above, or any other like means, to defraud their parents repay their parents’ care for them very badly, and, more like barbarians than Christians, return evil for good. They often bring poverty and disgrace on their parents and themselves. They are worse than other thieves, because they are more dearly valued and more freely trusted. Indeed, they are a very bad example to servants in the house, or to subjects in the commonwealth.

§. 25. Of children’s being content to be clothed according to their parents’ mind and liking.

IIII. A fourth branch of the aforesaid subjection of children concerns their clothing: that it be no other than what agrees with their parents’ good liking. It is noted that Israel185 made Joseph a robe. Does not the particular mention of that circumstance show that parents must have the ordering of their children’s clothing? This is also implied in the reason given for Tamar’s “robe of many colors,” namely,186 “because this is what the king’s virgin daughters wore.” And since Rebekah had the keeping of her187 son Esau’s clothes, it appears that his clothes were to his parents’ liking; otherwise he would have hidden them from his parents. In further confirmation of this, it is noted that his clothing was pleasing to his father.

Contrary to this is the vainglorious disposition of many children,188 who, to the grief and discredit of their parents, dress themselves both against the mind and above the means of their parents, and in a way unbecoming their parents’ place and calling. Among others, many ministers’ children bring much discredit on their parents by this. Let all such proud youths note how the Lord has threatened to punish even the king’s children who are dressed189 in foreign apparel.

§. 26. Of children’s forbearing to bind themselves to do anything against their parents’ consent.

V. The fifth and last branch with which I will illustrate the subjection of children named above will be the one expressly noted in the law: a child’s binding itself by a vow.

The law gives the parent power to annul his child’s190 vow. It is therefore a child’s duty to abstain from vowing without his parents’ consent.

Contrary to this are such vows as the papists lure children to make,191 namely vows of chastity, perpetual virginity, obedience to a monastic rule, voluntary poverty, and the like.

Even if by these vows children are not drawn to forsake their parents (which192 we proved above to be utterly unlawful), and even if these vows were lawful in their nature (which they are not, because they are against God’s law and ordinance, and against Christian liberty, and smack too strongly of Judaism, indeed of a worse superstition), yet they must not be made without their parents’ consent.

Just as unlawful are oaths and other such means by which children bind themselves to do things neither commanded nor forbidden, which their parents are not willing for them to do. What does this do but bring a snare on the consciences of children, and make it necessary for them to break one of God’s commandments? Either the third, in breaking their vow or oath, or the fifth, in disobeying their parents.
