192. §. 14.

Children Obeying Parents’ Instruction and Correction

The Fifth Treatise: Of Children · §§. 27–38

§. 27. Of children’s active obedience.

The affirmative and active part of a child’s obedience consists in making himself pliable to his parents’ will. This must be added to the negative and passive part of obedience named before, of refraining from doing things without the parents’ consent, to show a true childlike affection and disposition toward the parent. Passive obedience may arise from mere sullenness and stubborn pride. For there are many who will refrain from doing this or that without their parents’ consent because they are unwilling to ask for their consent: they would rather have their own wills crossed in the things they desire than be made subject to their parents’ will. What does this show but a stubborn pride and a disdainful heart? Besides, to refrain from doing an unlawful thing is only to abstain from evil. But it is required of Christians193 to do what is good, as well as to abstain from what is evil. This is what is commended in Jacob: he not only refrained from taking such a wife as would be a grief to his parents (in which his194 brother Esau had offended), but also obeyed his parents in195 taking such a wife as they wished him to take.

We will illustrate this general point by four particular instances, namely, by a child’s obedience to his parents’ commandments, instructions, reproofs, corrections.

§. 28. Of children’s obedience to their parents’ commandments.

I. Whatever lawful commandments parents give to their children, the children must be ready to obey them to the utmost of their power. “Obey your+ parents,”196 says the apostle to children.

Parents, by virtue of their place, have power and authority to command. Children therefore must obey, or else that power is to no purpose.

To show this by some particulars:

1. If a parent calls his child, or sends for him, the child must readily197 come, indeed even though he does not know the reason. Eli was in the place of a parent to Samuel; so the child, supposing that Eli called him,198 ran to him once, and again, and again. David,199 when he was sent for by his father out of the field to be anointed king, did not know the reason, yet he came.200 The twelve sons of Jacob, though grown men, yet when their father called for them, assembled themselves together before him.

2. If a parent is minded to send his child anywhere, or on201 any errand, though it is far off and may seem somewhat troublesome, yet the child ought to go and do it. The202 example of Jacob named before,203 and also the examples of Joseph204 (sent to see whether all was well with his brothers), of the ten sons of Jacob205 (sent by their father into Egypt), and of David206 (sent to visit his brothers in the camp), are commended by the Holy Spirit in this case. Of David it is noted that207 he “got up early … and set out as Jesse had commanded him,” which shows his ready obedience.

3. If a parent requires his child to wait on him, the child must208 do that too. When Abraham was going up to the top of Moriah, his will was that his servants should stay behind, and that his son Isaac should go with him and carry the wood for the sacrifice; and Isaac obeyed accordingly.209

4. If a parent gives any task, or commits any business, to210 his child, the child ought to perform it faithfully. This kind of faithful obedience is commended in Joseph,211 in the Rechabites,212 and in David,213 with many others. Joseph, because of his high position, was not free to go out of Egypt; yet, to perform what his father had charged him with, he asked leave. The Rechabites were tempted to break their father’s charge, yet they would not. David, when he was sent by his father from the sheep which had been committed to his keeping, took care to leave them “with a keeper”;214 and again, when a bear at one time and a lion at another came215 to the flock, he put his life in danger to preserve the flock. All these circumstances are noted in this way to set out the great care these children had to discharge the charge which their parents had committed to them.

§. 29. Of children’s disobedience to their parents’ commandments.

Contrary to this is a rebellious disposition in children, shown by these and similar practices:

1. By refusing to come at their parents’ call; or by coming (as we say) at their leisure, and making their parents wait for them.

2. By lazily and sluggishly offering vain and frivolous excuses when their parents would send them on an errand, like that sluggard who says, “There is a lion outside! I will be slain in the streets!”216 Such pretexts are “like vinegar to the teeth and smoke to the eyes.”217

3. By scorning to wait on their parents. For this reason they will slip out of doors and absent themselves when they imagine their parents will need their service in that way: they, if you please, will not be their parents’ servants. An ungodly notion!

4. By refusing to do what their parents enjoin on them and require of them, like218 the younger son who did not go to work in the vineyard at his father’s command. For the most part, those children offend in this who through pride think the business given them too lowly and base to do. Had David219 or the daughters of Reuel220 been of this mind, the one would not have returned to his father’s sheep after he was anointed to be king over Israel and after he had been called to the court; and the others would not have watered their father’s sheep, especially among such rude and rowdy louts as would drive them away without any respect for their place and sex.

§. 30. Of children’s obedience to their parents’ instruction.

II. Such wholesome instructions as parents give their children for the right ordering of their conduct, children ought conscientiously to obey. Solomon221 presses this point much. “Listen, my son,” he says, “to your father’s instruction, and do not forsake the teaching of your mother,” etc. And to move children all the more to do so, he sets before them222 his own example, showing that he required no more of them than he himself had performed. Moses,223 though grown to years and a prince among his people, showed his obedience to his father-in-law in this.

1. Parents have an express commandment to instruct their224 children (as we will show later).225 There is great reason, therefore, that their children should listen to them and obey them in this. The good instructions of anyone are to be regarded; much more those of parents.

2. Great wisdom may be gained by it. For the desire parents have for their children’s good makes them give the best226 directions they can to them, namely what they themselves have learned from others or observed by their own experience. In this respect Solomon calls him “a wise son” who “heeds his father’s instruction,”227 and he likens its fruit and benefit to a graceful ornament, to chains and bracelets, and to a crown of glory.228

3. Much joy and comfort is brought to parents by seeing229 their children observe their instruction; for “a wise son brings joy to his father.”230 Now this is something children ought to aim at: to bring joy to their parents’ hearts.231 Esau is blamed for grieving232 his parents.

Contrary to this is the proud and foolish attitude of those who think they need no instruction: their parents are too suspicious of them, they are wise enough by themselves, and if their parents would only leave them alone, they would do better. In this way they show themselves ungodly toward God, rebellious against their parents, and harmful to themselves. Such were Eli’s233 and Lot’s234 sons. Now note the vengeance that fell on them.

§. 31. Of children’s patience under their parents’ reproof.

III. The obedience of children must further235236 extend to their parents’ reproof: both by patiently bearing every kind of reproof, and by amending what is justly reproved. That shame which the Lord speaks of, which should be in a child237 when “her father had but spit in her face” (that is, had shown his anger by some outward sign), implies a child’s patient bearing of a parent’s reproof. This patience in a child must be shown to his parent whether the reproof is mild or bitter, just or unjust. In this respect a child must consider the person who reproves more than the matter or manner of the reproof. Jacob’s reproof of Joseph for his dreams, which came from God, was unjust;238 and the manner of uttering it, with many short pauses and in questions, implies some tartness. Yet Joseph’s patience was such that we do not read of one discontented word that he gave. But most memorable is the patience of Jonathan in this respect. His father Saul’s239 reproof of him was plainly unjust and bitter beyond measure; yet with what patience he bore it! All he replied was to make some small defense of David; he replied nothing against his father’s insulting words.

Great wisdom may be learned by this patience. For in this way a240 child can better judge whether his parents’ reproof is just or not. Though it is unjust, yet by it he may observe what displeases his parents; at least he may observe his parents’ weakness, and so know better how to conduct himself toward them.

Contrary to this is the practice of those children who, at every reproof of their parents, are ready to answer back. “Our parents241 are so wayward,” they say; “who can bear them?” If no one else could bear them, yet children should. For parents ordinarily bear such waywardness and unruliness from their children, especially while they are young, as no one else would or could.

Question. If a parent is mistaken in a matter and unjustly reproves his child, may the child make no answer?

Answer. Yes, he may, provided he does it mildly, reverently and at a fitting time, not too flatly crossing or contradicting his parent.

Objection. Christ rebuked his mother very bluntly for reproving242 him unjustly.

Answer. Christ, as God-man, was greater than his mother, and in that respect he blamed her with authority for her unjust reproof. The Virgin Mary was not ignorant of this, and therefore she was silent.

§. 32. Of children’s readiness to amend what is justly reproved by their parents.

If a child is justly reproved by his parents for his fault,243 both conscience toward God and obedience to his parent require that he readily put right what is amiss. Unless amendment of the thing justly reproved is added to patient bearing of reproof, that patience can be counted no better than pretense and plain mockery. When the father-in-law244 of Moses told him that what he was doing was “not good,” he amended it at once.

But on the contrary, many wicked and graceless children go on in their evil courses, though their parents rebuke them for it again and again. Eli’s reproof of his sons was just, yet no amendment followed. Now note the inference the Holy Spirit makes from this: “They would not listen245 to their father, since the Lord intended to put them to death.” By this it is implied that to despise the just reproof of parents is a clear sign and forerunner of God’s heavy judgment. Solomon calls the child who “does not listen to rebuke” “a mocker,”246 which points to a most obstinate sinner who cannot be reclaimed, and who for that reason is mocked by the Lord.247

§. 33. Of children’s submission to their parents’ correction.

IIII. Correction is a reproof in deed, a reproof in the highest degree, indeed the severest kind of reproof; so that submitting to it is a great trial of obedience. A child’s submission to his parent in this kind of reproof must be shown by the same means as in the former, namely:

1. By patiently bearing the correction his parent gives him.

2. By readily amending what he is justly corrected for.

The apostle notes the first of these as a settled case, a matter not to be denied, in these words: “We have had fathers of our flesh who corrected us, and we gave them reverence.”248 One special part of this reverence is patient endurance; therefore he infers from it, “Should we not much more submit,” etc.

Solomon sets out the second by an effect that follows on performing it. For having advised a parent to correct his child, he adds this reason: “He will give you rest; he will give delight to your soul.”249 How can this rest and delight be given except by the child’s amending what he is corrected for? A parent takes no delight in the pain and smart of his child, but in the fruit that follows from it. As a child’s transgression is a grief250 and vexation to the parent, so his amendment brings rest and delight. Now this effect does not follow from correction in itself, but from the good use the child makes of it. It lies therefore in the child, and so lies on him as a duty, to give this rest and delight to his parent by amending the fault for which he is corrected, as he brought grief to him by provoking him to use correction. In this way neither will the parent regret inflicting correction, nor the child regret enduring it.

So that a child may attain this degree of obedience, he251 must duly consider both the cause that moves his parent to correct him and the end his parent aims at in it. The cause is the love252 he bears his child. The end he aims at is his child’s good.253 If these motives do not produce obedience, what can?

§. 34. Of refusing, or abusing correction.

Contrary to this is disdain on the one side and obstinacy on the other. Disdain, when children scorn to be corrected by their parents; and so, when they cannot avoid it by any means they can use, they will mutter and murmur, fret and fume, rage and rave against their parents, and despise and hate them for it. Obstinacy, when they will not be bettered by it in the least, but keep running on in their wicked courses, and rather grow worse for being corrected. This may be counted the highest pitch of a child’s rebellion, for this is the last means a parent can use to reclaim his child from desperate courses. If this does not prevail, the law of God requires254 that a parent give up his child into the hand of the magistrate, so that he may be put to death.

So much for the separate branches of children’s obedience.

Its extent follows.

§. 35. Of children’s conforming their judgments to their parents.

The extent of children’s obedience is only implied in this epistle to the Ephesians, but it is expressed (Col 3:20) in these words: “Children, obey your+ parents255 IN ALL THINGS.” It is a large extent, but not to be taken absolutely, without any limitation; for the apostle himself notes a restraint in these words,256 in the Lord. So far as children do not transgress any of God’s commandments in obeying their parents, they ought to obey. This is to obey in all things, in the Lord.

The257 extent of children’s duties is the very same as that of wives’ duties, and the restraint also is the same; so the order observed there will be kept here also. Only other proofs, more pertinent to children’s place, will be brought to confirm those general propositions which may be applied to any inferiors. Many general reasons given there in proof of the propositions will be omitted here. Therefore compare this place with that.

So we see that parents’ authority is very large: there is no restraint on it but God’s contrary command, of which a child must be sure if he refuses to obey his parent in anything.

It is not enough for a child to say, “I have obeyed my parent so long and in so many things; I hope that if I have my own will in some things, I may be excused.” No: all things covers more than many things. So many are not enough. And though God’s will is exempted, your own will is not exempted. Though you may do nothing against God’s will, yet you ought to do many things against your own will, if it is contrary to your parents’.

Children must work at two things in order to attain this extent of obedience in all things.

1. They must work to bring their judgment and will into line with their parents’: to think fitting and suitable for them to do what their parents want them to do. Though Isaac thought it somewhat strange that he should258 carry wood up a hill to offer a sacrifice where there was nothing for a burnt offering, yet since it was his father’s will that he should do so, he thought it fitting enough for him to do so.

This subjection of judgment and will is to be given in all the particular cases of obedience set out259 before, as in their calling, marriage, clothing, allowance, etc. So children are to think that kind of calling, that particular match, that clothing and that allowance most fitting for them which their parents think fitting.

If the judgment is persuaded that a thing is fitting,260 and the will is inwardly brought to yield to it, outward obedience will be given to it more readily and cheerfully.

Contrary to this is the overweening opinion which many children261 have of their own judgment and will: they think they can discern better than their parents what is fit and proper for themselves. They imagine their parents to be too strict and precise, or too suspicious and distrustful, or too covetous and worldly. This makes them take whatever callings, matches, clothing and allowance they think best; from which many harms arise, which would all easily be avoided if they would lay down that presumptuous opinion and labor to follow the direction given above.

§. 36. Of children’s yielding to do at their parents’ command such things as in their judgment they cannot think very fitting.

2. Though children cannot think in their judgment that what their parents require is the fittest and most suitable, yet, being pressed to it by their parents’ peremptory command, they ought to yield to it in practice, saying to their parents, as Peter said to the Lord, “But because you say so, I will do this.” Jacob262 yielded to Rebekah in this way. He thought that by doing what his mother told him he would seem to be mocking his father; yet when she urged him, he did it.

Question. If a child can give a better reason than his parent, is he not allowed to refuse to do what he thinks unfitting, or at least to hold back from doing what he is commanded until he is better informed that it is fitting?

Answer. With reverence and humility he may give his reason why he thinks it unfitting, and ask his parent not to press it on him.

(Judah,263 one of the sons of Jacob, did this, and is not blamed for it), and parents ought in such a case to yield to their children (as Jacob264 did). But yet if, in things neither commanded nor forbidden, the parents are otherwise minded than their children, and want their children to yield to them, the children must yield.

For, 1. In things neither commanded nor forbidden, a parent’s command is a warrant to the child, because of this extent (all things); so that the parent may sin in commanding a thing which the child may do without sin. Who can clear Rebekah of sin in commanding Jacob to deceive his father? Yet I take it that Jacob cannot justly be blamed for obeying.

2. In this way children show a high esteem for their parents and very great respect toward them; they show how eager they are to please them and how afraid to offend them. When the will of parent and child agree, there is no such test.

3. By this means peace and love are better preserved between parent and child: a parent’s anger is stopped, its effects avoided, and many other harms prevented, which often happen when inferiors refuse to yield to their superiors who have authority over them.

Contrary to this is the wrongheaded peremptoriness of those who will do265 nothing against their own mind and will, however much their parents require it. This phrase266 (“If you will not send him, we will not go down”), which Judah used to his father, though in a good cause, was too peremptory for a child. Those who obstinately refuse to do the things that are against their own mind must come short of this extent, obey in all things. Indeed, they show that what they do is done for their own sakes, because they like it, rather than for their parents’ sake. What sort of obedience can that be thought to be? Yet this is all the obedience many children will give. If they do not think what their parents require is fitting, neither fair nor foul means will move them to do it; and by this many children greatly provoke their parents. Let such children know that it is in every way safer for them, at the pressing command of their parent, to do what they think unfitting than peremptorily to disobey their parents, which is worse than unfitting: it is unlawful.

§. 37. Of the restraint of children’s obedience.

The restraint of children’s obedience is expressed in this clause, in the Lord. This phrase gives a necessary limitation267 to their obeying their parents, who are only parents of our flesh, men and women, liable to err in their commandments and to require such sinful things as their children cannot perform with a good conscience. The limitation, then, which this clause (in the Lord) gives is this:

Children must give no other obedience to their parents than may stand with their obedience to God. The reasons the apostle gives prove as much: “This is right”; “this is pleasing to268 the Lord.” But to obey parents against the Lord is neither right nor pleasing to the Lord.

If, therefore, parents command their children to do anything269 which the Lord has forbidden them, they ought not to do it. On this ground Michal did well in letting her husband David escape out of the hands of Saul her father.270 I do not justify her way of carrying out the matter, with untruths and false tales; but her refusal to yield to her father’s mind and will is justifiable, and that in two respects.

1. Because the dispute was between her husband and her father. Now271 by God’s law a wife is to yield to her husband rather than to her father.

2. Because she knew her father sought to kill him. If she had then delivered him into her father’s hands, she would have made herself an accessory to murder. In this latter respect Jonathan also did well in refusing to fetch David at his father’s272 command.

So if a father commands his child to go to Mass, to perjure himself, to marry an idolater, to steal, to lie, or to commit any other sin forbidden by God, the child ought not to obey: those things cannot be done in the Lord.

Again, if parents forbid their children to do any necessary duty commanded by God, the child ought to do it despite the parents’ prohibition. We may well think that Ahaz, who set himself so violently to deface the holy things of God, to profane his ordinances, and to shut up the doors of God’s house, gave strict orders to his son that he273 should not repair them again; yet Hezekiah, as soon as he had power, repaired them all.

If a parent forbids his child to go to the Protestant churches, to hear a sermon, to pray in a language he understands, to give just weight and measure, to speak the truth when he is called to witness to it, and the like, the child must be of Daniel’s mind,274 and despite that prohibition do the things God requires.

§. 38. Of children’s sin in yielding to their parents against God.

Contrary to this limitation is, on the one side, a flattering eye-service in many children, who do not care what they do, whether275 it is good or evil, lawful or unlawful, so long as they may please their parents by it; and on the other side, a slavish fearfulness,276 which makes them dread their parents so much that they do not fear God at all. They would rather choose to sin, and so provoke God’s wrath, than do anything by which their parents’ wrath may be provoked. It is a brand set on evil kings that they277 walked in the ways of their fathers and mothers, and did wickedly278 as they counseled them. So their following and obeying their parents in evil was so far from lessening their sin that it rather made it worse. The preferring of father and mother before the Lord Christ shows that such a child is “not worthy” of Christ.279 In comparison with Christ, father and mother must be hated.280 But it is that undue and unchristian regard for parents above Christ that makes so many young papists, young swaggerers, swearers,281 liars, deceitful persons and people of wicked life.

To avoid the two extremes just named, let your heart be filled with a true fear of God, and also consider the difference between our earthly parents and our heavenly Father. They are only parents “of our flesh”;282 he is “the Father of our spirits.”283 They can only touch the body; he can cast body and soul into hell. They are over us only for a while; he forever. Their authority is subordinate to his; his is supreme and absolute in itself. They can give only a light, temporary reward; he, an eternal weight of glory. They cannot shelter us from his wrath; he can shelter us from theirs.

So much for those duties of children which concern their parents’ authority; those which concern their necessity follow.

Children Giving Back to Parents

The Fifth Treatise: Of Children · §§. 39–51

§. 39. Of children’s recompense.

The general head to which belong all the duties children owe their parents with respect to their Necessity is, in one word, Recompense. It is a duty by which children endeavor, as far as lies in them, to repay what they can for their parents’ kindness, care and cost toward them, and that by way284 of thankfulness. This makes a child think he cannot do too much for his parent; and well may he think so, for a parent does much more for his child before it is able to do anything for itself than the child can possibly do for the parent. So even if the parents’ authority were laid aside, the law of fairness would still require this duty of Recompense; and so do the law of piety and the law of charity. Therefore, of all duties, this is the most due.285 The apostle expressly charges children with it, bidding them “learn” to “requite their parents.”

Contrary to this is the neglect of parents in their need, which is more286 than monstrous ingratitude. As all ingratitude is odious to God and man, so this is most of all; and yet very many are guilty of it. In them the proverb is proved true that love is heavy. For it is the property of heavy things to fall down quickly but to rise slowly, and not without some force. So love falls down quickly from the parent to the child, but it rises only with difficulty from children to parents. For this reason another proverb says, One father will better provide for nine children than nine children for one father. Many children in this respect do no more for their parents than for strangers. Either they do not consider how much their parents have done for them, or else they imagine that what their parents did was mere duty, and needs no recompense. Shame on such barbarous and inhuman children!

§. 40. Of infirmities to which parents are subject.

The rule of the recompense named above is, on the one side,287 the parent’s Necessity, and on the other, the child’s Ability. So in everything in which a parent needs his child’s help, the child must give his best help, as far as he is able. Beyond one’s power nothing can be expected.288

A parent’s Necessity may arise from

  • Natural infirmities.
  • Chance misfortunes.

Natural infirmities are

  • Inward.
  • Outward.

Inward infirmities are weakness of judgment, a slippery memory, violent passions and the like, from which come perversity, irritability, suspiciousness, distrust, fear, grief, etc.

Outward infirmities are such as arise from some pressing temptation, as were Noah’s289 and Lot’s290 drunkenness; Lot’s291 and David’s292 uncleanness; Abraham’s293 and Isaac’s294 pretense; Jacob’s295 and David’s296 excessive lamentation, etc.

Some of these latter, which may seem most heinous and odious sins, are to be counted infirmities when those who commit them do not make a sport of them, nor delight to live and lie in them, as swine wallow and lie in the mire, but only at times, through some temptation, fall into them, as it were unawares; and after they have committed them, they are themselves more ashamed of them and more grieved for them than anyone else who sees them or hears of them.

With respect to the natural infirmities of parents, the duty of children is both to bear with them and also to cover them as far as they can.

§. 41. Of children’s bearing with their parents’ infirmities.

Children bear with their parents’ infirmities when they do not esteem their place or person any less reverently, nor perform any less duty to them, because of their infirmities.

This is the first particular branch of recompense. For children in their younger and weaker years are subject to many infirmities. If parents had respected them the less for their infirmities, and had taken occasion from them to neglect them, and would not have borne with them, surely they could not have been brought up so well. The great patience, long-suffering and much forbearance which parents have shown toward their children require that children, by way of recompense, show the like to their parents as occasion arises. It was a great infirmity in Isaac to prefer Esau, a profane child, to Jacob, a religious child, especially against God’s express word concerning Jacob; yet Jacob did not respect his father one bit the less for it, as appears by his297 fear of offending him, and by his298 readiness to obey him. Jacob’s299 unjust reproof of Joseph was no small infirmity, and yet the history that follows shows how much Joseph reverenced his father and respected him in every way. Saul’s infirmities were far more and much greater than any of theirs, yet what duty and faithfulness Jonathan his son showed him, even to their deaths! For300 he died with him.

We have in this the pattern of Christ himself. How great an infirmity his mother showed when she too rashly rebuked him while he was about a good work, a bounden duty, his Father’s business! Yet immediately after this it is noted that he “went down” with his parents “and was obedient to them.”301 This shows the honor he gave to his mother, in spite of her infirmity.

Those act contrary to this duty who take occasion from their parents’ infirmities to think basely of their person and302 their place, and so grow careless in duty, either refusing to do any duty at all, or else doing it carelessly, grudgingly, disdainfully and scornfully. Absalom303 made a supposed infirmity of his father the ground of his rebellion. Even if his pretext had been true, it would not have been sufficient cause for him to disgrace his father and rise against him, as he did. The law that threatens God’s vengeance against children whose eye “mocks a father and scorns obedience to a mother”304 makes no exception for parents’ infirmities.

§. 42. Of children’s covering their parents’ infirmities.

Children cover their parents’ infirmities both by passing them by (as we say) and taking no notice of them, and also by concealing them from others as much as they can. Scripture notes it as a property of love that it “covers over a multitude305 of sins.” Now in whom should love abound, if not in children? And who should show this property of love more than children?

Of passing by a parent’s infirmity and concealing it from others we have a worthy pattern in Shem and Japheth. When Noah their father lay drunk and uncovered in the middle of his tent, they, “walking backward” (so that they themselves might not306 see their father’s infirmity), “covered their father’s nakedness” (so that others might not see it). The blessing then promised on this occasion to them and their descendants shows how acceptable this duty was to God.

Contrary to this was Ham’s practice: he exposed and made307 known his father’s nakedness.308 The curse denounced against him for it shows how odious that sin was to God. There are too many of Ham’s cursed brood who spread abroad their parents’ infirmities and make such things known about them as would not otherwise be known. By this they bring much dishonor and shame on their parents (which can be no honor309 to the children), and besides, a curse from their parents on themselves, which the heathen counted very dreadful.

Still more contrary was Absalom’s practice: he raised a most malicious slander against his father, and by it turned his subjects’ hearts away from him. Too many, like Absalom, seek to raise a supposed310 reputation and honor for themselves by vilifying and disgracing their parents. But let them note Absalom’s end. Assuredly, if they persist in that course, a like end, or a worse, will be theirs.311

§. 43. Of children’s bearing with their parents’ chance needs.

Chance misfortunes are all kinds of crosses that are laid on a man by the providence of God: whether on his body, as blindness, lameness, sickness, etc.; or on his person, as captivity, banishment, imprisonment, etc.; or on his means, as poverty, destitution, etc. In all these children must bear with their parents, as in the infirmities named above, neither esteeming them less reverently nor performing less duty because of them. These are needs that are not sinful in themselves; and therefore, with respect to these, parents are to be borne with much more. Though Isaac was blind,312 Jacob did not respect him one bit the less. Though Naomi was poor, Ruth her daughter-in-law continued to do a child’s duty and service to her.

Contrary to this is the heartless disposition of children who313 take occasion from these chance needs of their parents to despise them. God has made an express law against despising those who are made helpless by any outward defect,314 as the deaf, blind, etc. If no one may despise another for these, much less may children despise their parents. Those who do so are worse than Ham, and may expect a heavier curse.

§. 44. Of children’s relieving their parents according to their need.

Besides bearing with their parents’ needs, children must give their parents relief and help in such cases as the parents need it from them. In sickness they must visit them, as Joseph315 visited his father. In time of mourning they must comfort them, as316 the children of Jacob did. In need they must provide what is needful for them, as317 the sons of Jacob did, who went to buy food for their father; and as Joseph318 did, who sent for Jacob into Egypt and there provided for him. It is noted of Ruth319 that she not only gleaned for her mother, a poor woman, but also saved for her some of the food that was given to herself to eat. In time of danger they must do what they can for their parents’ protection and preservation, as David320 in this respect took special care of his father and mother. Indeed, if God is pleased to321 take children out of this world before their parents, and their parents are left without help, the children must make what arrangements they can for their parents’ well-being after their own departure, as322 Christ did, who entrusted his mother to his disciple John a little before his death. These and similar duties are particular branches of recompense, and are all included under that323 requital which the apostle requires of children. And they are only a small part of the requital of all the pains, care and expense that parents have gone to for their children. Indeed, this one thing alone, that parents have brought children into the world, children can never sufficiently requite. Nature has taught this much not only to heathen men, but also to irrational creatures. Among such creatures the example of the324 stork is worth noting. For it is recorded of that kind that when the parent birds are old, the young ones feed them; and when through age they are ready to faint in their flying, the young ones help them; and when they are past flying, the young ones carry them on their backs. The325 Greek name of a stork is taken from that word which means to requite a parent’s kindness; or else this word is taken from that name: they both come from the same root.

Contrary to this is the opinion of the Pharisees, who thought that children, by dedicating their substance to the temple, might be freed from this duty of recompense to parents; this is what lies hidden in that Hebrew word Corban.326 They made a mere pretext of piety toward God the cause of open impiety against parents. Christ gives this verdict on them: “you+ nullify the word of God.”327328 The papists are of the same opinion, and so under the same condemnation.

Contrary also is the practice of those who, having the goods of this world, allow their parents to be in need. Saint John329 asks of one who “withholds his compassion from” his brother in that case, “how can the love of God abide in him?” How then can it abide in such a child? Not only those who let their parents starve offend in this extreme, but also those who let them live poorly and wretchedly while they themselves,330 like Dives, live in luxury and go splendidly dressed every day.

Those offend in a higher degree who bring their parents into extremities: into poverty by their lavish spending; into prison by pressing them to be their sureties; into excessive grief by their wicked doings, as331 the sons of Jacob did.

But what shall we say of such graceless children as dare to strike their parents?332 God’s law counts such a child unworthy of life, and sentences him to death.

And what can be said of killers of fathers and killers of mothers? Of old there was no particular law made against them, because it was supposed that no child could be so heartless and inhuman. In imitation of this, Solon,333 that wise lawmaker among the heathen, made no law against them; and when he was asked his reason, he answered that he thought no child would commit such a deed.

When such inhuman impiety later showed itself in the world, the civil law ordained this punishment: “If anyone kills his parent, let him not be put to the sword, nor to fire, nor to any other usual punishment; but let him be sewn into a sack with a dog, and a cock, and a viper, and an ape, and cast into the nearest sea or river; so that while life is in him, he may begin to lack all use of the elements, and be deprived of the air while he lives, and of the earth when he is dead.”334

Since this sin had been committed among the heathen, the apostle lists it among other most notorious and barbarous sins, 1 Tim 1:9. As murder is one of those sins which the earth can least bear, and which cries loudest to heaven for vengeance, so among the various kinds of murder this is the most unbearable, and cries the loudest.

So much for the duties of children which they are to perform while their parents live. It remains to speak of those which they are to perform when their parents are dead.

§. 45. Of children’s care to bury their parents when they are dead.

The duties which children owe to their parents after they are dead concern the body and the reputation of their dead parent.

It is the duty of children to bring the bodies of their dead parents to the grave with such seemliness and honor as may correspond to the place and reputation in which they lived.

So both the thing itself and the manner of doing it are to be observed.335

The thing itself, namely the burial of the bodies of the dead, has always been in use in God’s church, and it has been used as a means to maintain our hope of the resurrection of our bodies. Many of the heathen, who never dreamed of the resurrection,336 used to burn the dead bodies of their relatives; other heathen learned this manner of burial from the church, though they did not know its mystery. It is clearer than needs proving that God’s people, from the beginning of the world, have performed this duty of burial for their relatives; but it is not to the point in hand to dwell on the general. That it belongs especially to children to see this duty performed is now the point to be proved, and it is readily done by the approved examples of Isaac,337 Jacob,338 Joseph339 and others expressly recorded in Scripture.

And there is great reason for it:

1. It is a testimony of great love and good respect to the one340 who has died. Now who should show more love and greater respect than a child?

2. It is a kind of blessing341 promised by God to his saints to342 be buried, just as, on the other side, it is a curse343 threatened against obstinate sinners not to be buried. For this reason David344 blesses the men of Jabesh-gilead for burying Saul, and acknowledges it as a kindness done to Saul. Now who ought rather to procure a blessing for parents and do them a kindness than children, who are often blessed through their parents?

3. Since it is a great shame to have a man’s corpse lie above345 ground (for no carcass is more loathsome than a man’s if it lies unburied), children, who are most bound to cover their parents’ shame, are in this respect bound to bury their bodies.346

Contrary to this is the practice of those whose minds are so set on their parents’ goods that they wholly neglect their bodies. As soon as their parent’s breath is out of his body, they busy themselves so much about the things he has left behind that his corpse is ready to stink before any care is taken for its burial. Indeed, some will purposely keep their parent’s corpse above ground until it is extremely offensive, in order to receive some revenues, or debts, or other dues which must be paid before the corpse is buried. If the corpse must of necessity be kept above ground for some time, let it be embalmed, or so treated that it does not smell. Those who are careless of this show that they respect their parent’s wealth347 more than his person and honor.

For this reason those also transgress heinously who are so greedy for their parent’s estate that they cannot wait for his departure, but, like Adonijah, enter on their father’s estate and take possession of his goods before the breath is out of his body. By this they often cause great disquiet to him who would depart in peace.

Again, others bear an inward grudge and secret hatred348 against a brother or other kinsman whom their parent dearly loved, and for that reason dared not lay a hand on him in their parent’s lifetime. As soon as their parent is dead, they pick a quarrel with the one they hate, and so disturb and hinder their parent’s funeral. Esau intended such a plot,349 but God defeated it, which shows that God is displeased with it.

§. 46. Of the seemliness with which children ought to see their parents buried.

The manner in which children ought to see their parents buried must be with such seemliness as agrees with the commendable custom of the country and church where their parents die, and with such honor as in some measure corresponds to the rank and place of their parents while they lived (at least if it is not beyond the means the parent has left, or beyond the ability of the child who holds the funeral). Joseph was a great ruler in Egypt, and because of this his father was highly regarded when he came there; accordingly350 he carried him to his grave with great honor.

There are two extremes contrary to the seemliness351 and honor named above. One is an overlavish and prodigal extravagance and ceremony at their parents’ funeral, far above the parent’s rank and far beyond the means the parent has left, and far above the rank and ability of the child himself too. Some are cast so far into debt by the needless ceremony of their parents’ funeral that they are never able to recover themselves again, and so they bring more dishonor to their parents by the weakness of their own means than honor by the ceremony of the funeral. There may be great honor and much seemliness in a funeral where there are no extraordinary expenses: take Stephen’s funeral, for example.352

The other extreme is too lowly and private a manner of353 burying their parents, very unbecoming both to their parents and to their own rank and means. It arises from a mixture of pride and covetousness possessing their hearts. Pride makes them have no ceremony at all, because covetousness will not allow them to spend freely on it. So it comes about that they choose out unfamiliar places where neither their parents nor they themselves are known, and the dead of night, so that no one may see them; and they set an uncertain time, so that no friend may go with them. God often repays such proud, covetous children in kind, and causes them to be brought to their graves with the same dishonor.

§. 47. Of children’s paying their parents’ debts after their death.

As children must have regard for the body of their parents354 who have died, so also for their credit and good name, which is a thing of greater worth and honor: a thing by which they may bring a kind of blessing to their parents and make them live after their death.

Parents themselves cannot do anything when they are dead to preserve it; children therefore, being the living image of their parents, must endeavor to do it.

There are three things which children must make conscience of for the sake of their dead parents’ credit and reputation: one, to pay their debts; another, to suppress ill rumors; a third, to imitate their good example.

I. If the estate of parents, their goods or lands, comes to their children, the children’s duty is to pay their parents’ debts as far as they can, especially if those debts may be recovered from them by law. For what the law may force others to do in fairness and justice, conscience must move good children to do out of charity and as recompense to their parents. The Holy Spirit makes it a355 mark of the wicked that they “borrow and do not repay.” Therefore, to wipe that blot from the name of a dead parent, children must be ready in this respect to do what the parent himself, if he were living, would or should do. Indeed, if children are well able of themselves, they ought to pay all their parents’ debts, even though their parents did not leave enough to pay them. In this especially a childlike love is shown to the parent.

Contrary to this is the practice of those who strive to get all they can of their parents’ goods, and yet make no conscience of paying any debts at all unless the law forces them to. What they do in this case cannot be thought to be done for their parents’ sake, but rather for their own sake. Many have so little regard for their parents’ reputation in this respect that they secretly convey away and wholly conceal much of their parents’ estate, on purpose to cheat creditors. As this is a piece of plain injustice, so it is a cause of opening men’s mouths against their parents, to their discredit and shame.

§. 48. Of children’s suppressing evil reports against their dead parents.

The direction given before concerning children’s speech356 about their parents behind their backs may also fitly be applied to the care which children ought to have of the speeches and reports made about their parents after their departure. It follows, as from the less to the greater, that what children do for their parents’ reputation in their absence, behind their backs, they must do much more when their parents are dead. For then there is no hope, no possibility, that parents should do anything to right their own wrong in that respect: it lies on children, therefore, to do it.

They act flatly contrary to this who take occasion from their parents’ departure both to open their ears to receive any ill reports of them and to open their mouths to speak ill of them, spreading abroad all their infirmities and stretching their ill reports of their parents beyond the bounds of truth. They are ill birds that so foul their own nest. They know that their parents, being dead, can have no knowledge of it; and in this they show how little piety toward God or parent is in their hearts. But there is an ever-living, all-seeing and all-knowing Father who takes notice of all; and besides other vengeance, he will cause the same measure to be measured out to them as they measure out to their parents. There is nothing in which this proverb (“with the measure you+ use, it will be measured357 to you+”) is more often proved true than in children’s ingratitude358 to their parents. Every age has given many instances of it. (The very heathen observed it.) This shows God’s great indignation against it.

§. 49. Of children’s imitating their parents’ good example.

If parents have been persons of good conduct in their lifetime, religious toward God, just in their dealings with men, merciful to those who needed their help, doing much good in their place, and so ended their days with much credit, it is a special means of maintaining and continuing this credit of theirs for children to walk in their steps and to endeavor to be like them.

In this way a blessed memory of their parents is kept fresh and green (as we say), though their bodies have rotted. For when those who knew the parents see the like good qualities and actions in their children, they are reminded by it of the departed, and say, “Oh, how such parents still live! See a vivid and living image of them.” In this way Solomon, Asa, Jehoshaphat, Hezekiah, Josiah and other such good kings who came of the stock and lineage of David kept the memory of their father David fresh, fair and flourishing (long after his body had rotted), as is evident by these and similar phrases: he “walked in the statutes of his359 father David”; he “walked in all the ways of his father David”;360 he “did what was right … as his father David had done,”361 etc. There can be no better monument of a parent’s piety, uprightness and virtue than a child’s vivid likeness of them. Therefore,362 as a motive to stir up children to walk in the good ways of their parents, God has promised to show “loving devotion to a thousand generations of those who love Me and keep My commandments”; that is, to those who, having religious and righteous parents, walk in their steps.

Contrary to this are both those who are unlike good parents and those who are like evil parents. The former sort greatly damage and dishonor the reputation of their parents, as Rehoboam did, who by his foolish, harsh and unjust conduct made the people speak contemptuously of David.363

The latter sort keep alive in memory the evil name and the shame of their parents, and make them stink more and more: as the sons and successors of Jeroboam did, who by following his idolatrous course made it the more remembered, and caused this stain to remain on his title from age to age: “Jeroboam, who made Israel sin.”364

As the former stop the current and hinder the passage of the blessing of righteous parents, so the latter spread and open a way for the curse of unrighteous parents.

§. 50. Of the superstitious duty imposed by papists on children after their parents’ death.

To the two duties named above, burying the body and preserving the reputation of parents, the papists add a third and the heathen a fourth, neither of which is warranted by God’s word, but both are directly contrary to it.

What the papists add is that children, after their parents’365 death, ought to procure dirges, Masses, pardons, releases and such trifles for them, and make continual prayers to free them out of purgatory and bring them to rest in heaven. Of the emptiness of these prayers and the folly of the other trifles I have366 spoken elsewhere.

Scripture expressly teaches that after death the soul goes to the place appointed for it, of endless bliss or woe, so that there is no means of altering the one or of helping forward the other.

§. 51. Of the unlawfulness of children’s seeking to avenge their parents’ wrongs.

What the heathen add is that children, after their parents’367 death, should avenge such wrongs as were done to their parents in their lifetime. And they press this so far on children that they frighten them with their parents’ ghost, saying that if they neglect to avenge their parents’ wrongs, the ghost will follow them and not let them live in quiet, but trouble them continually. This notion arises from the corruption of nature, which is extremely prone to revenge; but it is expressly forbidden in Scripture, in these and similar prohibitions: “Do not resist an evil person,”368 “Do not repay anyone evil for evil,”369 “Do not avenge ourselves”370 etc. Yet some, to justify it, cite David’s371 charge to Solomon to take vengeance on Joab and Shimei after his death.

Answer. The charge which David gave, and Solomon’s carrying it out, was no matter of private revenge, but only a lawful execution of justice, which children may and ought to do. There were just reasons to move David to put off the execution of justice on the one and the other so long. Joab372 was too mighty to have justice executed on him in David’s time; and Shimei’s373 offense was committed in the time of David’s humbling, which made him swear that he would not himself take vengeance on him. Besides, Solomon executed justice on the one and the other, not for the wrongs they did to his father, but for other crimes which they committed in his own time: their former offenses were only remembered to add weight to the case.

So much for children’s duties. The manner of performing them is to be declared next.
