Children Honoring Father and Mother in the Lord

The Fifth Treatise: Of Children · §§. 52–64

§. 52. Of the manner of performing children’s duties.

The clause that374 pointed out the limitation of children’s duties also gives an excellent direction for the manner of performing them. It is this: in the Lord, that is, children must perform their duty to their parents in the way they would or should perform it to the Lord.

More particularly, it implies these six points:375

1. That their duties are performed in conscience, or for conscience’ sake, which is the same as for the Lord’s sake. For the Lord alone is Judge of the conscience and has power over it. This is how376 subjects must perform their duty to magistrates; much more must children perform it to their parents. The reason the apostle gives in these words, “this is pleasing to the Lord,” shows that children, in obeying their parents, must strive to approve themselves to God.

2. Their duties must be done in sincerity, that is, when children377 make a show of doing no more than they mean in truth and in heart. “Whatever you+ do, do it heartily, as to the Lord,”378 says the apostle. Parents usually deal with no one more heartily than with their children, and children must deal with their parents in the same way.

3. They must be performed cheerfully, with a willing and379 ready mind, for the Lord loves cheerfulness.380 In this lies a main difference between a filial and a servile, a childlike and a slavelike obedience.381

4. They must be performed reverently, as to those who bear the image of God. We spoke of this382 before.

5. They must be performed in such a way that in performing them no383 sin is committed against God. We also spoke of this384 before.

6. Constancy must be added to all the other virtues. For as the385 Lord himself is constant in all his ways and works, so he expects children to be constant in the duties he requires of them. He who begins well and does not hold on loses all the glory of his good beginning.

If the examples of all the good children commended in Scripture are weighed well, we will find that their duties, so far as they were acceptable to God, were performed in the manner described above, in all its branches.

§. 53. Of the failings of children in the manner of their obedience.

Contrary to this are these failings.

1. When children perform their duties from ulterior motives:386 for fear of their parents’ wrath and the punishment that follows it; in hope and expectation of a larger portion and allowance; at the urgent persuasion of relatives; and the like. These motives, taken by themselves, are not for the Lord.

2. When they perform them only outwardly, in show,387 as a mere formality, while their parents are present or may come to know of it. This is not done with respect to God, who searches the heart.

3. When they perform them grudgingly, with muttering,388 and disdainfully, as if their parents’ authority were a usurped power and not given them by God. Is this in the Lord?

4. When they perform them rudely and with bad manners:389 this shows that they do not consider the glory of God’s image shining in their parents.

5. When390 they do not care how they sin against God, so long as391 they may please their parents.

6. When, as if they regretted what they have done well,392 they refuse to do any more duty to their parents. They grow weary, thinking that God has laid too heavy a burden on them. Many show themselves more dutiful in their younger years than in their riper ones. What usually makes children weary of doing their duty is the great and long need of their parents, such as long sickness, long frailty, long poverty, and the like. It appears that such children look on their parents only as men who, as they imagine, can never repay their pains and cost. They do not look to God, who is able to repay all abundantly. So these do not perform their duty in the Lord.

§. 54. Of the equal respect that children are to have for both parents.

As the distinct duties of children have been set out, so I think it needful to declare distinctly who the persons are to whom those duties are to be performed. These are chiefly the natural parents, both father and mother; secondarily, those who are in the place of parents.

The first point to be noted, then, is that children are to have an equal respect for both their natural parents and perform duty to both alike. The law expressly names both: “Honor your father and mother.” We may well think that there was some just and urgent cause why the law, which holds an exceedingly great deal of matter in as few words as could well be used, should expressly name father and mother, when there is one word, parent, that includes both. Now what other reason can be given than the point in hand?

It is worth noting how the apostle is not content to have named parents, which implies both, but also adds the express words of the law, which name in particular father and mother. It is expressly recorded of Jacob that he “obeyed his father and mother.”393 Among the other writers of Scripture, Solomon expressly names both father and mother, almost twenty separate times in Proverbs.

There are many reasons to enforce this point.

1. Both parents are, under God, alike the means of their children’s394 being. Children come from the substance of both alike.

2. The care and pains of both for the good of the children are very great: I do not know whose are the greater. The mother’s pains and care in bringing forth the child are indeed the greater, and they may also be the greater in bringing up the child, especially while it is young, at least if she nurses it herself. Yet afterward the father’s exceed, in providing a fit calling, sufficient means of maintenance, and indeed a portion or inheritance for it, and that for the time after he himself is dead. So one way or another the child is equally bound to both, and accordingly God’s law makes no difference between them.

Objection. The wife is subject to her husband; therefore a child ought to prefer his father to his mother.

Answer. Though there is a difference between father and395 mother in their relation to one another, yet in relation to their children they are both as one, and have a like authority over them. Now children are not to look to the difference between their parents in their mutual relation as husband and wife, but to the authority both parents have over their children, and so to have an equal respect for both.

2. Objection. What if the father’s and the mother’s minds396 are contrary, and the one commands what the other forbids?

Answer. The thing commanded or forbidden must be considered. If it concerns something good or evil in itself, lawful or unlawful, then the parent who would have the lawful thing done, or the unlawful thing left undone (even if it is the mother), must be obeyed, for in this case she is backed by God’s authority. But if the matter is in itself neither commanded nor forbidden, then I do not doubt that the father must be obeyed. Yet the child must in no way show any contempt for his mother, but with all reverence and humility make it known to her that it is best both for herself and for him that his father should be obeyed. But if the father’s contrary authority does not come between, or if the father is dead, then a mother is to be obeyed in all things as fully and absolutely as a father.

§. 55. Of pretexts alleged for obeying father rather than mother.

Contrary to this, on the one side, is the childish doting of those who so wholly respect their mother and seek to please her that they pay little regard to their father, unless they are forced to it through fear; and on the other side, the scornful spirit of those who show respect only to their father, and altogether neglect their mother, if they do not despise her. For the most part, of the two, the mother is the less regarded. I take the reasons for this to be the following, and to them I will add particular means of removing the seeming force of those reasons, as antidotes or remedies to them.

1. The mother, because of her sex, is usually the weaker, and subject to more infirmities.

Answer. Children ought to look at their mother’s place and authority rather than at her person and infirmity. Then these would not in the least lessen their respect for the other.

2. The mother is more indulgent and tender to her children, and is more familiar with them; and familiarity397 breeds contempt.

Answer. This is the abuse of familiarity. Love should breed love, and love must be ordered according to the condition of the persons loving and loved. As children with one eye see the mother’s affection, so with the other they should see God’s image in the mother. Then (what was398 noted as the ground of all children’s duty) a loving fear would be worked in their hearts, which would cast out all contempt.

3. The mother does not have the power to reward or punish that a father has.

Answer. 1. This is not to obey in the Lord. No outward consideration should move a child to obey his parents so much as conscience toward God. If children duly considered God, how he has made no difference but commanded them to obey both alike, and how he is able to reward abundantly and to punish severely, that reason would be no reason.

4. The mother is subject to the father.

Answer. This was answered399 before.

As a general answer to these and all other such pretexts that can be alleged, let it be noted that the Lord not only charges children in express terms to fear their mother, but also (to press this point the more) at times sets the mother in the first place, thus: “Each of you+ must fear his mother,400 and his father.” This is not to be taken as if the mother were the more excellent of the two (in this respect the father is for the most part named first), but because it is the truest test of a child’s subjection to be subject to his mother. He who willingly and conscientiously subjects himself to her who is, in relation to her husband, the inferior; in sex, the weaker; in condition, subject to more infirmities; in her feelings, less moderate; in power, less able to reward or to punish, will (no doubt) much more readily subject himself to his father.

§. 56. Of the difference between children’s subjection to natural parents and to those who are only in the place of parents.

Besides natural parents, there are others whom God has so set over children that the children owe them childlike duty in conscience. In general these are those who are in the place of parents, and so perform, or at least ought to perform, the duty of parents to children.

They are of two sorts.

1. Those who are joined to a natural parent in marriage, commonly called stepfathers and stepmothers, or fathers-in-law and mothers-in-law.

2. Those to whom the government and charge of children are committed, commonly called guardians, tutors, governors; and also foster-fathers and foster-mothers.

Question. Is the same duty in every respect due to those who are in the place of parents as to natural parents themselves?

Answer. Not so. Such a prerogative belongs to natural parents, from whom children have received their being, that in many things in which children are bound to them by an absolute necessity,401 they are bound to the others, who are only in the place of parents, merely by the law of what is honorable, fitting and402 suitable. Hence it comes about that things which, when done by children rebelliously without or against the consent of their natural parents, turn out to be mere nullities, will stand in force though they are done without or against the consent of those who are only in the place of parents. Take as an instance contracts made about goods, lands and other such things in which parents keep a right; to these many good divines add403 contracts of marriage, of a calling and the like.

Yet even so, since in conscience we are bound to the things that the law of what is honorable and suitable requires (for “whatever is honorable, whatever is right … whatever is of good report”404 is to be done), great is the duty that children owe to those who are in the place of parents.

§. 57. Of children’s subjection to stepparents and parents-in-law.

Stepparents and parents-in-law are to be ranked in the first degree of those who are in the place of natural parents. There is very good proof in Scripture for children’s subjection to them. The respect that Moses showed to his father-in-law,405 and Ruth to her mother-in-law, and Christ himself to his supposed father, are commended for this very purpose. Subjection is seen in Christ’s example; reverence in Moses’; recompense in Ruth’s.

The marriage bond makes man and wife one flesh. Therefore406 the natural parent who marries another makes that other one with himself, and in that respect the other is as a parent to the children, and ought to be counted so by them.

The law of God makes it plain incest for a son to uncover407 the shame of his stepmother, or for a stepfather to uncover the shame of his stepdaughter. By this it appears that stepparents are, by God’s law, in the very place and stead of natural parents to their stepchildren, and accordingly are to be honored as natural parents.

Besides, a child does his natural408 father or mother a great honor when he respects the one they have made one flesh with themselves as he does his own parent. So to honor a stepfather or stepmother is to honor a natural parent.

Contrary to this is the mind and conduct of most children. Very few have a reverent, dutiful and childlike respect for stepfathers and stepmothers. For the most part they despise them in heart, grumble at them in speech, and are very undutiful in their behavior. So it comes about that they bring much grief to their natural parent, and often cause much discord and dissension between their natural parent and their stepparent, being set to work in this by Satan, who labors all he can to divide those whom God has closely united and made one flesh. Sad experience shows that second, third or any later marriages are seldom as happy and peaceable as the first, especially if either the one or the other, or both, have children. The cause of this, for the most part, lies in children who cannot bear stepfathers or stepmothers.

Objection. Nature cannot bear a stepparent as well as a natural parent.

Answer. 1. If not as well, yet do not despise them: there is a difference between extremes.

2. Conscience and religion ought to change corrupt nature. Look to God’s ordinance, and let the fear of God possess your heart, so that it may bring you to do what nature cannot.

2. Objection. Stepfathers and stepmothers seldom respect their husbands’ or wives’ former children.

Answer. This objection better suits the mouth of a barbarian than of a Christian. The gospel teaches us to be subject “not409 only to those who are good and gentle, but even to those who are unreasonable,” and not to “be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good.”

Scripture counts those who rise up against their parents-in-law410 among those who rise up against their natural parents, showing by this that the impiety of the former is as blameworthy as the impiety of the latter.

§. 58. Of children’s subjection to guardians, tutors, etc.

As for children’s subjection to governors, guardians and tutors, the apostle says that a child is under them.411 If by the law children are under them, in fairness they ought to be subject to them. It is expressly noted of Esther, even after the king had chosen her for his wife, that she “obeyed Mordecai’s command”412 (who was in the place of a guardian to her) “as she had done under his care.” This is a memorable pattern for this purpose. What pretexts might she have made for casting off all manner of subjection? Mordecai was only her cousin; she was now raised above him; she was a wife, and so subject to her husband; indeed, a king’s wife, and so herself a queen. Yet she was subject, and her subjection is commended. We read that the sons of the prophets413 greatly respected Elisha, showed him reverence and were obedient to him, because he was like a father and tutor to them. In this respect Elisha too was subject, as a child, to Elijah, whom he called414 father.

Guardians, tutors and other such overseers of children have a parent’s charge laid on them, as we will415 show later. There is great reason, therefore, that childlike duty should be given to them. Their honor must correspond to their charge and care.

Contrary to this is the notion of many lawless children who, when their parents are dead, or when they themselves are sent away and placed out from under their parents’ government, think they are completely free from all government and may live as they please. Their practice matching this opinion, they run into all wild living, and in time bring themselves to utter ruin. It is the downfall of many children that they do not regard their guardians, tutors and governors; and God in judgment brings many such unruly children to some fearful and shameful end or other. Let children therefore be wise, and not take too much liberty for themselves.

So far we have dealt with the duties of children in their separate kinds, the manner of performing them, and the persons to whom they are to be performed. It remains to speak of the reasons the apostle gives to enforce those duties.

§. 59. Of the place of parents, by which children ought to be moved to obey them.

The reasons the apostle uses to move children to perform their duty are four:

  • The first is taken from the place of the parent.
  • The second from the justice of the thing.
  • The third from God’s express charge.
  • The fourth from God’s promise.

I. The place of a parent is pointed out by this phrase, IN THE Lord. As it gives children a416 limitation and a417 direction, so it adds a spur to stir them up to perform their duty. For it shows that parents are to their children in the Lord’s stead. As evidence of this, God has418 imparted to them this glorious and honorable title (father), which is419 properly his own and belongs to him alone. Now then, since parents are to their children in God’s stead, and by virtue of their place bear God’s image, children who obey their parents obey God, and in refusing to obey them they refuse to obey God. This first motive is a strong motive. For who is so void of religion that he will not think it most fitting that God should be honored? Or who is so impious as to refuse to give duty to God? Here, then, children may learn in one main point how to honor the Lord and show themselves children of God. And let them know by this that disobedient and undutiful children, who resist the authority of parents, resist the ordinance of God,420 and bring judgment on themselves.

§. 60. Of the justice by which children should be moved to obey their parents.

II. The second reason, in these words, for this is right, though it is not of greater force, is yet more plainly and expressly marked as a reason, as the causal word (for) placed before it shows. It is a general reason drawn from common justice, a reason that may move all sorts, even unbelievers and pagans, and therefore Christians much more.

In saying, It is right, he implies three things.

1. That it agrees with all law: with the law of God, which421 is the fountain of justice; with the law of nature, which proceeds from it; and with the law of nations, which corresponds to it in many respects. The proofs from God’s word given above show that it agrees with God’s law. The precepts that heathen men have given on this point show that it agrees with the law of nature. And the many statutes of lawmakers in all ages show that it agrees with the law of nations.

2. That the place of parents requires as much. For RIGHT422 requires that everyone have his own, what is his due. Since it is therefore right that children obey their parents, that duty is due to the parents.

3. That parents deserve as much, for right presupposes deserving.423 What is done by right is done by way of recompense. The cause of this deserving is the love parents have for their children, and the pain, the pains, the care and the cost they have gone to in bringing them forth and bringing them up.

Since these things are implied in right, note what follows from the force of this reason:

1. Disobedient and undutiful children transgress against God’s law, against the common justice of all nations, and against the light of nature; so they are unworthy of the name of Christians. They are worse than unbelievers, indeed worse than the brute beasts.

2. They have no regard for the place of their parents; they disgrace the image of God, which their parents carry by virtue of their place; and they disturb the seemly order and rank that God has set among men.

3. They badly repay their parents’ care and pains for their good, and show themselves both ungrateful and heartless, two most monstrous and odious sins.

§. 61. Of God’s accepting children’s obedience.

The same apostle sets down the reason just named in another place in this way: “This is pleasing to the Lord.”424 By comparing that place with my text, I observe that

What is right is pleasing to the Lord. And again, What is pleasing to the Lord is right.

These two propositions are (as we say in the schools) convertible and reciprocal; each is true of the other in every way. That is why the apostle, in another place, joins them both together. For having exhorted children to repay their parents, he says, “This is good and pleasing in the sight of God.”425 Good426 or honorable is in effect the same as427 right.

This shows that dutiful children, as they do what is good, or honorable, and right to their parents, so in doing it they also greatly please God, so that they may be sure not to lose by it. They will receive a reward at God’s hand, even if their parents should pay little regard to their dutifulness. This is how God dealt with Jacob. His father-in-law repaid his faithfulness badly, but God looked428 on him and abundantly repaid all his pains.

This shows, again, that undutiful children, as they do not do what is right to their parents, but rather wrong, so they greatly displease God. They may be sure, therefore, not to escape unpunished, even if their parents, through too much indulgence, should leave them alone. Take as an instance the two impious children of Eli, Hophni and Phinehas, and the two rebellious children of429 David, Absalom and Adonijah.

This, therefore, adds force to the second reason, and moves children to do right to their parents by obeying them, as they have regard for God, his good pleasure or displeasure, and as they look for recompense or fear vengeance from him.

§. 62. Of God’s charge, how inviolable a bond it is to tie children to obey their parents.

III. The third, drawn from God’s charge, is not only noted in express terms, but for more weight the very words of the moral law are quoted (“Honor your father and mother”), and it is added that this is a commandment, indeed the first commandment, and that with a promise. All this is for the enlarging of the point.

Here then let us consider

  1. The reason itself.
  2. Its enlargement.

From the reason that it is God’s charge, I gather these three points.

1. That it is not an optional matter, left to children’s discretion430 whether they will obey their parents or not, but a matter to which they are bound in conscience, just as they owe allegiance to God himself, the great lawgiver. So in neglecting duty to parents, children sin even against God himself; for the same God who has commanded us to honor himself has commanded us, “Honor your father and mother.”

2. That this is a perpetual and a general law, a law by which431 all children of all times, places, sexes, conditions and ranks always have been, still are, and always will be bound. For the moral law has that extent: it is general for all persons, perpetual for all times. Therefore no children may think themselves exempt from it.

Question. What if children are grown up and not under their parents’ government?

Answer. There may be some difference, both in some parts of subjection and in the manner of subjection, between children who remain under their parents’ government and those who are freed from it. Yet as long as a child has a parent, whatever his age or condition, he owes an honor to his parent. Joseph,432 when he was a great governor of Egypt, a grown man with a wife and children, still performed the honor of reverence, obedience and recompense to his father. Solomon,433 when he was in a higher place than Joseph, an absolute king, did the honor of reverence to his mother.

3. That no man can give children any dispensation or exemption from their duty to parents. If anyone may, he must be either the lawmaker himself or one greater than he, one who has power over him. Now God is the author and giver of that law: “God spoke all these words,” etc.434 But is anyone greater than God? Has anyone power over him? Who, then, can grant children a dispensation in this matter?

From this, then, I draw these two conclusions.

1. That the pope’s dispensation is worth nothing. Those who make it valid must make him greater than God, which is a horrible blasphemy.

2. Even if parents themselves should not demand duty of their children, children would still be bound to perform duty to them, because of God’s charge. To this, therefore, children are to look. This shows that no less a penalty hangs over the heads of those who transgress this charge than the curse of the law, eternal condemnation.

§. 63. Of the title FIRST given to the fifth commandment.

In enlarging the reason just named, the apostle calls the commandment to honor parents the first with a promise. As this shows that it is the first that has a particular promise attached to it, so it is also the first that God gave of any duty to be performed to man. The very order of the Ten Commandments shows the truth of this. The reason is clear: the honor due to parents is the ground of all the duties required in the second table. For if duty is not performed to those to whom we are bound by some special bond, may we think it will be performed to those to whom we are bound only in general? Now of all those to whom we are first and most bound, and to whom we owe our first duty, our parents are the ones. Those, therefore, who are rebellious against their parents and refuse to do their duty to them will hardly perform duty to anyone else. There is little hope that a disobedient child will turn out a profitable member of church or commonwealth. Absalom, who was a rebellious child, turned out only a traitorous subject; and Hophni and Phinehas, who refused to listen to the voice of their father, turned out only sacrilegious priests. Therefore, if any precept of the second table is to be conscientiously observed (as all are, for the same lawmaker gave all, and Christ has said that the second table is like the first)435 then this one of honoring father and mother is to be observed among the rest, and above the rest, at least if any difference may be made in observing them.

But since this word (first) is set down not simply but with a promise connected to it (the first with a promise), we are duly to consider its promise, from which a fourth reason arises.

§. 64. Of God’s promise moving children to obey their parents.

The fourth reason, taken from God’s promise, is both stated in general and illustrated in particular. It is stated in this clause, (first with a promise). It is illustrated in the third verse.

As for the general: God’s promise made to the performance of any duty cannot fail to be a strong motive to stir us up to perform it. By this means men stir up and urge one another436 to perform anything. So kings, when they would gladly have their subjects do this or that, promise them such and such rewards; so masters spur on their servants, parents their children, and one man another. If the promises of men encourage us to perform the things they charge us with, how much more ought the promise of God! Men437 are deceitful and may be double-dealing, professing one thing with their mouths and intending another in their hearts, and never meaning to perform what they promise. But God is faithful and true: his words are as deeds, his promises as performances, so that he never makes a show of more than he means to perform. Again, man’s power is limited. Though he truly intends what he promises, yet he may fail in the performance, either because he did not know his own power, but thought when he made the promise that he could do more than in the event he finds he can do; or because he is later hindered or disabled by some occurrence. But God’s power cannot be so restricted or hindered. Besides, men may be taken away before the time for performing their promise has come; but God lives forever and does not change. If, then, man’s promises are any motive to anything, much more are God’s, who always remains the same. Between God and man there is no proportion, no comparison.438

This motive greatly commends God’s fatherly indulgence toward us, and the earnest desire he has for our good. For he has such power and authority over all his creatures that the mere knowledge of his will ought to move them to perform any duty he commands; and if they do not obey, he might execute vengeance on them at once. But considering that we are his children, and need many inducements to draw us on little by little, he deals with us accordingly. He does not stand wholly and only on his authority, but adds promises to it (for this is a commandment with a promise). If, in spite of all this, children refuse to obey their parents, could not the Lord justly reason with them about the matter, as he once did with the Israelites in another case, and say, Judge between me and these children:439 what more could I have done that I have not done? I gave them an express charge to honor their parents; I laid it down in the first place, as a main and principal charge; to encourage them to keep it, I added a promise of good to come to themselves. What more could I do? Do not those who regard none of these things justly deserve vengeance? So, since this is a commandment with a promise, we see how children who disobey their parents are both rebellious against God, because of the commandment they transgress, and injurious to themselves, because of the promise they make void and of no effect. On this particular promise, see more in the first treatise, §. 97, 98, etc.
