The Sixth Treatise: Of Parents

Parents Loving, Praying, and Providing for Children

The Sixth Treatise: Of Parents · §§. 1–25

§. 1. Of the heads of parents’ duties.

Eph 6:4.

And you+ fathers, do not provoke your+ children to wrath, but bring them up in the nurture and admonition of the Lord.

Next after children’s duties follow parents’ duties, which the apostle lays down in this fourth verse. In it he notes:

  1. The duties

  2. The parties

    1. Those who are to perform the duties, fathers.
    2. Those to whom they are to be performed, children.

The duties are set down

  1. By prohibition.
  2. By precept.

The prohibition points out one extreme, which is too much rigor (do not provoke to wrath).

The precept, following on the prohibition, points out another extreme, which is too much laxness.

The precept itself lays three duties on parents.

  1. To nourish children, namely with food, clothing, and other such necessities (Nourish them.)
  2. To nurture them, namely with good discipline (In nurture.)
  3. To instruct them, namely in the ways of God (And admonition of the Lord.)

Nature teaches irrational creatures to do the first; civilized life teaches rational men to do the second; piety teaches Christians to do the third.

All the separate points which I shall deliver concerning parents’ duties may be referred to these heads.

So that parents may better discern how one duty follows another, I will proceed in this order. The fountain of all the duties, and the streams that flow from it, will be set out.

The streams will be divided into two rivers.

In the first are those general duties that are to be done continually.

In the second, the particular duties that are to be fitted to the different ages of children.

There are two principal general duties.

  1. Faithful prayer to God.
  2. Upright walking with God.

All the particular duties may be included under this one head, a provident care. And this concerns

  1. The infancy of children,
  2. Their youth,
  3. The time of their placing out,
  4. The time of the parents’ departing out of this world.

§. 2. Of the love which parents owe to their children.

The fountain of parents’ duties is love.440 This is expressly commanded them. Many approved examples of it are recorded, such as Abraham’s,441 Isaac’s,442 Rebekah’s,443 and others.

There is great reason why this affection should be firmly fixed in the hearts of parents toward their children. For great is the pain, the pains, the cost and the care which parents must undergo for their children. But if love is in them, no pain, pains, cost or care will seem too much. In this the wise providence of God appears, who by nature has fixed love so firmly in the hearts of parents that if there is anyone in whom it does not abound, he is counted heartless. If love did not abound in parents, many children would be neglected and lost. For if parents do not look after their children, who will? If no one looks after them, they must perish, for they are not able to help themselves. As God by nature has planted love in all parents, so Christians ought, even for conscience’ sake, to nourish, increase and fan this fire of love, so that they may be made more eager by it to do every duty cheerfully. The more fervent love is, the more readily every duty will be performed.444

Objection. As too much fire is dangerous, so is too much love.

Answer. True. Therefore, as in other things, so in this, the golden mean must be kept. There is no duty so holy and necessary that it cannot be perverted. Let the extremes be avoided, and the middle way will be better kept.

§. 3. Of what is contrary to love.

The extreme contrary to love in the defect is lack of natural445 affection, which is counted in the446 catalogue of notorious sins. Though love of children is engraved by nature in man’s heart, yet many put it out completely through covetousness, lust, vainglory, superstition, idolatry and other vices. So it comes about that instead of the good which they should do for their children, they bring much harm on them. Some do not spare the precious life of their children. Among these, barbarous idolaters go furthest in this kind of heartless cruelty, sacrificing their children and offering them up to devils. To this the great bloodsucker Satan of old brought not only the heathen, who, being ignorant of God, served the devil, but also the447 Israelites, to whom Jehovah, the true God, made himself known and expressly448 forbade this cruelty, and that449 on pain of death. See how superstition and idolatry blind the eyes of men!450 Those who have been among the savages in Virginia, Florida, India and other such places testify that such cruelty was still practiced in their time. And it is given as a main reason why, despite the vast lands they have, they increase no more in number: because many of their children are offered up in sacrifice from time to time.

Reasonable men show themselves in this more unreasonable than unreasoning beasts, which do everything they possibly can to preserve their young.

Though not so high, yet too high on this ladder of heartlessness451 do those climb who hate their children, and that (which makes the sin sinful beyond measure) for their piety and integrity: as many popish and profane parents do who have truly religious children, who for that very reason ought to be loved all the more.

The extreme in the excess is too much doting on children,452 as is done by those who love them so beyond measure that they count nothing of any worth in comparison with their children. Even God himself is lightly regarded, his worship neglected, his word transgressed, all duty to others left undone, and their own souls forgotten, through care for their children. Is not this sheer apish kindness? For apes kill their young with hugging. This is no love, but plain foolish doting. But what may be said of those who are so hellishly infatuated with their children as to commit incest or buggery with them?

§. 4. Of parents praying for their children.

The first and best stream which flows out of the fountain of love named above is faithful and fervent prayer. This extends to all things, at all times, throughout the whole course of the child’s life. It is the first and the last duty which parents ought to perform for their children,453 the one which they must do without interruption: “Pray without ceasing.”

Though prayer is a general duty which all Christians owe454 one another, yet it belongs to parents in a distinctive way, and of all others they are the most bound to it. For the promise which God makes to a parent is extended to his seed and children, as these and similar Scriptures show: “to be your God and the God of your seed after you”;455 “so that it might be well with them and with their children”;456 “This promise belongs to you+ and your+ children.”457 Parents therefore may call on God for their children with the greatest assurance of faith. For God’s promise is the ground of faith: as far as God’s promise extends, so far our faith may and ought to extend itself. From this has come the commendable custom of children’s asking458 their parents’ blessing, which implies a desire that their parents would pray for God’s blessing on them.

This duty of prayer must be performed before parents have children (that they may have some, as Isaac,459 Hannah460 and others did461); and as soon as children are conceived, especially when they perceive them to be alive and stirring in the womb (as Rebekah462 did); and again when they are born (as Zechariah463 did); and throughout the whole course of their life (as Job464 did); and when the parents are going out of this world and leaving their children (as Isaac465 did).

There is no one thing in which and by which parents may do more good for their children than in and by true prayer. God has sanctified prayer as a means of receiving every needful blessing from himself, the fountain of all blessing. If therefore God’s blessing is of use to children (what atheists they are who do not believe it!), then so is prayer, by which it is obtained.

§. 5. Of vices contrary to parents’ praying for their children.

The very neglect of this duty is a sin contrary to the duty466 itself, and there are many parents who stand guilty of this sin. Some think it needless to pray for a child before it is born, not considering that it is conceived in sin. When it is born, they leave this duty to the midwife, whereas it properly belongs to the father. When it has grown to any maturity, they put it off on the child to pray for itself. And when they are on their deathbed, they think it enough if they can pray for their own souls. Such parents show little true love to their children, but less faith in God.

But what may we say or think of such impious parents as467 do not fear to utter fearful curses against their children? God often, in wrath and vengeance, hears such curses, to the woe of parent and child; and by this he shows his great indignation against them for it.

§. 6. Of parents’ endeavoring to be righteous so that they may leave God’s blessing to their children.

Another general branch proceeding from parents’ love for their children is that for their children’s sake they endeavor to walk uprightly before God and to please him. I note this all the more because I find the reward promised to righteous parents extended to their children. “The generation of the upright will be blessed,”468 says David. And Solomon says, “Blessed are his children after him”;469 and again, “A good man leaves an inheritance to his children’s children.”470471 This motive is therefore urged by the Holy Spirit to stir parents up to all righteousness.

The Lord extends the reward of righteous parents to their children in this way to show his great pleasure in righteousness and his high approval of it. Read for this purpose 1 Kgs 11:34 and 2 Kgs 10:30.

1. Objection. “The righteousness of the righteous man will fall upon him.”472

Answer. That is meant of a man’s personal righteousness, and of grace itself, which is not imparted to children, rather than of its fruit: that is, that faith in Christ, the fear of God, obedience to God’s word, or any other personal grace which is in righteous parents, will not justify or save their children. For “the righteous will live by his own faith.”473 Yet this does not prevent the benefit and blessing of righteous parents from falling on their children, according to the extent of God’s promise.

2. Objection. We find it proved true by experience that the children of some righteous parents are cursed, and Scripture gives us many examples of it, such as Cain,474 Ham,475 Absalom,476 and others like them.

1. Answer. Such children, by their unworthy and degenerate conduct, forfeit God’s covenant and477 so deprive themselves of its benefit.

2. Answer. Many good reasons may be given why God should sometimes alter his course and withhold his blessings from the children of his servants, such as these:

1. So that God’s gifts and blessings should not otherwise seem to come by natural descent from the parent rather than by free gift from God.

2. So that parents should not be drawn by it to neglect the means of good education.

3. So that children themselves, trusting too much in their parents’ righteousness, should not take too much liberty and grow licentious.

4. So that God’s free election should not seem to be restricted by it.

3. Objection. If this is so, what motive can it be to parents to labor after righteousness for their children’s sake?

Answer. God reserves to himself a freedom to order his blessings as he pleases and to bestow them on whom he will, and so he sometimes blesses the child of a wicked parent (for example, Hezekiah)478 and denies his blessing to the child of a righteous parent (for example, Amnon).479 Yet because it is his very usual course to extend his blessing (according to his promise) to the children of the righteous, it is a strong motive to those who desire the good of their children to endeavor after righteousness all the more for their children’s sake. For in this way they use the means which God’s word warrants and sanctifies for obtaining God’s blessing for their children. Therefore leave your children a good memory rather than much wealth.

§. 7. Of the wrongheaded course which covetous and unjust parents take for the good of their children.

Contrary to this is the course of those parents who think to provide well for their children by unrighteous means. For many not only drudge and toil too anxiously and distrustfully to scrape together great heaps of money, or a great store of land, or other capital for their children, neglecting the duties of piety and mercy, but also defraud others by unjust and wrongful practices to make their children rich. This improper way of providing for children is so common that this proverb has arisen from it: Happy are those children whose parents go to the devil. A cursed proverb! For what else can it mean but this: that those who do not fear God, nor take care for their own salvation, will have the most regard for the outward condition of their children, and be the most eager to make them great and rich in this world? Note in this how many ways they reveal their notorious folly.

1. They prefer the outward condition of their children to the eternal salvation of their own souls. Indeed, even to God himself.

2. They place the happiness of their children in the goods of this world,480 than which nothing is more vain.

3. They make themselves drudges for their children, and so debase themselves below the dignity which belongs to them because of God’s image on them.

4. With much pains, care, grief and fear they spend a long time gathering what their children will squander in a short time, most dissolutely and prodigally.

5. They make themselves vassals of Satan and seek to be made rich by him, whereas in truth “the blessing of the Lord enriches.”481 So they take a wrong course to get wealth. If it is said that many are made rich in this way, I answer that as482 God gave a king to Israel, so he gives wealth to them in wrath, and in wrath he will take it away.

6. They bring God’s curse into their house and leave it to their children, so that these are the riches that are “hoarded to the harm of” their owners. Therefore do not let care for your children draw you into any covetous or unjust practices; but know that he who made your son made you also, and he who has given you the means of nourishment will also give your children sufficient help.

§. 8. Of parents’ provident care for their children.483

The head to which all the particular duties which parents owe to their children may be referred is a provident care for their children’s good. This extends to all times and to all things.

To all times: to the infancy, youth and adulthood of their children; and that not only while the parents live, but after their departure.

To all things: namely, those that serve both the temporal good of their children and also their spiritual good.

Children are of the very substance of their parents, and therefore parents ought to seek their children’s good as far as their own.

The patterns of holy parents recorded and commended in Scripture vividly set out this provident care.

But we will illustrate this general duty in the particulars, and declare in order how parents must provide both for the temporal and for the spiritual good of their children at every stage of their age.

Those who at any time, in anything, are negligent and careless of their children’s good, fall into the contrary of this general duty. The heinousness of these offenses will appear in the particulars.

§. 9. Of a mother’s care over her child while it is in her womb.

The first age of a child is its infancy. I will therefore first show how parents must see to the temporal good of their children in it, and then to their spiritual good.

The first part of a child’s infancy is while it remains in its mother’s womb. Here, therefore, the duty lies chiefly on the mother. As soon as she perceives that a child is conceived in her womb, she ought to take special care of it, so that (as far as lies in her power) the child may be safely brought forth.484 (The heathen philosophers, by the light of nature, observed this to be a duty and prescribed it to mothers.) A mother, then, must take tender care of herself when she is with child. For since the child is lodged in her and receives nourishment from her (as plants from the earth), her well-being contributes much to the good and safety of the child; but the harm that comes to her makes the child the worse, if it is not a means to destroy it. Why was the charge of abstaining from wine, strong drink and unclean things485 given to Manoah’s wife, but because of the child which she had conceived?

In this case there is a double bond to make mothers take care of themselves.

  1. Their own,
  2. Their child’s good.

Husbands also in this case must be very tender toward their wives, and helpful to them in all things needful, both because of the duty which they owe to their wives, and also because of what they486 owe to their children. Why was Manoah so eager to hear for himself the direction named above which the angel gave to his wife? And why did the angel repeat it to him again, but to show that it belonged to him to see that she observed it?

Those who, through violent emotion, whether of grief or487 anger, or through violent motion of the body, as by dancing, struggling,488 running, galloping on horseback, or the like, or through disorder of the body, by eating harmful things, by eating too much, by too much fasting, or by too much bashfulness in concealing their desires and longings (as we say), cause any abortion or miscarriage, fall into the offense contrary to the duty named above. If women were persuaded that they are bound in conscience to this duty, they would, I think, take more care of themselves. For if through their fault they themselves or their child are lost, they make themselves guilty of that loss; if both are lost, they make themselves guilty of the blood of both, at least in the court of conscience before God.

But those who purposely take things to do away with their children489 in their womb are guilty of blood in a far higher degree, indeed of willful murder. For what has received a soul formed in it by God, if it is unjustly cast away, will be avenged.

So far as husbands are careless of their wives when they are with child, denying them things needful, they are accessories to the harm which the woman or child suffers, guilty of the sin, and liable to the judgment.

§. 10. Of providing things needful for the child as soon as it is born, and of the cruelty contrary to it.

The next stage of a child’s infancy is while it is in swaddling bands and is still a nursing child. In this also the care lies especially on the mother, yet so that the father must give what help he can.

The first duty required here is that a sufficient supply of all things needful for a child in that weakness be provided beforehand. What the particulars are, women know better than I can express. For my part, it is enough to lay down the duty in general, which is commended to us in that worthy pattern of the Virgin Mary. Though she was very poor, and forced to travel far, and gave birth in a place where she was a stranger, where she was so little regarded that she was not given a place fitting for a woman in her condition, but had to content herself with a stable at a common inn, yet she provided for her child. For it is said, “She wrapped Him in swaddling cloths,” Luke 2:7.

Contrary to this is the practice of such wicked and heartless women as leave their newborn children under stalls, at men’s doors, in church porches, and many times even in the open field. It is noted as a point of heartlessness in the ostrich that “she leaves her eggs on the ground and lets them warm in the sand”; for which reason she is said to be “hardened against her young, as if they were not her own,” Job 39:14, 16. Much more hardened are the wicked women named above. The eagle is490 counted a heartless bird, because she thrusts the young which she has brought forth out of her nest. Are not such mothers, then, much more heartless? They often lay their children out in public places, for others to show the mercy which they themselves do not have. The civil law judges this to be a kind of murder.

§. 11. Of nursing children.

Among other needful things, the milk of the breast is fit for young babies, and they are to be nourished with it. I think no one doubts the rightness of this. In all ages and in all countries it has been counted the best food there can be for young babies. The metaphor which Saint Peter uses, taken from young infants, in these words (“Like newborn babies, crave pure spiritual milk”)491, confirms as much. So also does the desire which such infants have for the milk of the breast; and the ability and readiness that are in them to suck; and God’s providence in causing a woman’s breasts to give such milk; and the constant practice of nourishing little infants in this way, commended in the Scriptures; and (to conclude) the natural instinct which many irrational creatures have to nourish their young in this way.

Those who out of sheer curiosity (where no urgent necessity requires it) try whether their children can be nourished like birds, without the breast, offend against this duty. They reject the means which God has ordained as the best, and so set their shallow understanding against his unsearchable wisdom.

§. 12. Of mothers nursing their own children.

There is no great question about nourishing children with breast milk; therefore I have passed over it with a light touch. The chief question in doubt concerns the person who is bound to this duty: namely, whether the mother is bound to do it herself or not.

There are many strong arguments to press it on the consciences492 of mothers, and to show that (as far as they are able) they are bound to nurse their own children. Some are taken from the light of God’s word, and some from the light of nature.

In many places God’s word implies by just consequence that it is a binding duty. In other places it expressly commends it by the practice of holy women. And in yet other places it takes it for a granted truth and a settled case, not to be denied.

I. The consequences by which the word implies this duty are these:

1. In the blessing given to Joseph, old Jacob speaks thus: “the Almighty … blesses you … with blessings of the breasts and493 womb.” By the blessing of the womb, what can be meant but children? By the blessing of the breasts, what but milk, by which those children are nourished? It is as if he had said: I will bless you with such women as will both bear you children and also nurse the children they bear. The consequence, then, is this: as it is a blessing to have children by a true, lawful wife, so it is a blessing to have those children nursed by the same wife, their mother.

Objection. Those who have other women to nurse their children have the blessing of the breasts.

Answer. By the same reasoning it may be said that those who have other women to bear them children have the blessing of the womb. But the joining of these two branches of blessing together shows that both must be taken in the same way: so that as the blessing of the womb is to have children by a man’s own wife, so the blessing of the breasts is to have them nursed by his wife. If it is a blessing for the woman who bears the child to nurse it, then mothers are bound to perform this duty.

2. It is pronounced as a curse that women should have “wombs that494 miscarry and breasts that dry up.” If it is a curse for women to have dry breasts, then women must not knowingly make them dry, which all mothers do who do not nurse their children.

3. Manoah’s wife, when she was promised that she would bear a son, was given this charge: “Do not drink wine or strong drink,” etc. Those things were especially harmful to her milk. So it is implied by this that she should order her diet so that she might nurse her child well and have good milk for him.

4. God by his good providence brought it about that the mother of Moses (though she was forced to cast out her495 child) should nurse her own child. Indeed, the mother herself was eager to do it, and therefore appointed her daughter to watch who would take it up. These two circumstances imply that it belongs to a mother to nurse her children.

5. The apostle lays this down as a mark of a good woman,496 who in her place has been careful to do her duty and is therefore fit to do service in God’s church: (“if she has497 nourished her children,” or word for word, “if she has fed her children”). Now the proper food for young babies is breast milk, which, by the apostle’s rule, the mother must give.

6. The same apostle commands mothers “to love their498 children.” How can a mother better express her love for her young baby than by letting it suck at her own breasts? As this is a testimony of love, so it is a means of preserving and increasing love; for daily experience shows that mothers love best those children whom they themselves nurse.

Add these separate consequences together, and we shall find the duty in question very strongly enforced by them.

  1. It is promised as a blessing that mothers will nurse the children they bear.
  2. It is threatened as a curse that women will not be able to nurse.
  3. An angel directed a mother to conduct herself so that she might have a good supply of milk for the child she was to bear.
  4. God by his special providence showed that the child’s own mother was the best nurse for it.
  5. It is the mark of a good woman to perform this part of her particular calling, namely, to nurse her own child.
  6. Women ought to do for their children all the best duties of love that they can.

Therefore mothers ought to nurse their own children.

II. Some of the worthiest patterns, by whose example this duty is commended to mothers, are these.

1. Sarah nursed Isaac.499 This example is to be noted especially by those of the higher sort, such as the wives of rich men, the wives of honorable men, and the like. For Sarah was an honorable woman, a princess, a rich man’s wife, a beautiful woman, aged and well advanced in years, and the mistress of a household.

Are not these the excuses which many mothers plead for not nursing their children themselves?

2. The virgin Mary nursed Jesus. This example is to be noted especially by those of the lowlier sort, for the virgin Mary was young, poor, persecuted, and forced to move and flee with her child from country to country. Are not these the excuses which other mothers plead?

These two patterns not only commend the duty, but also strip all mothers who neglect it of every excuse.

To these may be added the examples of Hannah,500 of David’s mother,501 and of many others. What if I also add the example of that true, natural, loving mother who stood before Solomon’s throne to plead for her child? She says this of herself: “I got up to nurse my son,”502 etc. If this had not been a good motherly duty, she would not have pleaded it then and there.

III. The places of Scripture which take this duty as a matter granted and a settled case are such as these.

1. Where Sarah says, “Who would have told Abraham that503 Sarah would nurse children?” In this phrase she sets out God’s blessing in giving Abraham a son by her. Now since she expresses the blessing in this phrase of nursing, she takes it for granted that the mother who bears children must nurse them.

2. Where David says, “You made me hope upon my504 mother’s breasts,” he not only implies that his mother nursed him, but by the phrase makes it a settled case that the child who sucks must hang on its mother’s breast.

3. Where Solomon says, “O that you were to me like a brother who505 sucked at my mother’s breasts!” he also takes it for granted that brothers and sisters, as they come out of the same womb, so should suck at the same breasts: the breasts of her out of whose womb they came, their own mother’s breasts.

4. Where the woman said to Christ, “Blessed is the womb that506 bore You, and blessed are the breasts that nursed You!” she takes it for granted (as it was the usual practice in those days) that the breasts of the woman whose womb bore him were the ones that507 nursed him.

These arguments we have from the light of God’s word. Others we may have from God’s works and the light of nature, such as these:

1. God has given women two breasts fit to contain and hold milk, and nipples on them fit to have milk drawn from them. Why are these given in this way? To be laid out for display? There is no warrant for that in all God’s word. They are given directly for the food of the child that comes out of the womb. For until the child is born there is no milk in the breasts; soon after it is born, milk ordinarily flows into the breasts; indeed, a great part of the food which women eat turns into milk. Those who dry up this spring, and do not allow their children to share in its benefit, make this wonderful work of God’s providence vain.

2. The nourishment on which the child fed in its mother’s womb, and by which it was sustained there, turns into milk and comes into the breasts when the child comes out of the womb. From this we may gather that of all women’s milk, the milk of the woman out of whose womb the child came is the fittest for it.

3. Together with the milk passes some taste of the508 affection and disposition of the mother. This makes mothers love best those children whom they have nursed; and often, too, children who have sucked their mothers’ breasts love their mothers best. Indeed, we may observe many who have sucked another woman’s milk love those nurses all the days of their life.

4. Other things are nourished by what they are bred from. The earth out of which plants grow supplies nourishment to those plants; trees that bring forth fruit yield sap to that fruit, by which it grows to ripeness; irrational creatures, and among them the most savage wild beasts, such as tigers and dragons, and even sea monsters, nurse their young. For this reason the prophet says of women who do not nurse509 their children that they are more cruel than those sea monsters, “like an ostrich in the wilderness.” For the cruel ostrich and the hateful cuckoo are the two kinds of creatures noted for leaving their young for others to nourish: the ostrich leaves her eggs in the dust; the cuckoo leaves hers in other birds’ nests. Other creatures (if nature does not give them milk and teats, as to birds it does not) feed their young in other ways, yet by themselves.

5. Shall I add another argument which daily experience confirms, namely, God’s blessing on this motherly duty?510 Commonly, children who are nursed by their mothers thrive best. Mothers are most tender toward them, and cannot bear to let them lie crying without taking them up and quieting them; whereas nurses will let them cry and cry again if they are about any business of their own. For who are commonly chosen to be nurses? Poor country women who have much work to do and little help, and so are forced to let the child lie and cry, many times until it is ready to burst. Children nursed by their mothers are for the most part brought up more cleanly and neatly, and are freer from diseases; not so many die; I am sure not so many are lost through negligence. The number of children put out to nurse who die every year is very great. It has been observed in many country villages that most of those who die there from time to time are children put out to nurse. Are not mothers who might have nursed their own children, if they would, accessories to the death of those who are lost through the nurses’ negligence?

For these and other such reasons, heathen women, and even511 savages, have in all ages been moved to nurse their own children; and some heathen philosophers have urged and pressed the necessity of this duty. It was never more neglected than among those who bear the name of Christians.

Let mothers of whatever rank or degree know that (except in a case of necessity) they have no warrant to send their children out to others to nurse. We do not read in all of Scripture of any holy woman who ever did it.

§. 13. Of the objections for sending children out to a wet nurse.

Objection. Many nurses are mentioned in Scripture, as Rebekah’s512 nurse, Mephibosheth’s nurse, Joash’s nurse, and others.

1. Answer. The nurses mentioned in Scripture were commonly dry nurses. Rebekah’s nurse went with her before she was married: how can it be thought that she was a wet nurse? Could they tell when Rebekah would have a child? Or, when513 she had one, that Deborah (the nurse mentioned there) would have milk for her? It is said that Naomi “became a nurse to” Ruth’s514 child. Now Naomi was old; long before this she was past childbearing, and she had been without a husband for many years. How then was it possible for her to nurse the child at the breast? She was therefore a dry nurse, as were the other nurses mentioned in Scripture.

2. Answer. The mothers of those children who are said to have had nurses (if those nurses were wet nurses) may have been dead; or, if living, unable to nurse for lack of milk or nipple, or for some other such defect; or, if able, they sinned in sending their children out.

3. Answer. Though it is said that there were nurses, yet it is nowhere said that a mother sent her child out to be nursed.

2. Objection. Pharaoh’s daughter sent out the child whom she515 took as her own, to be nursed.

Answer. She did not bear this child, nor was she its natural mother, so this is beside the point. Indeed, it tells against the objectors, because the true mother of this child nursed it.

3. Objection. The metaphor taken from nurses516 is often used, and applied to God and to God’s ministers.

1. Answer. Using a thing by way of comparison and likeness does not wholly justify it: take for instance the parable of the unjust steward, and that of a thief.517

2. Answer. The metaphor may be taken from a dry nurse as well as from a wet nurse. For the comparisons are not drawn from nursing at the breast, but from bearing and carrying in the arms, as dry nurses usually carry children.

3. Answer. The metaphors are most fitly taken from mothers who are nurses to their own children.

4. Objection. Many mothers do not have such skill in nursing as nurses have.

Answer. Let them learn, seeing it is their duty.

5. Objection. Mothers of great wealth and high position cannot endure the pain of nursing, nor take the pains of handling young children as they must be handled.

1. Answer. The greatest there are must set themselves to do the duty which God requires at their hands, though it costs them pain and pains. Note Sarah’s example, recorded above.

2. Answer. By this it appears that if other women could carry their children in the womb nine months and endure the pain of labor for them, they would hire them to do it. But seeing they do the one (that is, carry and bring forth their own children with hard labor), why should they not do the other? If they say there is an unavoidable necessity of carrying and bringing forth their children, I answer that conscience ought to move them to nurse those children whom necessity forces them to bring forth. By this latter duty, of nursing children, God puts women to the test, whether they will, for conscience’ sake, do a duty which they can decline if they will. But because God knew that many will do no more than necessity lays on them, he has made it impossible for women to carry and bring forth their children by another.

3. Answer. If women would set themselves cheerfully to perform this duty, much of the supposed pain and pains would be lessened.

4. Answer. Though they do not send their children out to nurse, they may for their own ease employ a nurse, provided they nurse the child themselves.

6. Objection. A mother who has a trade, or who has the care of a household, will neglect much business by nursing her child; and her husband will save more by giving half a crown a week to a nurse than if his wife nursed the child.

Answer. No outward business belonging to a mother can be more acceptable to God than the nursing of her child. This is the work most properly belonging to her special calling; therefore all other business must give way to it, and it must not be left for any other business.

As for the husband’s saving by sending the child out to nurse, no gain can give a dispensation against a binding duty.

7. Objection. It will wear down tender, fair women, and make them look old too soon.

1. Answer. God’s ordinance must not give way to women’s squeamishness. Sarah was fair and old; the Virgin Mary was fair and young.

2. Answer. Drying up a woman’s milk will wear her down more than her child’s nursing on it. For nursing is a means both of better health and of greater strength, for bearing children as well as for nursing them. Barren women, and childbearing women who send their children out to be nursed, are the most subject to sickness and weakness. The drawing out of a woman’s milk by her child is a means to get and keep a good appetite, which is a great preserver of good health.

8. Objection. Husbands are disturbed in the night and kept from their sleep by their wives’ nursing their children.

1. Answer. By this reasoning, neither mothers nor other nurses who have husbands should nurse children.

2. Answer. Since children come from the loins of the father as well as out of the womb of the mother, fathers must be content to endure some disturbance as well as their wives, and all the more so that they may pity their wives the more, and give them what help they can.

9. Objection. Many husbands will not allow their wives to nurse their children themselves.

Answer. Because it is a binding duty, wives must use all the means they can, by themselves or through others, to persuade their husbands to let them perform it. They must take care that they do not make this a pretext to cover their own sloth and unwillingness for this duty. They must not make themselves accessories to their husbands’ fault by providing a nurse and sending the child away themselves. If their husbands insist on their authority and can by no means be persuaded otherwise, the wives must be merely passive, and allow the child to be taken away.

10. Objection. Many poor women support their households by nursing other people’s children.

Answer. If they were not employed that way, they could take pains at something else. But the gain of one must not make another neglect her duty.

11. Objection. Some mothers cannot nurse; they have no milk. Others cannot do it very well, because they have no nipples, or they have sore breasts, or are sickly, or perhaps they have such a disease that the child, if it nursed on their milk, would draw it into itself, and so the nursing might turn out very dangerous to the child.

1. Answer. God requires no impossibilities. Therefore in setting out the duty I put in this caution: (as far as they are able).

2. God requires “mercy, not sacrifice.”518 If, therefore, it is truly the case that the mother’s nursing the child will be dangerous to herself or to the child, she may and ought to refrain. For nursing is only as sacrifice, compared with preventing danger, which is mercy. But women must take care that they do not claim inability and danger without just cause. Some are themselves the cause of their lack of milk, because they will not let it be drawn down, or because they will not use means (for there are means) to get and increase milk. There are means also to raise the nipples where the breasts are very flat. Refusing to nurse often causes some illness in a woman, and sore breasts, which might be prevented by the child’s nursing. If the soreness is only in the nipples, a mother may safely nurse the child by enduring a little more pain. Many mothers have nursed their children when blood ran from the child’s mouth because of sore nipples, and yet both mother and child have done very well.

12. Objection. Several children nursed by their mother have died one after another.

Answer. A due and thorough inquiry must be made by those who are skilled. If any cause is found in the mother, then the rule holds, “mercy, not sacrifice.” But if none can be found, the outcome must be left to God’s providence, and an uncertain result must not be a hindrance to a known duty.

So the answering of the objections named above makes the point all the clearer.

§. 14. Of the father’s duty in encouraging his wife to nurse her child.

The duty required on a father’s part in this respect is that he encourage his wife, and help her with all needful things for performing this duty. It is noted of Elkanah that he allowed his wife to stay at home while she nursed her son, and would not force her to go up to the tabernacle as his other wife did, but gave her all the ease and contentment he could, saying to her, “Do what you think is best.”519 And of Abraham it is noted that after Sarah had finished nursing the child, he “held a great feast,” even “on the day520 Isaac was weaned”; and one purpose of it was to testify his rejoicing at God’s blessing on her motherly duty so well performed.

§. 15. Of the faults contrary to a mother’s nursing her child.

All those mothers offend against this duty who, for any ulterior motives, when no necessity requires it, send their children out to be nursed by others.

  1. Some do it for ease and quiet, because they cannot bear to have their sleep broken, or to hear their child fuss and cry.
  2. Others do it out of squeamishness, because they are unwilling to bare their breasts or to soil their clothes.
  3. Others out of pride, imagining that their beauty would be impaired, and that they would look old too soon.
  4. Others for gain, because they can have a child nursed more cheaply away from home than at home, where at least they must hire one more maid.
  5. Others for pleasure, so that they may more freely ride out and meet their friends.
  6. Others for other ulterior motives.

All of which shows much self-love, little love for their child, and little regard for God. They can be counted only half-mothers, for nursing a child is as much a mother’s part as bearing it and bringing it forth.

§. 16. Of a father’s fault in hindering his wife’s nursing of her child.

All those fathers who forbid their wives to nurse their children, or grieve them by complaining of the trouble, disturbance and expense, or do not provide needful things, or do not encourage them all they can to do it, make themselves accessories to the fault of mothers named above. The mother’s pain and pains are both the greatest; what fathers can endure in it is, by comparison, only a small thing. Their fault therefore must be the greater if they are in any way the occasion of their child’s being sent out to nurse. I have noted this all the more because husbands are for the most part the cause that their wives do not nurse their own children, partly by allowing it and partly by egging them on to send their children out. If husbands were willing for their wives to perform this duty, and would persuade and encourage them to it, and give them what help they could, then where one mother now nurses her child, twenty would do it.

§. 17. Of parents’ joint care about their children’s baptism.

There is a further duty to be performed by parents to their children even in their infancy, and that concerns their spiritual good. It is this:

Parents ought to see that their children are rightly baptized in due season.

This is indeed a common duty belonging to both parents, but chiefly to the father, and that for two reasons.

1. The father is the chief and principal governor of the family, and has the greatest charge; accordingly he ought to have the greatest care, even in such matters as are common to both.

2. The mother at that time is weak because of her labor and delivery, and in no condition to have her head much troubled with many cares, much less able to make arrangements herself for such weighty matters. Yet the husband should make known to his wife (if she is not extraordinarily weak) what he intends concerning the place, time, manner and other such circumstances of baptizing the child, and consult with her about the name, the witnesses and such points. And if the husband is too slow and negligent, the wife ought, so far as she is able, to remind him of his duty in this, and to stir him up, by herself or through someone else, to perform it.

§. 18. Of the reasons to move parents to see their children baptized.

That parents are bound to see to their children’s baptism, these reasons show.

1. The commandment of God concerning circumcising521 children, in whose place baptism now succeeds under the gospel (Col 2:11, 12). God’s commandment to this duty was first given to Abraham, and that for himself and all his posterity to observe (Gen 17:10). After this it was laid down in the law as an enacted statute, Lev 12:3.

2. The practice of the Jews in a faithful and constant observance of this ordinance: as of Abraham; of Zechariah and Elizabeth; of Joseph and Mary; and many others.

Objection. The children who were born in the wilderness were not circumcised.

Answer. They had no settled dwelling place in the wilderness, but were always on the move, so that it would have been dangerous for the children to have been circumcised. In that extraordinary case this rule prevailed: “I desire mercy,522 not sacrifice.”

3. The practice of Christians, who, believing, were baptized themselves,523 and their whole household with them. Under whole household children must surely be included.

4. Christ’s embracing and blessing such children as were524 brought to him, and his rebuking those who would have kept them from him.

5. The promise of God made to them. For seeing God is so525 gracious as to extend his promise to our children, our care must be to obtain the seal which God offers for the confirmation of that promise.

6. The right they have to God’s kingdom. Baptism526 is an evidence of that right of theirs. It is parents’ duty to get them that evidence. If children have a just title to any lands and revenues, or to any earthly honors and dignities, parents will do what they can to make that title sure to them even in their infancy. Much more careful should they be to make that rich and glorious inheritance, which is reserved for them in heaven, as sure to them as they can; and there is no better means of bringing this about than baptism.

7. Their conception and birth in sin.527 Children drew contagion from their parents; therefore there is great reason that their parents should see them washed with the water of regeneration.

8. The comfort which will arise from the performance of this duty to Christian parents, and indeed to the children themselves too, when they come to the age of understanding. When parents see the covenant of God surely sealed and confirmed to their children, they cannot help rejoicing greatly in it (if, at least, they bear any love to their children). And it must also greatly comfort the child when (having come to understanding) he knows that from his infancy he has carried the seal and pledge of his regeneration.

9. The constant, continued custom of the true universal528 church, which ever since the apostles’ time has given the sacrament of baptism to children.

§. 19. Of parents seeing that their children are rightly baptized.

Since there are such forceful motives to stir up parents to perform this duty (and the motives show it to be a weighty duty), I will further show how this duty ought to be performed.

Two things ought to be observed in children’s baptism.

  1. That it be done rightly.
  2. That it be done in season.

In performing it rightly, some things are necessary, and some advisable.

The things of necessity are chiefly these:

1. That the child be baptized by a minister of the word.529

2. That it be baptized with the element of water, the only element sanctified for this purpose.

3. That the form prescribed by Christ (Matt 28:19) be530 used, “in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit,” by which the unity of the Godhead and the trinity of persons is plainly set forth.

4. That the proper rite of applying the water to the child’s body be used, so that at least the child’s face is sprinkled with it.

The things that are advisable are these:

1. That the child be baptized in a public place, where God’s people ordinarily meet together, set apart for the worship and service of God.

2. That such a time be chosen that an assembly of saints may be present.

These two circumstances should be observed all the more because baptism is one of the solemn parts of God’s public worship, a pledge of our incorporation into the body of Christ and the communion of his saints. Therefore it is to be performed with the more solemnity (as a matter of great moment), before many witnesses, with the help of the faithful prayers of an assembly of saints.

§. 20. Of parents’ care to give a fit name to their child at his baptism.

A third very advisable matter about a child’s baptism is that parents be careful to give a fit name.

It belongs to parents to give the name to their child. For so531 holy parents (whose pattern in Scripture is commended to us in this respect) have done from time to time. And for their warrant to do it, it is worth noting that when God was pleased to appoint a name for a child, he charged the parent to name him so, saying to him, “You are to give him the name”532 so-and-so.

It is also evident that the time of baptism is the fittest time for giving the name.533 Under the law, children’s names were given at their circumcision; and so under the gospel it has been the practice in all ages, and that for these reasons.

  1. That their names may be a testimony of their baptism.534
  2. That as often as they hear their names, they may be reminded of their baptism.
  3. That they may know how they are given to Christ by name to be his soldiers, and that therefore there must be no deserting him.
  4. That they may also be assured that, being baptized with water and the Spirit, they are registered by name in heaven.

Now because names are given so solemnly, and are of such good use,535 it is most proper that fit names be given to children. And for proof of this, let the names be observed which Scripture records as given by God himself, and by such holy men and women as were guided by his Spirit; and we shall find them to be holy, sober and fit names.

For the direction of parents in this duty, I will set down some sorts and kinds of names that are fit and becoming for Christians.

1. Names which have some good meaning, and among them such as are warranted by Scripture, as John (the grace of God), Jonathan (the gift of God), Andrew (manly), Clement (meek), Simeon (obedient), Hannah (gracious), Prudens (wise), and the like, so that their name may stir them up to strive after the virtue it signifies.

2. Names which in times before us have been given to persons of good note, whose life is worthy of our imitation, as Isaac, David, Peter, Mary, Elizabeth, and the like, so that the names may move them to imitate those worthies.

3. Names of our own ancestors and forebears, to preserve a memory of the family. This appears to have been an ancient practice even among God’s people, since the relatives wanted Zechariah’s son to be named Zechariah;536 and when the mother had just cause to name him John, they answered, “There is no one among your relatives who bears this name.”

4. Common names of the country, which custom has made familiar, as Henry, Edward, Robert, William, and the like among us.

§. 21. Of parents’ care in bringing their children to be baptized in due season.

Though Christians are not so strictly tied to a set day as the Jews were to the eighth day, yet from that strict direction given to the Jews we may well gather that it is not fitting for Christians to put off the baptizing of their children beyond eight days. For a young child of that age may be baptized with more ease and less danger than circumcised.

The most seasonable time, I take it, is the day on which God’s537 people, in the place where the child is born, usually assemble publicly to worship God next after the child’s birth, if at least it does not fall within two or three days after it, which is rather early for both mother and child.

Whether we consider the honor of God (the riches of whose mercy are vividly set forth in the sacrament of baptism) or the good of our child (who in that sacrament receives a pledge and seal of that rich mercy of God), baptism is of great consequence, and therefore the first opportunity of performing it is to be taken. For by their diligence and due speed in it, parents give evidence both of their zeal for God’s glory and also of their earnest desire for their child’s spiritual good.

§. 22. Of parents’ faults in neglecting their children’s baptism.

Contrary to the aforesaid duty of parents about baptizing their children well are many failings, such as

1. The corrupt opinion of Anabaptists, who deny the lawfulness of baptizing children. The arguments noted above are enough to stop their mouths.

2. The practice of Separatists (who come too near to Anabaptism), who, objecting to the ministry and orders of our church, do what they can to keep their children from that sacrament. To that end they take their wives, when they are about to be delivered, to a strange place where they are not known, and soon after the delivery they secretly carry wife, child and all away, so that the magistrate cannot have their child baptized against their will. And having no ministry of their own, nor means to carry the child overseas, they keep it unbaptized many years. Where is the evidence of their faith in God’s promise, of their538 respect for God’s ordinance, and of their desire for their child’s spiritual good? Though it is a great wrong to children to be kept from baptism, yet the sin lies on those parents who do not obtain baptism for their children, especially at that age when their children cannot object to it.

3. The perverse opinion and practice of certain ancient heretics, who instead of baptizing children with water had them branded with a hot iron. They grounded their error on a false interpretation of this phrase, “He will baptize … with the Holy Spirit and with fire.”539

Answer. 1. They err in taking this word (fire) literally and in its proper sense, when it was meant mystically and metaphorically.

2. They err in applying to the outward action of a minister what was meant of the inward working of Christ. By this misinterpretation of theirs they thwart the main aim of the one who first used that phrase, which was to show the difference between540 all other ministers and Christ Jesus.

4. The opinion and practice of those who use other forms of baptism besides this one: “in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.” Their opinion and practice are grounded on certain concise phrases used by the apostles, such as these: “baptized in the name of Jesus Christ,” “in the name of the Lord,” “in541 the name of the Lord Jesus,” etc.

Answer. Those phrases set forth the very substance and inward matter of baptism rather than its form.

5. Their opinion and practice who do not care by whom their children are baptized, whether heretics, idolaters, laymen or women. Little do they regard the comfort of conscience and the strength of faith that arise from this: that a lawful minister, in God’s place and name, as God’s ambassador, puts the seal of God to his covenant.

6. The practice of those who (from I know not what fussiness or show of rank) must have their children baptized at home in their private house. This manner of baptizing takes much away from the honor of that high ordinance, which ought to be performed with all the seemly solemnity possible.

7. Their practice who bring their child to church to be baptized, accompanied only by the midwife and three witnesses. It would be almost as good to be baptized in a private house. For it is not the walls of the church, but the assembly of saints, that adds to the honor of the sacrament, and that is most of all to be regarded.

8. Their practice who, for show of rank, or to have great persons as witnesses, or for such ulterior motives, put off the baptizing of their children longer than is fitting: some two or three weeks, some two or three months, some longer. By this they show too light an esteem of this sacrament, because they prefer circumstances merely for show to a matter of such great moment. God often shows his just indignation against such people by taking away their children unbaptized before the time they set for the baptism has come.

9. Their practice who do not care what heathenish, idolatrous,542 ridiculous names they give their children. What respect do they show either to God, in whose name their child is baptized, or to the holy sacrament itself, or to the congregation of saints before whom the name is given, or to the child himself, who is to carry that name all his life?

§. 23. Of parents providing things needful for the life and health of their children.

So much for the duties of parents concerning their children’s infancy. Those that concern their childhood follow.

The childhood of a child is reckoned from the time it begins to have any discretion and understanding until it is fit to be placed out: that is, as long as it ordinarily lives under its parents’ government.543

The duties which parents must perform to their children during this time may be gathered under these two heads.

  1. Care to bring them up.
  2. Care to place them out.

In training them up well, regard must be had both to their temporal and also to their spiritual good.

Two things are required of parents with respect to the temporal good of their children.

  1. To nourish them well.544
  2. To nurture them well.545

Under nourishment are included all things needful for546 health and life, which parents ought to provide for their children, such as

1. Food, which Christ takes as a settled case, and from which he draws his argument to show that God will provide for his children: “What father” (he says) “if his son asks for bread, will give him a stone?” etc. Matt 7:9, 10, 11.

2. Clothing, for it is expressly noted that Israel made his son a coat (Gen 37:3).

3. Recreation, which is needful for health, especially in young children. When Zechariah, in chapter 8, verse 5, told the Jews, and that by way of blessing, that “the streets of the city will be filled with boys and girls playing there,” he implied that it is a lawful and fitting thing, which parents should allow their children. But yet the time, measure and kind of recreation must be well ordered.

4. Means for recovering health when they are sick. It was for this end that Jeroboam547 sent his wife to the prophet on behalf of his son, who was sick; that548 the ruler came to Christ for his son also, who was at the point of death; and that many others came to him for their sons and daughters who were ill.

Whatever other things are needful, parents must provide for their children as far as they are able;549 otherwise the apostle counts them worse than unbelievers.

Both fairness and necessity require this much of parents.

Fairness, because children owe all their pains and service to their parents while they are under them, and are wholly at their command, and for that reason have no means to provide needful things except by their parents’ help. Parents therefore in all right must be helpful to them in this.

Necessity, because if the life and health of children are not well provided for, no duty, no service can be expected at their hands.

§. 24. Of parents’ too great stinginess and carelessness toward their children.

There are two extremes contrary to the aforesaid provident550 care of parents for their children’s good:

In the defect, covetousness.

In the excess, lavishness.

Some parents fail so far in the defect that they almost starve their children for lack of necessities. They do not give them enough wholesome food, nor fitting and decent clothing, but let them go in tatters and rags like beggars’ brats. If they are sick, God may restore them if he pleases, but the parents will use no means. When they are well, they allow them no time to refresh themselves with any recreation, but hold them in too strictly. There is not only a lack of charity in such parents, but plain heartlessness, even more than in the most cruel beasts. For the wild beasts provide for their young with much tenderness.

§. 25. Of parents’ too great lavishness and indulgence toward their children.

Others go just as far beyond in the excess: feeding them too daintily, dressing them too showily, tending them with too much pampering, and letting them spend too much time in sport and play. Many and great are the harms that follow from this, such as

1. Those who in their childhood are daintily fed and too much pampered, besides being for the most part the most sickly, will in time grow so squeamish and so choosy about their food that their parents will not know what to provide for them, or when to give it to them. “The soul that is full loathes honey.”551 Indeed, if a stranger comes to the table where such a child sits, he may soon see that the child has been too daintily fed. If children are fed at first with ordinary, moderate fare, they will afterward both be in better health and condition, and also accept more contentedly and thankfully whatever is provided for them. But excess breeds diseases both in body and in mind.

2. Vanity in clothing also greatly corrupts young children. For there is in them, even from the cradle, a natural inclination to outward finery. Now for parents to deck them out, what is it but to blow up the fire of that vanity, and make it rise into such a flame as may in time badly scorch the parents themselves and utterly consume the children? And yet how common a fault this is! How monstrously many parents offend in it! What foolish fashion is used by the boldest swaggerers and the loosest harlots that they will not bring their children to, and that when their children cannot tell one fabric or color from another? What can this proclaim but the parents’ pride and folly? Proud maids are often the instruments of decking children out (especially when they are little ones) more than is fitting; but yet the blame lies on the parents for allowing it.

3. Tending children with too much pampering keeps them children too long, and too tender, and often spoils a good constitution of body. Some are so overly tender of their children that if a child complains ever so little, or refuses its food (though out of daintiness or fullness), the physician must at once be sent for, and the apothecary sent to, and the child is made much worse with a supposed and apish kindness.

4. Too much sport makes them wild and rough, unfit to be trained up to any good calling, and it drains their spirits and wastes their strength too much. Yet many parents do not care how much time their children spend in sport and how little in learning. They think it dulls their children too much to be kept at school, or at any learning; whereas in fact too much play makes them more foolish, and learning would greatly sharpen their wits.
