Parents Nurturing, Teaching, and Training Children

The Sixth Treatise: Of Parents · §§. 26–41

§. 26. Of nurturing children well.

I refer good nurture in part to the temporal good of children, because (as we shall hear later in the particulars) it is a special means of the outward, temporal welfare of the child even in this world. Unless this is added to nourishing, in what do rational men and women exceed irrational beasts? The cruelest beasts of all are very tender (as we heard before) toward their young, nourishing them and providing all things needful for them until they can fend for themselves. But as God has given man a rational soul, an understanding head, capacity, teachableness and aptness to learn, so parents ought to make use of those abilities and gifts. Otherwise, for lack of use, they may in time be lost, and so children turn out little better than brute beasts. In this respect the proverb is true, better unfed than untaught. Experience shows that a good education is better than a great portion. The Holy Spirit presses this point very much on parents, as we shall hear later in the particulars. For I will handle these three points.

  1. The kinds of nurture.
  2. The time when it is to be done.
  3. The means of doing it well.

§. 27. Of parents’ neglect in nurturing children.

Contrary to good nurture is too much liberty, which often brings much woe and utter ruin on children. It is the greatest enemy of good education that can be, and the nurse of all vice. Yet many parents do not mind letting their children live as they please: all the care they take is that they are fed and clothed. This is a common fault of both rich and poor parents. The rich claim that their children need no education, because they have enough to leave them, not knowing that education is a special means to make them keep that enough and use it well. The poor claim that they are not able to bring up their children to anything, not considering that the Lord by his providence has so ordered the affairs of men that, as there are fit employments for the greatest, so there are also552 for the lowliest, which may be followed without much cost. So the fault lies wholly in the negligence of parents. And if as a result children fall into any wild living, their parents will answer for it.

§. 28. Of parents teaching their children good manners.

The nurturing of children mentioned above consists

  1. In teaching them good manners.
  2. In training them up for a good calling.

Not only heathen men and other moralists, who were merely natural, civilized men, but also the Holy Spirit himself has prescribed many rules of good manners, and has urged and pressed them much.

1. The word nurture553 mentioned by the apostle in this text which we have in hand implies as much; and so does the phrase which Solomon uses, “Train up a child in the way he should go”554: that is, teach him how to order the course of his life.

2. The many555 precepts about reverencing our superiors and conducting ourselves with respect toward one another are rules of good manners. There are very many of these in Scripture.

3. Those rules are556 commended by many examples of holy men recorded in Scripture.

4. Those who have557 failed in the rules of good manners and behaved rudely are reproved by the Holy Spirit.

Nor is it without good reason that this point is so set forth. For

1. Good manners are a very becoming and seemly thing. But558 it befits Christians to do “all things decently.” That decency is to be applied not only to the affairs of God’s church but also to the whole course of our life. In this respect we are commanded to “walk559 decently,” that is, to order all our actions and the whole course of our life with good manners.

2. They are a thing of good report, and that to both parents and children. Now we must do “whatever is of good report.”560

3. They work a kind of delight, love and admiration in those who see them, as is noted of the Queen of561 Sheba when she saw the seemly bearing of Solomon’s servants, and of the Egyptians when they saw the orderly562 seating of Joseph’s brothers.

4. They are an outward ornament to piety and religion, and make it much more respected. In this respect Saint Peter exhorts believing wives to order their conduct well563 before unbelieving husbands, and Saint Paul exhorts Christians of every sort to “walk decently toward outsiders.”564

Since the Holy Spirit has urged the point of good manners in this way, we must not think it a matter merely for show and a needless point, but a binding duty.

§. 29. Of the objections against good manners.

1. Objection. Religion and grace do not consist in good manners. Many who have not a spark of the fear of God in their hearts are able to conduct themselves very orderly and courteously in their outward behavior.

Answer. Though grace does not consist wholly in it, yet grace cannot well be without it: it is a great ornament and beauty to grace. And though good manners may be separated from the fear of God, yet the fear of God will not be separated from good manners. Restraining grace may be in him who has no renewing grace; but renewing grace presupposes restraining grace, just as reason presupposes sense, though sense may be without reason. If those who do not fear God can conduct themselves with seemliness and good manners, what a shame it is for those who seem to fear God not to do so! Will not those be a witness against these?

2. Objection. Good manners are a hindrance to grace: those who are most diligent in teaching or practicing the one are commonly most negligent in the other.

Answer. This is a mere quibble. I am sure that grace is no hindrance to good manners. If any make good manners a hindrance to grace, it is their fault.

3. Objection. Good manners are to grace as mint, dill and cumin are to the great and weighty things of the law.

Answer. Grant that it is so; yet, seeing both may stand together, why should they be separated? Christ’s rule is this: “These you+ should have practiced, without neglecting the others.”565

4. Objection. Many who make a great show of religion are very rude and unmannerly.

Answer. If there is only a show of religion in them, no wonder they have no manners. If some examples could be shown of those who are truly religious and lack good manners, their pattern is no precedent; much less can it prove that to be no duty which God’s word has set down as a duty. Many who perform some duties well fail much in other duties. Who comes anywhere near following God’s word as he should in everything?

§. 30. Of parents allowing their children to be brought up without manners.

Contrary to parents’ care in teaching their children good manners is laxness: when parents allow their children to grow up rude, not caring how they behave at home or abroad, toward their parents or toward others. An unmannerly upbringing makes children crooked, perverse, stubborn, churlish, surly and snarling in disposition; as, on the other side, good nurture in this respect breeds a frank and generous spirit, amiability, courtesy and kindness. If those who are brought up without manners are children of those who profess the true religion, they bring a stain on their profession of faith. Indeed, they dishonor God, as if he were the author of unmannerliness and confusion,566 against which the Holy Spirit protests. And they make themselves and their children a scorn in the eyes and mouths of profane persons, who will be ready to point and say, “Look at the children of professing Christians, how unmannerly they are brought up, and how badly taught: they do not have so much as good manners in them.”

To avoid this blemish, schoolmasters and all who567 have the charge of training up young children must help parents in teaching children good manners.

§. 31. Of parents training up their children for some good calling.

The second branch of good nurture is training children up for a good calling. This charge (“Train up a child in568 the way he should go”) aims directly at this. Parents have performed this duty from the beginning of the world, and the Holy Spirit has commended their performance of it. Adam brought up his sons to separate callings: one was “a keeper of sheep,”569 the other “a tiller of the soil.” The like is noted of Jacob’s570 sons, of Laban’s571 and Reuel’s572 daughters, of Jesse’s573 son, and of many others.

Much good may arise from this to parents themselves, to their children, and to the people and places where such children574 will live.

1. A good calling is a special means for children to maintain themselves and their family, to relieve those who are in need, to ease their parents, and (if their parents’ need requires it) to relieve and maintain them.

2. It is that way in which God’s angels have a charge to575 keep them while they walk in it.

3. It is a means in which and by which they may be of service to the commonwealth where they live.

4. It is the best place in which the general duties of Christianity may be most clearly shown and best performed.

5. It is the best ordinary means that can be prescribed to keep a child from the vanities of youth, from immoderate pursuit of pleasures, from unlawful games, from idleness, from bad company, and such like evils. As these are sins in themselves, so they are occasions and provocations to other most grievous and monstrous sins, and turn out to be the very bane of youth.

Objection. Many parents have good lands to leave to their children: what need is there of a calling for such children?

Answer. 1. Much land may soon be consumed by those who do not have the skill to use it well.

2. Maintenance is only one end of a calling, and not the chief and most principal one.

3. More good may be done by skill in a calling than by a great store of land.

4. We are born for others as well as for ourselves. It is not enough, therefore, to say, “I have enough to maintain myself.”

§. 32. Of parents’ care in choosing a fit calling for their children.

Having shown that the point in general is a duty, I will576 add some directions for performing it better.

1. Children are to be trained up in those things which are the groundwork of all callings, such as reading, writing, and the principles of learning. Whatever the particular calling is, these will be of great use to anyone. Many who were not taught them at first would give much for them afterward. Parents at first might teach their children these things with much ease and small expense, which afterward cannot be577 so well learned, partly for lack of leisure, and partly because the abilities of those who are grown in years are not as fresh and fit to learn as they were in childhood. Those things are not to be despised as small without which great things cannot stand.

2. The calling for which children are trained up must be lawful, approved by God’s word, and not against its general rules. So they may keep a good conscience in practicing it.

3. The calling must be fit for the child who is trained up578 for it. As there are various callings, so there are various abilities in different children: some are fittest for callings of understanding and learning, others for callings that require an able and strong body. In this the wise, ordering providence of God is much commended, for in this way men are much more useful to one another. Now, in choosing a fit calling, a child’s best ability, where it chiefly lies, whether in the exercise of mind or of body, is to be duly observed; and also his inclination, to what calling he is most disposed.

4. Among fit callings (for there may be many), that which579 is best and most excellent is to be preferred. To this purpose I may fittingly apply what the apostle says, “eagerly desire the best gifts.”

On this ground let parents be exhorted to train up such580 children as they find fit for the great and weighty calling of the ministry. There is no calling in which anyone may do more good, and in which (if they are able and faithful ministers) they can receive more comfort and contentment. This exhortation is all the more to be heeded because, in comparison with those who are trained up for other callings, so few are trained up for this one.

§. 33. Of parents’ faults contrary to their duty of training their children up for a calling.

On the contrary, many parents offend greatly by not training up their children for a calling as they should. And the offense in this respect is committed in many ways, as

1. When parents allow their children to live like little masters at home and pass all their youth in idleness. So they turn out mere drones and caterpillars in the commonwealth. If they have an inheritance, they soon waste it; if they have none, they often turn out either thieves or beggars. They will fall in with any company, the readiest prey for the devil that can be; for they are like the house “empty, swept clean, and put in order,”581 and when the evil spirit spies it, he at once enters it with seven other spirits worse than himself.

The wise lawgiver among the heathen is said to have ordered582 that a child who had been taught no craft by his parents should not be forced to support them, even though they were old or poor. I cite this not to justify the law (for it is against the Christian rule of overcoming evil with good) but to show how the very heathen judged the neglect of this duty a great fault in parents.

2. When parents neglect to teach their children in their childhood the general and common grounds of all callings, some out of stinginess, others out of carelessness. In this way poor men make their children unfit for many means by which they might well maintain themselves, and rich men make theirs unfit for public office and for good society. Indeed, poor and rich alike are in this way reared all the more in ignorance, and made all the more unfit to profit by the preaching of the word and other means of spiritual edification.

3. When parents bring up their children in unwarranted and unlawful callings, such as to be of popish and idolatrous orders, to wait on papists, to be stage players, keepers of gambling houses, etc. Some (which is horrible to think of) train up their daughters to be common harlots; and some583 (which is yet more horrible) train up their children to be sorcerers and witches. How can they keep a good conscience in these, when the very works of their calling are sin? Is this not to thrust them headlong into hell? Those who thus bind their children to the devils’ sacrileges are their spiritual murderers.

4. When parents have no regard at all for the fitness of the calling: as when they train up for learning children of able bodies but dull and slow capacity, with a stuttering tongue and other such imperfections, and in learning they turn out mere dunces and lose all their time, or are not able to make use of the learning they have; or when they train up children who have a great inclination to learning, and are very fit for it, in some other trade, which, after many years spent in it, they are forced to leave.

5. When parents seek only the most profitable trade, and never think of educating their children most to the honor of God. How can such parents expect God’s blessing on the means used for their children’s good? This is why among papists so many are trained up for church orders and offices, and so few among Protestants. For there is very great maintenance and revenue for such among papists, but little in comparison among Protestants.584

§. 34. Of parents teaching their children piety.

Parents are to see to the spiritual good of their children, and that in their childhood, as well as to their temporal good. Therefore parents must train up their children in true piety. This is expressly commanded in my text under the phrase admonition of the Lord. Under the law God both directly585 commanded it, and that very often, and also ordained various outward586 rites, and caused many visible and extraordinary587 monuments to be set up, so that children might be moved by them to ask their parents the mystery of them, and parents might take occasion from that question of their children to588 teach them the ordinances of the Lord.

This express charge of the Lord is further commended by the practice which holy parents have given it from time to time: witness the examples of Abraham,589 David,590 Bathsheba,591 Lois592 and Eunice, with many others.

1. Piety is the best thing that a parent can teach his child. For as reason makes a man differ from a beast, and as learning and civility make a wise and sober man differ from savages and ruffians, so piety makes a sound Christian differ much more from the most civilized and well-ordered natural man there can be. Learning, civility, calling and portion are all nothing without piety. Now it is a special point of wisdom to seek the best good that we can, for our children as well as for ourselves. Indeed, this is a clear sign of a parent’s true love for his child.

2. There is a necessity for children to be taught piety, because593 they are not born but made Christians. By nature they are utterly destitute of all piety; for by nature “every inclination of the thoughts of man’s heart is altogether evil all the time” (Gen 6:5), and in that respect “man is born like a wild donkey’s colt” (Job 11:12). So a man would be better unborn than not taught piety.

3. The charge and office of parents bind them to teach their594 children piety, for they are made watchmen over their children by God. If, therefore, their children live and die in impiety through their parents’ negligence, their blood will be required at their parents’ hands: witness the example of Eli.595

Objection. This duty belongs to ministers.596

Answer. 1. God has given parents an express charge about this, as we heard before.

2. In the family a parent is all in all over his child: a king, a priest and a prophet. Therefore what a minister is to do in the matter of instruction in the church, a parent must do at home.

3. Children need daily instruction. The parents’ pains in this respect must be added to the minister’s, and both together are little enough.

4. Parents, having more familiarity with their children than ministers have, must surely know their capacity and disposition better, and so may know better in what manner to instruct them: whether to give them milk or solid food, whether to deal mildly or roughly with them.

5. Instructions from parents are commonly received more kindly than those from others, and children will relish them better when they come from their parents. They say that a plant will grow best in the soil from which it first sprang; so instructions coming from those who both brought us forth and first brought us up are likely to do the most good.

6. There is no means like this to breed love in a child’s heart: to be an instrument of bringing piety into it. Now who should seek a child’s true love more than a parent? In this respect a parent is more bound to this duty than a minister.

7. It is impossible that a minister who may have many hundreds of children under his charge should instruct them all well. It is therefore needful that each parent look after his own children.

As these distinct answers satisfy the objection, so they serve as so many more reasons to enforce the duty. Therefore, to proceed in adding other reasons:

4. It is only right and just that parents teach their children piety,597 because they598 conceived them and brought them forth in iniquity. If they allow them to lie and die in that corrupt condition, they are more cruel than the ostrich and the dragon.

5. Children are most truly God’s: they are born to God.599 He is600 most truly their parent; in comparison with God, fathers and mothers of the flesh are only nurses. They must therefore nurture them in “the admonition of the Lord.”

6. Piety is what will make the child, more than any other thing,601 most obedient and grateful to his parents. For so there is a double bond to bind him: 1. His birth. 2. His new birth; especially when the cause of the one has also been the cause of the other.

7. Nothing can settle the heart of a wise parent on his602 deathbed concerning his children more than the assurance that piety is planted in them. For then he may commend them to God’s providence with stronger confidence, and expect his blessing on them after he is dead with greater assurance.

8. Parents, by teaching their children piety, are a special603 means of propagating true religion from age to age and from generation to generation. No better means can be thought of. For if all parents were careful of their duty in this respect, then, as there is a succession of children, and by it a preservation of mankind, so there would be a succession of those who fear God, and by it a preservation of true religion. My children who are taught by me may become fathers of children, and so teach their children what they have learned from me. Indeed, after them grandchildren may become fathers of other children and teach their children the same, and so on from age to age, others after them. This is the means on our part: in our time we must do our part, and for those who come after us, leave the outcome to God.

Not only the great benefit of this point but also the all too common neglect of it in most families has moved me to dwell on it the longer and to press it the more forcefully. For performing it better, I will add some directions.

§. 35. Of directing parents how to teach their children true piety.

1. Whatever principle of piety parents teach their children,604 they must be sure that it is grounded on God’s word. This phrase (admonition of the Lord) implies as much.

In this way parents will be sure to feed them with good, wholesome spiritual food, such as will serve for their spiritual nourishment and eternal life. In this respect principles of religion grounded on God’s word are called sound, or wholesome, or healthful words:605 and that both with respect to their matter and substance, and with respect to their effect: they cause and preserve good, sound, spiritual health. We know that natural men take care to give their children such food as is wholesome for their bodies (for will a father606 who is evil give his child a stone or a serpent, and not what is good?). Conscience must move religious parents to have the same care for the souls of their children as nature teaches all parents to have for their bodies. If parents are careful to draw the principles in which they instruct their children out of God’s word, they will be sure not to poison their souls with any error, heresy, superstition or idolatry.

2. When children begin to read, let them read the holy Scripture.607 So Timothy was trained up “from infancy” (2 Tim 3:15). In this way children will suck in religion with learning; for there is a secret power lurking in the holy Scripture (which is God’s own word), more than in any books of men, so that through God’s608 blessing there may by this means be an inward work of grace in children even in their young years. Besides, no books are easier than many parts of Scripture, and no histories more wonderful and delightful than the histories of Scripture. It is the advice of an ancient father that young children be made acquainted with the words and names of holy Scripture; that, in place of tales and fables, choice histories of the Bible be made known to them; and that they be instructed in the Proverbs of Solomon.

3. Let children be catechized constantly, from day to day. “You shall teach them continually to your children,” says the law. What is done daily is said in Scripture to be done continually, as the sacrifice which was offered daily was called a continual offering. Here let this caveat be noted: in giving this spiritual food, parents should deal with their children as skillful nurses and mothers do in feeding infants. They will not cram more into their mouths at once than their stomachs are able to digest, but will rather feed them often with a little. So it is not fitting for parents to be too tedious: that will only dull a child’s understanding, and breed weariness, and make the child loath to be instructed again. It should rather be “precept on precept, precept on precept, line on line, line on line,609 a little here, a little there.” In this way they will learn with ease and delight; and, this being done often, in time a great measure of knowledge will be gained by it. If a vessel has a little mouth, we do not usually fill it by pouring whole pailfuls on it, for so all may be spilled, and it may receive little or nothing; but we let the liquid fall in little by little, according to the capacity of the mouth. So nothing is lost, and the vessel is filled the sooner. This is how children are to be dealt with.

4. To the set times of catechizing children let other occasions610 of teaching them piety be added: as at table, by comparing the spiritual food of their souls to the bodily food by which their bodies are nourished; when they are walking outdoors, by showing them the stars, how they keep steadfast in their course, and the trees, how they bring forth fruit in their season, and how all things are for the use and benefit of man, and so making spiritual uses of them. Note the direction which the law gives parents for this purpose: “You shall talk of My words to your children611 when you sit at home and when you walk along the road, when you lie down and when you get up.”

5. Let parents explain to their children the mysteries of those612 outward rites which God has ordained in his church, such as preaching, baptizing children, administering the Lord’s Supper, resting from work on the Lord’s day, and the like. This was expressly commanded under the law. Visible rites are great helps to the weak understanding of children when they are plainly explained and applied. Indeed, they are also special means of keeping in memory the mysteries contained under them, as coarse threads or wires are means to preserve pearls strung on them. As often as children see the rites, they will be reminded of the mysteries implied under them.

6. To this may be referred the declaring of such great and613 wonderful works as God has done for his church in former times, especially such works as have been done in their own time; and if any memorials of them remain, make them known to children. This direction was also given under614 the law, concerning the monuments set up for the great deliverances that God gave his people. In particular, when the day of the Gunpowder Treason is observed, parents ought to teach their children the reason for observing that day. And as God does any great works of mercy or of judgment, point them out to children. When there is great famine, plague, or any widespread death, instruct children in the causes of it; when there is victory, plenty, peace or the like, teach children where these come from. Outward things that the senses can perceive work best on children.

7. Let religious schoolmasters be chosen for children, and so likewise615 other masters to whom children are sent, and religious houses where they are placed. Hannah entrusted her firstborn child to old Eli, a good, religious high priest.616 If masters themselves are religious, there is good hope that they will instruct those under them in piety; and if they do, what a help that will be to parents! If both parents and masters join in it, it must surely be very profitable to the children. If parents should fail, masters might still make up the lack well.

8. Let parents be a good pattern and example to their children617 in piety. “As for me and my house,” says Joshua, “we will serve the Lord”618: he sets himself first as a guide to the rest. “I will walk in my house with integrity of heart,”619 says David, by which he would make himself an example to his children, as to others of his family. Example is a real instruction, and adds a sharp edge to admonition. A religious parent will do much more by practice than by precept. For children are much inclined to follow their parents: let them go before, and children will soon follow after. Practice is a clear proof of the necessity of the precept given.

§. 36. Of parents’ faults contrary to their duty of teaching their children piety.

Many are the failings contrary to the care of teaching piety named above. For

1. Most parents care only for the temporal and worldly good of their children: so long as their children may be well fed and clothed, and brought up in some profitable calling by which they may well maintain themselves in this world, little thought is620 given or care taken for their spiritual life in this world or eternal life in the world to come. In what are these parents better than heathen? Job was otherwise minded: he was more concerned for their souls than for their bodies.

2. Many are so far from teaching piety that they teach their children profaneness, pride, wild living, lying, deceit, and such like principles of the devil. It would have been better for such children to have lived among wild beasts than under such parents. As the children are thrust headlong into hell by this, so their blood will be required of their parents.

3. Others think it enough that their children are taught a religion, but it does not matter to them what religion. Such are those who, having rich but popish relatives, commit their children to the education of those relatives, in hope of some temporal benefit which their children may reap from them. If they were as careless of their children’s bodies, they would be counted little better than murderers; and is not the soul more precious than the body?

4. So far are many from catechizing their children, and that daily, that they do not teach them even the Lord’s Prayer, the Creed, and the Ten Commandments. In this the papists will rise up in judgment against them, for they are very diligent in teaching their children Pater noster, Ave Maria [Our Father, Hail Mary], and such like Latin principles, which the children cannot possibly understand.

5. Few use the outward helps named above, such as the holy rites appointed by God, the great and glorious works of God, and his extraordinary works of mercy or judgment, to instruct their children by them. As they themselves do not care to take notice of any such thing, so they do not care whether their children do or not.

6. Some so prefer a little money to the true621 good of their children that they do not care to what schoolmaster they send their children, whether he is profane, or popish, or unlearned, especially if he is a kinsman or one of their friends. Few will do so in the case of their health or outward condition, but will rather get the best physician or the best lawyer they can. Children often learn such evil qualities from their schoolmasters as they can never shake off again.

7. Many turn out very bad patterns to their children, and set a very bad example by profaneness, dissolute living, swearing, drinking, playing at unlawful games, etc. These parents, as they brought forth their children in sin, so lead them on toward hell. Their evil example is not only a hindrance to the good instruction of others, but also makes all their own counsels (if at any time they do give any good counsel) in vain. For the left hand of evil example622 soon pulls down more than the right hand of instruction can build up again.

To conclude: those parents whose children are not brought up in the instruction of the Lord show plainly that they regard neither the salvation nor the damnation of their souls.

§. 37. Of instructing children as soon as they are capable.

So much for the kinds of nurture. Its time follows.

In handling the time of623 good nurture, I will show

  1. When it ought to be begun.
  2. How long it ought to be continued.

1. Parents ought to begin to nurture their children as soon as they are capable of any instruction, just as young birds are taught by their mothers to fly as soon as their wings can carry them.624 “Train up a child,” says Solomon, that is, while he is young and tender; and again,625 “He who loves his son disciplines him early.” So Samuel was sent when he was very young to be trained up under Eli (1 Sam 1:24); and Solomon was instructed by his father when he was “tender” (Prov 4:3); and Timothy was taught the Scriptures626 from a young child, or infant.

There are both privative and positive reasons to press this point: privative, with respect to the harms that may be prevented by it; positive, with respect to the good that may be gained by it.

1. Many are the evils to which children are prone by nature, just as rank ground is apt to bring forth many weeds. For “every inclination of man’s heart is evil from his youth,”627 and “foolishness is bound up in the heart of a child.”628 If, therefore, they are not well nurtured early, what can be looked for but the fruits of evil and folly? But timely nurture will prevent such fruits, and be an excellent preservative against their own natural corruption, against Satan’s temptations, and against the allurements or discouragements of the world.

2. Continuing in evil makes children obstinate and629 inflexible in it. Eli’s sons, being allowed to go on in wickedness until they came to ripeness of years, would not afterward “listen to their father.” What creature can be tamed if it is not begun with while it is young?

3. When children first begin to be capable of instruction630 they are most pliable to follow the direction of their parents, as is evident from the ordinary course of nature in all things. Clay, wax and other such things take any impression while they are soft; twigs are bent any way while they are tender; birds and beasts are easily tamed when they are young; grain sown early brings a timely and plentiful harvest.

4. What is learned in childhood is retained longest:631 “Train up a child in the way he should go, and when he is old he will not depart from it.” A jar keeps longest the scent with which it is first seasoned; and by experience we may note that old men best remember the things which they learned in their childhood. Indeed, by educating children well from their infancy much labor may be spared afterward; for the constant practice of virtue turns it into a law.632

Objection. To teach children while they are young is only like teaching a parrot or some such irrational creature: they may learn what is taught them, but they cannot understand it.

1. Answer. Though children do not have so deep an understanding while they are young as they have when they come to riper years, yet as soon as they are capable of instruction they grasp what is taught them much better than irrational creatures can.

2. Even if that were granted, it would not follow from it that it is better for them not to be taught while they are young. For, first, it is better that they should be shaped and squared to a good course before they can discern between good and evil than be allowed to run on in evil until they get a habit in it, which, once it is got, will hardly be cast off. Secondly, teaching them before they can well understand helps their understanding much. What can be the reason that the children of kings and great men are commonly of more understanding at 12 or 14 years of age than the children of poor and lowly men at 17 or 18, but that they are instructed sooner and better? Thirdly, as their understanding comes to more and more ripeness with age, they will more and more grasp what at first they did not understand so well. When schoolboys first learn their Latin rules, they learn them merely by rote, without understanding their meaning,633 but afterward come to make very good use of them. Therefore children are to be instructed early, both for the benefit that may be reaped later, as grain is sown in winter to yield a crop at the following harvest, and to prevent the harms that may come about, so that they do not get the upper hand over their parents against their parents’ will.

§. 38. Of mothers’ distinctive care in nurturing young children.

By the way, let mothers especially note this point of timely nurture, as a point belonging to them in particular. The634 grandmother Lois and the mother Eunice first taught Timothy; Bathsheba635 taught Solomon when he was young. Solomon often warns children636 not to forsake their mother’s teaching.

By this he implies that mothers should teach their children, especially while they are young. This duty belongs so much to a mother that Solomon637 lays the blame and shame of its neglect on her; on the other side, the honor of nurturing children well goes especially to the mother. It is to this purpose that the638 particular names of the mothers of the kings are recorded in Scripture, suggesting by this that mothers were a main cause of the piety or impiety of such children. Solomon and Absalom both had one father, but different mothers. May we not well think that Solomon’s mother’s care to instruct him was a special means of his piety, and that Absalom’s mother’s neglect of this duty was some cause of his impiety? It is expressly noted of Ahaziah’s mother that she “was his counselor in wickedness,” which made him as wicked639 as he was. Experience at home confirms as much: for if father and mother are of different religions, most of the children will follow the mother. For while children are young, their mother is most in their sight: she feeds them, she clothes them, she tends them when they are unwell (when the Shunammite’s child, being ill, said to his father, “My head! My head!” he said to a servant, “Carry him to his mother.”)640 Her precepts and practice are therefore best heeded by the children in that respect, and she has the best opportunity to persuade them to what she likes best. So what they learn in their younger years they commonly learn from their mothers; and what they learn then for the most part sticks closest to them and is retained longest by them, as was noted641 before.

I have not pressed this point on mothers in particular as if I exempted fathers from all care of nurturing their children at the beginning. For in my text the apostle names fathers; and Solomon says that his father taught him even while he was tender; and David felt the smart of neglecting his other children. It is therefore (as has been proved before) a joint duty belonging to both. Fathers therefore must do their best, and see that mothers do theirs too, because the father is governor over child, mother and all.

§. 39. Of letting the best time for nurture slip by.

Contrary to this is the negligence of most parents, who let the best years, in which their children are most teachable, pass by in unruliness, vanity and folly, and so lose what can never be recovered, most precious time. This is why, when they set about reclaiming their children, they find them exceedingly perverse and headstrong: much like a strong, big limb of a tree, which, if a man sets about straightening it, he cannot easily make bend; and though it bends, it will not keep standing as he would have it; indeed, it may well break rather than bend much. Such a branch was Adonijah. It is clear that he was not well nurtured in his childhood, for from his childhood “his father had never once reprimanded him.”642

The father’s putting this duty off on the mother, and the mother’s putting it off on the father, is a great cause of its neglect. If both of them were persuaded that it belonged to them both, and for that reason would help each other as far as they could, children would be much better instructed.

§. 40. Of parents continuing to nurture their children.

As parents must begin early to nurture their children, so they must keep on with it as long as they retain any government over them; indeed, as long as they remain their parents. There may be some difference in the manner of performing this duty: for children are to be treated as children, and those who are grown in years and of riper understanding are to be dealt with accordingly. Yet parents must always have a care for their well-doing. The word used in my text and translated children is a general word which in Scripture and other643 writers is used to set forth all sorts of children, of whatever sex, age or rank they are. In handling the duty of children we644 showed that children owe subjection to their parents as long as they both live. Therefore, by the rule of relation, an authority also remains in parents over their children for as long, and accordingly they ought to have a fatherly care for their good. On this ground Eli did well in admonishing645 his children after they were married. His fault was that he did not go far enough in doing his duty: he did something, but not all that he should and might have done. Job is commended for the care he had over his children when they were grown in years: for day by day he sent for them and sanctified them, and that after they had separate houses of their own and lived apart; and he did this all their days.

For the performance of what is now urged, parents must so conduct themselves toward their children from time to time that they always keep the reins in their own hands, and646 retain a power to curb their children as they see occasion. As their children grow up in years, they may slacken the reins more and more, but never let them go entirely and throw them loose on their children’s necks.

§. 41. Of parents’ folly in letting go all their power over their children.

Contrary to this is the folly of those who put themselves in their children’s power and let go all their authority over them. Many647 parents who have done this, having found by woeful experience the injury and harm that followed from it, have much repented their folly and used means of redress, but all too late. For an injury is much more easily prevented than redressed. All the power that David had could not hold Absalom in after he was permitted to have648 horses and chariots and men at his command. If David had continued as he began, to keep him within bounds and always hold him under, all the treasonous plots which Absalom put into action might easily have been prevented. Our times afford too many examples of parents’ folly in this respect, and of the injuries following from it.

So much for the time of nurture. Its means follow.

Parents Admonishing and Correcting Children

The Sixth Treatise: Of Parents · §§. 42–49

§. 42. Of adding admonition to instruction.

The means of furthering the good work of nurture649 are chiefly two.

  1. Frequent admonition.
  2. Due correction.

Both of them are implied in this text: one in the word translated admonition, which (according to the derivation of the650 Greek word) is a putting of a thing into the mind, an urging and pressing of it; the other in the word translated nurture.651

Now both of these are to be joined together, as being very helpful to each other. For admonition without correction is likely to prove mere futility, and correction without admonition will be too much austerity.

The duty which the first of these sets forth is this:

Parents must often whet instruction upon their children. They652 must not think it enough to tell their children what they ought to do; to instruction they must add admonition, and, as it were, beat into their children’s heads the lessons which they teach them, so that these may make a deeper impression on their hearts. In this way their instructions will be like the “words of the wise,” which are “like nails firmly fastened,” or nails fast knocked653 in. They remain firm where they are once fastened, and cannot easily be plucked out. For as many blows knock a nail in up to the head (as we say), so many admonitions settle good instructions in a child’s heart, and cause the heart to be established in what is taught,654 which is a thing to be labored after. The general exhortation to “be urgent in season and out of season”655 may be applied to this purpose; but more pertinently that656 direction which is given particularly to parents, of whetting God’s words upon their children.

It is to this purpose that Solomon is accustomed to double his instructions and urge them again and again, as: “Listen … to your father’s instruction, and do not forsake the teaching”;657 “accept my words and hide my commandments within you; … incline your ear …, direct your heart,” etc.658 Indeed, he often repeats the very same precepts.

The understanding of children is fickle, and their memory weak. If they are instructed only once, or seldom, or carelessly, what is taught will soon slip away and do little or no good.

For the better performing of this duty, parents must think of the best means they can to fasten their instructions on their children, and observe their children’s inclination and disposition, and see by what they are most moved. Constant exhortations and powerful persuasions are included under admonition, and each in its kind is to be used as occasion requires.

§. 43. Of parents’ weariness in instructing their children.

Contrary to this is the practice of those parents who soon grow weary of instructing their children. The apostle lays it down as a general caution in good duties that we “not grow659 weary.” If we must grow weary in no good thing, shall parents grow weary in doing good to their children? Yet how many there are who, having once taught their children, think they have done duty enough in that way: if their children will take it, they may. They are unwilling to take too much pains in often urging the points which they have taught them.

So that teaching vanishes away, and it turns out, as we say in the proverb, as good not to do it at all as to be never the better for it. This is one point in which old Eli failed. For he gave his children very good instruction; but because he stopped there, it was neither accepted by God as a sufficient discharge of his duty, nor were his children any the better for it. If this was a fault in him, even though his children had come to years of discretion and to ripeness of understanding, how much greater is the fault in those whose children are still young?

Objection. If a child does not take instruction at first, he is plainly of an unruly and perverse disposition; all the pains that can be taken will be lost.

Answer. It may be childishness rather than perverseness, or some weakness rather than obstinacy. Considering the necessity of good nurture, no pains should be thought too much. There is more perverseness and unruliness in such parents as grow weary of doing this duty than in such children as are not moved at first; for this is a means ordained by God to cure this unruliness.

§. 44. Of parents reproving their children.

The other means of helping nurture is correction.

This is of two sorts: verbal, by words, and real, by blows.

The former is reproof, and it must always go before the latter, which is most usually and properly called correction.

Reproof is a kind of middle thing between admonition and correction: it is a sharp admonition, but a mild correction.

It is all the more to be used because it may be a means of preventing strokes and blows, especially with well-disposed and good-natured children (for “a rebuke cuts into a man of discernment deeper than a hundred lashes cut into a fool”),660 and because it may be used when it is not so fitting to use strokes and blows, as when children have grown to full age.

The many good fruits which the Holy Spirit notes as coming from due reproof show that it is a duty which parents ought to make conscience of, as they desire to promote the good of their children; and all the more because many good fruits come back to the parents who reprove, as well as to the children reproved. As for the good of those who are reproved, it is said, “The reproofs of discipline are the way to life”;661 they bring “understanding”662 and make men “prudent.”663 As for the good of those who reprove, it is said, “To those who rebuke there will be delight”664 (that is, much comfort and cause for rejoicing, so that they will not need to regret what they have done) “and a blessing of good will come upon them”; that is, either a blessing of good men, who will bless, praise and commend them, or a blessing of good things, and that from the Lord, who will reward them for this conscientious performance of their duty.

On these grounds665 holy men have not held back from rebuking their children as there was occasion. Though Eli666 did something in this duty, yet because he was not more severe in it, he brought destruction both on himself and on his children.

The direction noted in §. 40 and 47, and in Treatise 4, §. 35, may be applied here.

§. 45. Of parents pampering their children.

Contrary to this is the excessive doting of parents on their children, when they are unwilling to give them a harsh word. David (though otherwise a very wise man) showed much folly in this, for he never once displeased Adonijah “by saying, ‘Why do you act this way?’” And it is very likely that he pampered his other rebellious son, Absalom, in the same way. Note the fearful outcome that followed from this, both for the father and for the children. Though their father would not displease them, yet they did not care about displeasing their father, indeed about grieving his heart and vexing his soul. All foolish doting parents may look for the same at their children’s hands. For, first, parents highly displease God by neglecting this duty; therefore in just retribution God will give their children over to667 displease and vex them. Secondly, neglect of reproof is a means of making children rude, presumptuous, rebellious, and so careless about pleasing their parents. Indeed, all things in which children offend through lack of upbringing will be required at their parents’ hands.

§. 46. Of correcting children.

The latter and more proper kind of correction, which is by stripes and blows, is also a means appointed by God to help the good nurture and upbringing of children. It is the last remedy which a parent can use: a remedy which may do good when nothing else can.

The Holy Spirit both expressly commands it and very often presses it, in these and similar phrases: “Chasten your son”;668 “Correct your son”;669 “Do not withhold correction from a child”;670 “Strike him with a rod.”671 If there were no other motive, this would be sufficient. God’s charge was such a motive to Abraham that at it he would have sacrificed his son;672 and will you not correct your child at God’s command?

It is further commended by God’s own example, which is set forth not only in some particular instances but in his general, constant dealing with all, and that as a special token and fruit of his love. For “the Lord chastens the one He loves,673 and He chastises every son He receives. If you+ do not experience chastening like everyone else, then you+ are illegitimate children and not true sons.” Let this example of God be well weighed, for it is of great weight. Who can better tell what kind of dealing is fittest for children than God? Who can better nurture children than God? Who more truly aims at and secures the good of children than God? Indeed, who is more tender toward children than God? If God, the Father of spirits, deals like this with his children in wisdom and love, fathers of the flesh must not think to show wisdom or love by doing the contrary. Their wisdom will be folly, their love hatred. On these grounds it is taken as granted that parents (who care for the good of their children as they should) chastise their children as need requires. For it is said that the674 Lord corrects whom he loves, “as a father the son in whom he delights.” If parents did not use it, it would be no good inference to say, “as a father.” Again, it is said, as a thing beyond dispute, “we have had fathers of our flesh who corrected us.”675

The grounds of the justice of this duty concern partly the676 children corrected, and partly the parents who correct. As for children, it frees them from much evil and works much good in them.

Correction is like medicine to purge out much corruption677 which lurks in children, and like a salve to heal many wounds and sores made by their folly. In this respect Solomon says that “foolishness is bound up in the heart of a child, but the rod of correction drives it far from him”;678 and again, “Lashes and wounds scour evil, and beatings cleanse the inmost parts.”679 Because of the inward working of this medicine, correction is further said to preserve a child from death680 (“if you strike him with a rod, he will not die”), and that not only from temporal death (as many children are preserved in this way from the magistrate’s sword) but also from eternal death681 (“you will deliver his soul from hell”). Note this, you+ pampering parents, whose excessive leniency is very great cruelty. For may we not justly count him a cruel parent who would allow diseases, boils, sores and wounds to remain, increase and fester in his child, and give him no medicine, nor apply any plasters or remedies to him? Or rather, one who sees his son running into a flaming fire or deep water and would not hold him back? Just as cruel, and more cruel, are those who allow their children to run on in evil rather than correct them.

Objection. Who can bear to make his own child smart and to put him to pain?

Answer. The future fruit is to be considered more than the present pain. Potions, pills and corrosives are nauseating, bitter and painful; but because there is a necessity of using them, and great injury is prevented by their use, wise parents will not refrain from them because of the bitterness and pain that is felt. The apostle fitly answers that objection in this way: “No chastening682 seems enjoyable at the time, but painful. Later on, however, it yields a harvest of righteousness and peace.” This may be applied to parents’ corrections as well as to God’s.

The good which correction brings to children is noted by Solomon in this and similar phrases: “A rod of correction imparts wisdom.”683 For it makes children observe what is good and what evil, what is commendable and what blameworthy, and accordingly to do the good and leave the evil, which is a great point of wisdom.

Objection. Instruction will do this better.

Answer. Instruction may give them more knowledge, but it is correction which brings them to practice what they know, which is the684 chief point of wisdom.

As for parents, due correction of their children both frees them from many harms and also brings them685 much quiet.

1. It spares them much trouble. For many admonitions, often repeated and driven home again and again, will not make many children heed wholesome and good advice as much as a little correction will. They are much more sensitive to a smart than to words.

2. It prevents much grief, shame and vexation. For “a foolish son brings grief to his father and bitterness to her who bore him.”686 But it is687 “the rod of correction” that drives foolishness away, and so prevents that grief and bitterness.

3. It frees them from the guilt of their children’s sin, so that they are not accessories to it, as Eli688 was. For correction is the last remedy that a parent can use. If he can do no good by that, it is presumed that he has done his utmost; and so, though the child dies in his sin, yet the parent has delivered his own soul.

The quiet which is brought to parents by correcting their children is shown by Solomon in this way: “Correct your son, and he will give you rest; he will give delight to your soul.”689 For children well nurtured, and kept in a filial awe by correction, will conduct themselves so that their parents may rest fairly at ease and not trouble themselves (as they do with children left to their liberty). Indeed, like trees well pruned and ground well tilled, they will bring forth pleasant and abundant fruit; and so their parents will have just cause to rejoice in them.

§. 47. A direction to parents in correcting their children.

To use this biting corrosive of correction well, parents must have regard to the matter for which they correct, and to their manner of correcting.

With respect to the matter, these three things must be noted.690

1. That they are sure a fault has been committed, so that there is just cause for correcting; otherwise more harm than good will come of it. If a corrosive is laid where there is no sore, it will make one. If correction is unjustly given, it may provoke to wrath, but will do little good. This is the point in which earthly fathers are blamed and shown to be unlike God,691 because many times they correct “at their own pleasure,” which is a point of great injustice.

2. That the fault is made known to the child corrected, and he is clearly convicted of it. Correction must be for instruction, which it cannot be unless the child knows why he is corrected; for if he does not know his fault, it is all one to him as if he were corrected for no fault. God proceeded like this at the first with the serpent,692 with Eve, and with Adam. So judges proceed in punishing wrongdoers. Indeed, so men will deal with a dog. Should they not much more do so with a child?

3. That the faults are especially such as the parents can show their children (at least if the children are of enough discretion) to be against God’s word, such as swearing, lying, pilfering and the like. For 1. These are the most dangerous faults, and therefore to be purged out more carefully. 2. In this way the child corrected will be the more clearly convicted of his fault, will condemn himself the more, and will bear the correction more contentedly.

With respect to the manner of correcting, four general and four693 particular rules are to be observed.

The general rules are these.

1. An eye must be kept on God’s manner of correcting his children, and in particular on God’s correcting of the parent himself. No better general direction can be given, for God’s pattern is a perfect rule.

2. Prayer must be made by parents for themselves and for their children: for themselves, to be directed in doing it; for their children, to be bettered by it. So good physicians will do in giving medicine. Prayer is to be used in all duties, and especially in this. For a parent is apt, partly through his own intemperate anger and partly through the child’s impatience, to fall into one extreme or the other. This is not to require of all that whenever they take up the rod they go and make a solemn prayer, but that they lift up the heart for direction and blessing.

3. Correction must be given in love. “Do everything694 in love”; much more this, which carries an appearance of anger and hatred. In love parents will give medicine to their children, and splint a joint if need be. God corrects his children in love;695 so must parents. Love will make them do it with tenderness and compassion.

4. Correction must be given in a mild mood, when the feelings696 are well ordered and not disordered by anger, rage, fury and other such passions. Disturbed passions cast a mist before the understanding, so that a man cannot discern what is enough and what is too much. When anger is stirred, correction must be put off. God corrects in measure.

The particular rules are these.

1. Due order must be kept. Correction by word must go before correction by the rod. “I rebuke and discipline,”697 says the Lord. In this way a parent will show that he takes no delight in striking his child, but that it is necessity that forces him to it. In this way a parent shows himself like God, “who does not willingly afflict,” Lam 3:33. Physicians, when they give strong medicine, will give a preparative first; rebuke may serve as a preparative. Good and compassionate surgeons will try all other means before they come to lancing and searing.

2. Due regard must be had to the one corrected. If he is young and tender, lighter correction must be used. Solomon often mentions a rod as most fitting for a child, for that is the lightest correction. So if the child is of a pliable and well-disposed nature, soon checked, the correction must be moderated accordingly. If he is well grown, and is also headstrong and stubborn, the correction may be more severe.

3. Due regard must be had to the fault. Sins directly698 against God, open, notorious, scandalous sins, known sins, sins often committed, in which they have grown up and of which they have gotten a habit, are to be corrected with greater severity.

4. In correcting his child’s faults, a parent must look at his own; so more compassion will be worked in him.

§. 48. Of parents’ too much indulgence.

Contrary to this duty of correcting are two extremes.

  1. Too much leniency.
  2. Too much severity.

Many so pamper their children that they will allow them699 to run into any misbehavior rather than correct them. They cannot bear to hear their children cry, and therefore their children must be humored in all their whims and evil desires. These parents bring shame on themselves and harm on their children; for God is often forced to correct such children. God’s chastisements are heavy, and they often fall on parent and child both, as appears by the judgment on Eli and his sons. For such parents make themselves accessories to their children’s sins, and also to the judgments laid on their children. God says of such parents that they honor their children above God. It is therefore a foolish indulgence which makes parents regard neither God’s honor nor their own or their children’s safety.

Mothers for the most part offend in this. They are so far from performing this duty themselves that they are much offended with their husbands if the husbands do it. And to proclaim their folly to all the world, they cannot commit their children to a tutor or schoolmaster without a strict charge that he not correct them.

Objection. Correction makes children dolts and blockheads.

Answer. If God’s Spirit deserves more credence than such foolish women, that objection is utterly false; for we heard700 before how correction gives wisdom and drives out foolishness.

2. Objection. Mothers may be borne with all the more in this, because they carried their children with long trouble and brought them forth with great labor.

Answer. That may be a good motive for them to seek the true good of their children, so that their trouble and labor may not be in vain; but not to uphold their children in the broad way that leads to destruction.

§. 49. Of parents’ too much severity in correcting their children.

Those who offend in the other extreme, of severity, are, of the701 two, the more heartless parents. They offend directly against the first branch of this text (Do not provoke to wrath). Nothing provokes more than immoderate severity. For

1. It shows no love in the parent, but rather hatred, or at least wrath and other such disordered feelings.

2. It does not soften the child’s heart, but rather hardens it.702

3. It makes him dull and numb, and utterly perverts the right and true end of correction.

4. It often makes a child think of doing some injury to his parent or to himself.

So that parents may take all the more heed of this extreme, I will briefly note in what ways excess in severity is shown.

It is shown when correction is given

1. For no fault. In this case, however light the correction is, it is too severe.

2. For small faults, in wrath and fury. Though the stripes are few and light, yet the parent’s behavior is too much severity.

3. To children who are young and tender, or soft, mild and well-disposed, as if they were older and the most obstinate and perverse that could be.

4. Too often, for everything done amiss; whereas parents703 should seem not to see or hear many things which they do see and hear.

5. Too hard, so that the child is lamed, or hurt in some way so that he will feel it as long as he lives.

649. III. The means of nurture.

650. νουθεσία. See Treatise 1, §. 120.

651. παιδεία. See Treatise 1, §. 119.

652. Annuncia, praecipe, impera, suade eis, etc. Aug. de salut. docum. cap. 29. [Declare, enjoin, command, persuade them, etc.]

653. Eccl 12:11.
