Parents Directing Children into Adulthood

The Sixth Treatise: Of Parents · §§. 50–70

§. 50. Of parents’ care in providing fit callings for their children.

Having laid down those duties of parents which especially concern the childhood of children, I proceed to set out those which concern their riper years, when they are to be placed out in the world.

Here we must note

  1. The kinds of those duties.
  2. The means of performing them.

The kinds may be brought under two heads.

1. Providing fit places and callings for them in which to exercise their gifts.

2. Providing fit marriages for them.

We heard704 before how children were to be trained up and fitted for some good calling even in their childhood. Now further, when by virtue of a good education they are able to discharge the functions and duties of a calling, and are well grown up in years, so that it is time they should be set to some particular calling:

Parents ought to provide fit callings for their children, and fit705 places for them to exercise the gifts which they have gained by nature or education. For example, if children have been brought up in learning, parents must use what lawful and honorable means they can to settle them in such a place and course that they may profess and exercise their gifts, according to their different kinds, whether divinity, law, medicine, or the like. Or if they have been brought up in any trade, parents must provide that they may set up (as we say) and exercise their trade. The first two children that were ever born of woman, Cain706 and Abel, were placed out in different callings; and without doubt their places were so ordered by their parents. The same may be gathered from these phrases: “Esau became … a man of the field, while Jacob … dwelt in tents.”707708 It is noted of Samuel that he made his two sons judges. Had they been as faithful in using their places well as their father was careful in providing them, they might have lived well themselves and done much good to others. Jesse, having many sons, took care of this: for709 he sent his three eldest sons to the war and placed them in a soldier’s course of life;710 his youngest he made a shepherd, which in those days and places was a calling of greater esteem than it is with us now.

1. In this way they will make use of the ability which they have gained by711 their parents’ provident care and their own diligence; otherwise that ability may soon be lost. Does not daily experience show that many who were well trained up by their parents in learning, so far that they were fit to enter the ministry, have in time, for lack of a place and employment, so forgotten everything that it is as if they had never been trained up in learning? And so it is in other fields of learning.

2. In this way they come to do much more good in church or commonwealth. Until men are placed in distinct callings, they are only being fitted and prepared for the times to come. I do not deny that both church and commonwealth may reap much benefit from the pains and labor of the young who are being trained up under others. But those are most strictly counted members of the church and commonwealth, and active instruments of their good, who have some particular, distinct calling by which they do good to others.

3. In this way they come to live by their own means, and to be able to relieve others as well. All the time of their education they are commonly at the expense of others; or at least, though they may gain much by their pains, the gain goes to others. They themselves for the most part have only a bare maintenance, food, drink and clothing (as we say); they have little to lay up for themselves for the time to come, or to give to others for the present.

4. In this way they come to train up others for the times to come, as they themselves were trained up. By this a continual and perpetual succession of all kinds of callings is preserved from one time to the next, and so family, church and commonwealth are upheld and maintained. In a short time all callings and functions would utterly decay if a continual supply were not made in this way.

§. 51. Direction for parents in providing callings for their children.

Two special cautions are to be observed by parents in712 providing callings for their children.

1. That the callings provided are such as their children have been trained up for, and are in some measure fitted and able to perform the duties of: as to provide a minister’s place for him who has been brought up in learning and has studied divinity; and so in other callings, such that their children may be masters of their craft in them. In this way their children will do all the more good in them, both to others and to themselves. Bezalel and Oholiab were chosen to build the tabernacle because they were filled with skill to do all kinds of work.713 Likewise the servants of Hiram were chosen to cut cedar trees for the temple, because among the Jews there was no one714 as skilled at cutting timber as the Sidonians. Pharaoh was careful to have capable men put in charge of his livestock.715

2. That such means are used for providing a calling that parents, in using them, may call on God in faith for his blessing. Those who are brought by lawful means into a calling for which they are fitted are set in it by God, as is implied by this phrase, “as God has called each one,” etc. A lawful entrance into a calling is a matter of great importance. He who enters in this way may, in rightly using it, cast himself on God’s blessing and expect it with strong confidence, saying as the prophet did, “Lord, I have not pushed myself forward; You716 know.”

§. 52. Of the extremes contrary to a parent’s lawful care in providing fit callings for his children.717

The extreme in the defect, contrary to a parent’s provident care in providing a fit calling, is a careless neglect of children after they are well educated, leaving them to fend for themselves.718 It is noted of the birds of prey that have sharp talons that as soon as they see their young ones able to fly, they flap and beat them with their wings and drive them out of their nests, and after that take no further care of them. We must not be like such cruel birds: reason and religion teach us otherwise. Good education is a good duty, but not a parent’s whole duty. Stopping here may make all the earlier care and pains of little use.

Objection. This should be left to God’s providence.

Answer. Means rightly used are subordinate to God’s providence, and by them God shows his providence and brings his counsel to pass. To neglect the means is to thwart and cross the divine providence. It is therefore well done to rely on God’s providence, but ill done to neglect the means of bringing it about. God’s blessing is best discerned in the use of means.

The extreme in the excess is a wrongheaded greediness in719 parents to bring their children into a calling. This shows itself in two ways.

1. When they do not care how fit their children are for the720 place, so long as it is a place of gain and honor. Experience shows that this is the bane of church and commonwealth. Through it the same thing happens in the body politic as would happen in a natural body: if the hand should take it upon itself to see, or the leg to hear, or the foot to taste, what could be expected from that but the ruin of the body? Tradesmen often ruin themselves, their families and their relatives by taking up trades in which they have no skill, or of which they are not masters. The more excellent the calling is, the more harm is done by this greedy wrongheadedness. This extreme is as much worse than the former as it is worse to do much harm than to do no good.

2. When they make no conscience of the means which721 they use to bring their children into callings, but get what they want by unlawful means: as by simony to obtain a church office (from which perjury also often follows), or by bribery to obtain a public office.

These crooked means take away the difference between fit and unfit persons, for the most unfit there are may buy a place with money. Besides, though children are ever so fit for these callings, there is little hope of any blessing from God when the first entrance is made without him, indeed against his will and word. Who can think that God has placed such a one in his place? If God has not placed him, with what faith can he seek a blessing? With what hope can he expect a blessing? By this means much terror is brought on many men’s consciences, and they are often in great perplexity, not knowing whether it is best for them to keep or to give up the722 place.

But, to settle that doubt by the way: if one who has entered unlawfully is fit to perform the work of his place, it is then safest for him to seek pardon for the former offense and reconciliation with God, and, on true and unfeigned repentance, to keep the place (if at least the law under which he lives confirms him in it), and to be all the more faithful in discharging its duties.

§. 53. Of parents’ care in providing fit marriages for their children.

God has further laid a charge on parents to provide marriages723 for their children. For this is what the prophet says to parents in the name of the Lord: “Take wives for your+ sons and give your+ daughters in marriage.”724 And the apostle says this: “If anyone thinks he is acting improperly toward his virgin, if she is past the prime of her youth, and need so requires, let them marry.”725 This direction was given in times of persecution, when because of the present necessity it was better not to marry. If, then, a parent ought to take care (when need requires) to provide a marriage for his daughter, much more ought he to do so in times of peace. Holy parents commended by the Holy Spirit have been careful to perform this duty, such as Abraham,726 Isaac,727 Naomi,728 and others; indeed, Hagar729 had learned this duty in Abraham’s house. But the perfect pattern (which surpasses all other examples) is that of730 God himself, who provided a fit match for his son Adam.731

1. Children must not marry without their parents’ consent (as was732 shown before); parents therefore must take care to provide for them in time.

2. Parents stand in God’s place to their children; they must therefore take on themselves this care of God’s.

3. Marriage is the means which the Lord has sanctified to keep our bodies chaste and undefiled. As parents therefore desire to keep their children from uncleanness and pollution, they must take care that this means is used. Not only holy apostles but also733 heathen philosophers, and that by the light of nature, have found this to be the fittest course.

4. This is also a means both to734 increase the commonwealth and to735 preserve a holy seed, and to establish new families, and so to continue the parents’ own houses and name.

§. 54. Direction to parents in providing marriages.

Two cautions are to be observed by parents in providing marriages for their children.

1. That the match which they provide is suitable. So God said when he was about to provide a match for Adam: “I will736 make for him a suitable helper.” Therefore737 the match provided must not be too near of kin, of a contrary religion, of too unequal an age, or of too great a disparity in condition. These things will hinder love and cause disdain and hatred of one another.

2. Though the match may seem suitable in the parent’s eyes, yet he must not force his child into it. Could a fitter match have been found for Rebekah than Isaac? Yet Rebekah’s family738 asked her consent. I do not deny that parents may use every kind of fair means to move their children to yield to what they see is good for them. But if they cannot move them to yield, they are to refer the matter to God, and not force them against their children’s minds. When God had made a most suitable match for Adam, he “brought her to him,” namely to see how Adam would like her. For the closest bond of all is between man and wife: a man must “leave his father and mother and739 be united to his wife”; man and wife must always live together. There is great reason, therefore, that at their first joining together there should be a mutual liking for one another, so that there is not a perpetual dislike ever after. And though the authority of parents ought in this case to be inviolable, yet a middle course is to be held, so that the parties may join themselves together willingly, with mutual consent.

§. 55. Of the extremes contrary to parents’ care in providing fit marriages for their children.

The extreme in the defect is when parents carelessly let their children pass the prime of their youth, and never consider whether need requires that they should marry or not. Their children may wait long enough before such parents seek out a match for them, unless one is brought to them; and when one is offered, though it is ever so fit, yet unless they can make some advantage of it for themselves, they will hardly agree to it. So they drive their children to seek out marriages for themselves and to make them without their parents’ consent, or else to live in discontent,740 if not in uncleanness. Through the carelessness of parents in this respect children are often made a prey to the devil, and for this parents will give an account to God on the day of judgment.

The extreme in the excess is741 when parents, out of a covetous desire to get great and rich matches for their children, marry them before they are of the age of discretion to like or dislike, to know what is suitable or unsuitable, or able to perform even the essential duties of marriage. Such unlawful marriages seldom prosper.

Those offend in a like excess who, for outward advantages, match their children with such as are by nature unfit for marriage, with idiots, with742 idolaters, with profane persons, or with anyone at all, for they do not care whom. And if their children do not like these matches, they will do all in their power to force them into them. Many evils ordinarily follow from such marriages, such as utter dislike between husband and wife, continual complaining of one another, seeking after divorce or some other separation, wishing, indeed plotting, one another’s death. Parents, being the cause of them, make themselves accessories to all these evils.

§. 56. Of parents providing capital for the callings and marriages of their children.

A special outward means by which parents may be better able to provide fit callings and marriages for their children is to lay up beforehand some capital, or a sufficient portion, for their children. This is included in that general provision of which the apostle counts the man who neglects it “worse than an unbeliever.”743 But it is noted more expressly in these words, “parents ought to lay up for their children,”744 and commended in Abraham’s745 example.

While children are under their parents they have no means to lay up anything for themselves, for all their service is for their parents. But because of the times in which we live, it is needful for setting up in a good calling, and for obtaining a fit match, that children have some capital and portion. It falls therefore on the parents, and it is their duty, to provide it.

Objection. Christ forbids laying up treasures on earth.746

Answer. If the aim of that place is rightly noted, it will appear that Christ does not there forbid the thing itself wholly, but

1. The mind of him who lays up: namely when it is full of fretting and distrustful thoughts, fearing that in time to come he will not have enough. To this purpose Christ sets forth God’s providence over the birds and747 lilies.

2. The manner of laying up, when temporal things are preferred to spiritual and heavenly ones. Therefore he adds this precept: “But lay up … treasures in heaven,” etc.748

3. The measure, when men never think they have laid up enough, but scrape together whatever they can come by, justly or unjustly, and save more than is needed, keeping back even necessary things from themselves and others, to make a great store and portion for their children. The word for749 treasuring up (which Christ uses there) implies an immoderate measure.

Among other needful cautions to be observed by parents in laying up for their children, these three are especially to be noted.

1. That they come justly by what they lay up, and lay nothing toward a child’s portion which is in any way unjustly gotten; for “ill-gotten treasures profit nothing.”750 They may turn out to be a fire to consume the parents themselves, their children, their house and their whole posterity.

2. That they do not covet too much to make their children rich, and for that purpose live poorly and shabbily themselves, indeed deprive themselves of many necessities. This is an egregious751 piece of folly, which Solomon strongly rebukes.

3. That all needful duties of charity to the poor, and of justice to the church and commonwealth, are performed, and that the pretext of laying up for children hinders none of these.

§. 57. Of the extremes contrary to a parent’s providing portions for his children.

The extremes contrary to the aforesaid duty are these:

1. When parents live to the utmost extent of their means, and from time to time spend all their revenues or all their gains, and so are scarcely able to make ends meet at quarter day or at the year’s end. What capital or portion can they lay up for their children?

2. When parents live above their means, and spend their ordinary gains or revenues dissolutely, and are forced to run into debt for other necessary affairs. Many are so far from helping their children in this way that they are a main hindrance to them, urging their eldest son especially, who is their heir, to be bound as surety for them, and so lay such a burden on his back that (to use the common phrase) they make it crack.

3. When parents have enough for themselves and their children, and yet dote so covetously on their wealth that they will not spend a penny to help them into a calling and marriage, but say they are keeping it all for them. What a wretched and foolish disposition this is, that they should always lay up more and more for their children, and yet refuse to give them any part of it in their greatest need, when it might be of the greatest benefit to them! God often deals with such covetous misers and thwarts their purposes by making strangers enjoy what they greedily hoarded up.

§. 58. Of parents’ last speech to their children.

The last duty which parents owe to their children is when they cease to be parents, that is, when they are going out of this world. Their duty at that time, in general, is to do what lies in their power so that it may go well with their children after their departure. Both752 the reasons often urged by the Holy Spirit to stir up parents to obey God, taken from the reach of God’s blessing (in this kind of phrase, “blessed are his children after him”)753 and God’s754 promises made to that purpose, prove as much.

For the better performing of this duty, three general points, tending both to the temporal and to the spiritual good of children, are to be observed, and two particular points tending most to their worldly welfare.

The three general points are these.

  1. Good direction.
  2. Faithful prayer.
  3. A wise choice of some friends to be as parents to them.

1. For755 direction. When parents see their time drawing near, they ought to pass on some wise and wholesome precepts to their children, the better to direct them in their Christian course. So did Isaac756 and Jacob.757

Objection. These patriarchs had an extraordinary spirit of prophecy, and by virtue of it foretold to their children things to come.

Answer.758 They bore a double role: one of a prophet, the other of a father. As prophets, they had an extraordinary spirit; as parents, they performed an ordinary duty. By their extraordinary spirit they foretold things to come; the ordinary duty which they performed was to direct their children how to conduct themselves in those times to come. For their prophecies were not only predictions but also instructions, to direct and teach them what to do. What they did by an extraordinary spirit in extraordinary things, we must do in ordinary duties by the ordinary spirit of understanding and wisdom which the Lord gives us. But the direction which Isaac759 gave to Jacob when he sent him to Laban was no extraordinary prophecy; nor was the direction which David,760 when he was old, gave to Solomon, and again761 when he lay on his deathbed. Now these things are written in this way for our imitation. And there is great reason to imitate those holy men in these things. For

1. The words of a dying parent are commonly the most regarded: his last words make a deep impression762 (Joseph’s brothers press this on him). If ever, therefore, there is a fitting time for a parent to give good instructions to his children, it is when parents are about to depart from their children for good.

2. In this way a parent will show his true love and his earnest desire for his children’s good. For now they cannot think that he seeks his own ease and profit more than their good, as at other times some are ready to say of their parents’ instructions and admonitions, “Our parents know what is good for themselves.”

That the last words of parents may be delivered to their children all the more seasonably and763 profitably, they must note on the one side what evils their children are most prone to, what temptations they are most assaulted with, what snares they are most likely to fall into; and on the other side, what virtues and graces they most need, and where they fail most; and they must order and frame their last words accordingly. Note as a pattern in this Isaac’s764 counsel to Jacob when he sent him to Laban and thought he would never see him again, and David’s765 to his son Solomon.

§. 59. Of parents’ last blessing to their children.

II. Concerning the prayers of parents for their children, I noted766 before that this is a general duty never to be omitted. Yet here I mention it again in particular, because a parent’s blessing consists especially in it, and this is the most proper time for parents to bestow a blessing on their children, as Isaac,767 Jacob,768 David,769 and others did. Let parents therefore, as they commit their own souls into God’s hand, so commit their children to God’s grace and blessing. God’s providence is a good inheritance: many children prosper exceedingly by it, though they have only small outward means; whereas others, who have great means used for their good, come to ruin, God’s curse following them. Now no means can be thought of to obtain God’s blessing, or to hold back his curse, like the faithful prayers of parents for their children, especially when parents are leaving their children and going to God.

§. 60. Of parents’ care to entrust their children to some faithful friends.

III. The third general point, choosing some faithful friends to entrust their children to, is especially on behalf of those who are not of sufficient age and discretion to look after themselves, or after the weighty affairs which belong to them. The friends who are chosen in this case ought to be such as the parents themselves have found by good experience to be honorable, wise, faithful and loving to them and theirs; and these the parents are to set in their own place for the good of their children. David used this means when he was old, on behalf770 of his son Solomon. Many children have found much help by it. Such friends may make up well for the departure of parents. They are all the more needful the more unstable and unbridled youth is, and the less able children are to help and guide themselves.

§. 61. Of parents’ neglect of their children for the time to come.

Contrary to a parent’s provident care for the good of his children after his departure is the carelessness of parents for the time to come. They think the world is gone with them when they are gone, and therefore they will take no thought for the times that will come after them, as if it were enough for everyone to look to his own time. There may seem to be more self-love in such parents than love of their children, because their care ends with their own time and does not extend to the time and continuance of their children. That is why not a word of direction and exhortation comes out of their mouths to their children when they are departing; there is no blessing that they will leave behind them; no friends will be appointed by them to be as parents to their children. “Let God provide,” they say. But where matters are referred to God’s providence without the use of those means which God has warranted and commended by his word, there can be little hope that God will take care of what is entrusted to him in that way. Such men do not depend on God’s providence in faith, but make the very name of it a pretext to cast off that care which God requires of them as a bounden duty. As there is little love of their children in such parents, so there is less zeal for God’s glory. For a parent’s care for his children’s welfare, especially for their continuing to fear and serve the Lord after his own departure out of this world, is a special means of preserving the fear of God in the world and passing it on from age to age. So this neglect is a greater fault than many are aware of.

§. 62. Of parents making a will before they die.

The two particular things to be observed by parents for showing their provident care over their children for the time to come, even after their departure, especially with respect to their worldly estate, are these:

  1. That they make a will.
  2. That they leave their estates to their children.

1. It has been an ancient and commendable practice, both among771 God’s people and among others who have been guided by common civility, that those who have any estate, when they grow old or sick, or have any occasion to expect death, make their last will and testament. This is set forth in the Old Testament under this phrase (“Put your house in order”). It is a duty expressly772 commanded by God, and not without good reason. For

1. A parent’s will is a special means of settling peace among his children after his departure, and of making them content with the allowance which he has set out for them, because by the will they know it was their father’s pleasure that they should have such and such a portion. If disputes should arise, a will is still a means for the law to settle them quickly, without any tedious and costly lawsuits. For the apostle takes it as a settled case that “no man cancels or adds anything to a man’s will.”773

2. After a parent has made his will, he may settle himself more quietly for heavenly contemplation and preparation for death; think of such good instructions as are most fit to give his children as his farewell; await the moment of his dissolution more willingly; and submit himself more patiently to the very stroke of death.

In performing this duty, a man must both observe a fit time774 and take good advice. The fit time is while his understanding is sound and his memory perfect, so that he may call to mind his debts, what he owes and what is owed to him, as well as what goods he has to bestow, and may order his estate with discretion and wisdom. And because his true meaning may be perverted through the quibbles which many unscrupulous lawyers and others are likely to raise, it is fitting to have the advice of those who can express his meaning in such distinct words and phrases that they will be beyond challenge. Matters of weight are to be managed wisely.

§. 63. Of neglecting to make a will.

Contrary to this is the daily practice of too many parents, who are not willing to make any will at all; or else, in vain hope that they may live longer, and, when they are sick, in the notion that they may recover, or at least keep the use of their understanding and memory longer, they put off making their will until it is too late. And so they die without a will, or make such a will as gives more ground for lawsuits than if they had made none at all: either because there is doubt whether he who made it had his understanding and memory or not, or because his will is so abrupt and ambiguous that his meaning cannot be known. The harms that follow from these neglects775 are many, such as:

  1. Disgrace to the deceased.
  2. Quarrels among his surviving children.
  3. Squandering a great part, if not the whole, of his estate in lawsuits.
  4. Depriving many creditors of the debts due to them.

The reason which makes many put off making their will is a foolish notion that if a man’s will is once made, then he must die at once. But what ground do men have for any such notion? If sickness grows on a man, his mind is unsettled as long as his will is unmade; and his mind being unsettled, the medicine given to him cannot work so well, so that his death may be hastened all the more for not making a will. Besides, if his speech fails before his understanding, the thought that he will now die without a will may so trouble him that his departure will be very unquiet and distressing.

§. 64. Of parents leaving their estate to their children when they die.

It was776 shown before that parents were to lay up a portion for their children for their entrance into a calling and marriage. There is a further duty required of them when they are going out of the world, namely that they leave their whole estate777 to their children. (When I say whole, I do not exclude works of charity, nor payment of debts, which is a point of justice; but I include more than is given as portions or capital in their lifetime.) That estate especially which parents have received from their forebears they are most bound to leave to their children. It is expressly recorded that “Abraham left everything778 he owned to Isaac.” God’s law provided for this among the Jews, for a man was not allowed to sell his land so as to cut it off from779 his posterity. This was what made Naboth refuse to sell his vineyard to Ahab, as his answer implies: “The Lord forbid that I780 should give you the inheritance of my fathers.” Because it was the inheritance of his fathers, that is, he had received it from them, he thought it unlawful to deprive his children of it. This phrase (“if we are children, then we are heirs”) takes it as a granted781 truth that children have a right to their parents’ estate; and if they have a right to it, they must not be deprived of it.

God gives wealth to parents only for their lifetime, and in that time they are only like guardians of God’s children, and are accountable to God. So they do not have an absolute power to do with it what they will; they must use it, keep it and leave it according to the directions of the great Lord and master.

To this end parents must order their manner of living according782 to the portion which the Lord has appointed to them and by his providence bestowed on them. They must (as the proverb says) cut their coat according to their cloth. Of the two, it is much better for parents to live below their means than above them. This is provided that they neglect no duty of charity or justice, nor through miserliness and stinginess behave in a way unbecoming the place in which God has set them and the means which he has bestowed on them. He who lives somewhat below his means has opportunity to lay up portions for his other children (if he has many) and to keep his inheritance whole for his eldest (besides many other good works of charity, as God gives occasion), which he who lives above his means cannot do.

§. 65. Of the harms which improvident parents bring their children into after their death.

Contrary to this branch of a parent’s provident care are many courses of improvident parents. For

1. Some parents squander and waste all their estate in their own lifetime, making it end with themselves. They are unworthy to receive any inheritance from their ancestors. Their fault is double:

1. In spending prodigally beyond their means.

2. In wronging their children and depriving them of their right. For particular persons succeeding one another are only like separate links of a continuing family, which are joined one to another by God’s providence. This chain is not to be broken at any man’s pleasure; but for its preservation, what has been received from the predecessors must be left to the successors.

2. Others leave their estate to their children, but so burdened with debts, bonds, recognizances and statute bonds that their children would be better without it than with it. For having it makes them live at a corresponding rate and brings many burdens on them. Besides, the debts in which they are bound make them servants to their creditors,783 and in time they will be forced to sell everything, or lie in prison like captives.

3. Others, though they do not deal so harshly with their children, still deal too harshly with them by stripping and plundering their inheritance as much as they can. They will not refrain from any present gain they can make, though it tends ever so much to the prejudice and damage of their children after them: like those who cut down all the timber and wood they can, and take all the heart out of their land.

4. Among these may be counted those parents who by sheer negligence allow things to go to decay for lack of timely repairs. So it comes about that damage which in the parents’ time might have been prevented by laying out a few shillings cannot be made good with many pounds.

5. Those also who do not care in their lifetime to clear the titles of the things which they leave to their children, but leave everything so unsettled and open to lawsuits that it often costs the children more in lawsuits to maintain the inheritance their parents leave them than the inheritance is worth; and after all their pains and cost they lose the inheritance too, whereas the parent, who knew more than the child can, might with small pains and expense have settled and cleared everything well.

These are harms that many children have been brought into by the improvidence of their parents. They are all the more to be made known, so that those who come after may be the more provident for their children.

§. 66. Of parents’ impartial regard for all their children.

So much for the duties of parents. The persons to whom those duties are to be performed must be considered distinctly.

The parties to whom parents are to perform all the aforesaid duties are expressed under this word (children), which784 has no special regard to priority of birth, to bodily constitution, to the parent’s affection, or any such thing, as if only firstborn, well-formed, beautiful, darling, or such children were meant; but all who are begotten and born of parents, all their children, are meant. From this I observe that parents ought to have an impartial regard for all their children, and perform their duty to all without distinction and equally. For proof of this we have God’s pattern, who counts all his children dear or beloved children. The Greek word translated785 dear is very emphatic: it is strictly applied to an only child. The Seventy who translated the Hebrew Bible into Greek render with this word that phrase only son:786 for where in Hebrew it is said to Abraham, “take your son, your only one,” they translate it, “take your son, your dear one,” or your beloved one. Other Greek authors also apply the same word to an only child, and indeed to an only eye: as when a man has only one eye, they call it a beloved eye. This word, then, shows that God so regards all his children as if all were only one, all a firstborn, all a darling child. So rare a virtue is this impartial regard (rare in its excellence, rare also in its scarcity) that throughout Scripture I can scarcely find a perfect pattern of it787 among the sons of men. Many examples of the contrary may be given, as we shall hear later. But the rarer it is, the more we must strive after it, so that we may resemble God’s fatherhood.

1. All our children come from our own flesh and788 body. Why then should we regard one child above another, any more than we do one eye or one ear above another? We are as tender over one as over another, though it may be that we have more use of one than of another.

2. All our children are committed to us alike by God: the same precepts and directions are given for all alike, and the same account is to be given for all. If a king should commit many of his children to one nurse, would he not be offended (and justly) if she should put such a difference between them, through a foolish partiality, as to favor some and neglect others?

§. 67. Of parents preferring a dutiful child to a disobedient child.

Objection. What if one child is more pious toward God and parent, and another more rebellious? May a parent not regard that one more than this one?

1. Answer. He may take notice of their different conduct, and accordingly reward the one and punish the other, and yet keep an equal desire of doing good to both of them alike. For punishing the rebellious child is a parent’s duty, an evidence of love, and a means of doing him good.

2. Answer. It is no partiality in a parent to like grace and goodness in a child, and for the sake of grace and goodness to love his child all the more; as also, for impiety and obstinacy in rebellion, to have his heart the more estranged from his child. This is rather a virtue in a parent. Partiality is when one child is preferred to another out of ulterior and improper motives.

§. 68. Of the prerogative of the firstborn son.

Question. May a parent not prefer his firstborn child and heir to his other children?

Answer. We must distinguish between a father’s settling of his estate on his children and the ordering of his affection toward them. A parent’s affection, his care for their good education, his desire for their true good, and his faithful prayers to God may be as great toward his younger children as toward his eldest son and heir, and yet he may bestow the greatest patrimony on the heir; which is no partiality.

2. Question. Is it then just and fair that the eldest son should have a greater patrimony than any of the rest?

Answer. It is most just and fair. For

1. God has appointed it so: indeed789 he made it one of the prerogatives of the firstborn to have a double portion. On this ground Joseph,790 who was the firstborn of the true wife, had a double portion; and as a testimony of this his posterity made two tribes.

2. The laws of all nations ordain as much.

3. Our law gives the whole inheritance of freeholds to the eldest son, and in that respect it is due to him. For in civil and temporal matters this rule is true: we live by law. I take it to be a matter of conscience for a parent to leave to every child what is due to him by law. Nor is it without good reason that the law ordains that a parent’s whole estate of freehold land should descend to the heir. For

1. There is an excellence in the firstborn, as is evident from Jacob’s words to his eldest son: “You are my firstborn, my might, and the beginning of my strength, excelling in honor, excelling in power.”791 And for this reason792 God took the firstborn as his own.

2. By this means houses and families are upheld and continued from age to age. How needful it is for the establishment of a commonwealth that families should be continued in this way is evident both by experience, to all who have even half an eye to see where the stability of a commonwealth lies, and also by the many laws which God ordained among the Jews for this purpose, such as

1. That793 no land should be wholly cut off from a family.

2. That794 if anyone was forced through poverty to sell his land, his next of kin was to buy it.

3. That795 if a man who had sold his land could by no means redeem it again, he was to have possession of it again in the Year of Jubilee.

4. That796 if daughters were heirs they should not marry outside their father’s tribe; and this reason is given: “so that every Israelite will possess the inheritance of his fathers.”

Objection. By leaving the whole inheritance to the eldest, he may be made a gentleman and all the others beggars.

Answer. For this reason parents ought to be all the more provident for their other children: in training them up to callings, or laying up portions, or settling other estates on them besides the main inheritance, or in arranging that sufficient portions are raised out of the eldest son’s inheritance, in case God takes the parents away before they have otherwise provided for their children.

From this answer a third reason may be gathered to show that it is a beneficial law for the commonwealth that the heir should have all the land. For this law makes parents more careful in training up their younger sons to various callings which are profitable to a commonwealth. If every child were to have a part of his father’s lands, they would all depend on it so much that none of them would apply themselves to such callings as are means of men’s livelihood.

§. 69. Of parents’ partiality toward some children.

Contrary to the aforesaid duty of a parent’s equal regard for all his children is partiality in fathers and mothers, shown in various ways. For

1. Many parents have their darling children, to whom so797 much affection is shown that in comparison none is shown to the others. While some are hugged in the bosom, others are neglected as if they were none of their own, but born out of wedlock. The heartlessness of the eagle is noted in this respect: she flaps and drives one of her young ones out of the nest, and feeds only the other as her own. Many evils come from such partiality in parents, such as these:

1. Such parents give those who observe it occasion to suspect that the children who are so little regarded are not their own.

2. They cause envy, malice and much contention to arise among children. “When Joseph’s brothers saw that their father798 loved him more than any of them, they hated him and could not speak peaceably to him.”

3. They provoke God to inflict some judgment on those children who are so pampered and preferred above the rest, so that the parents may better see their folly.

This sin of parents’ partiality is all the greater when, for outward reasons, they prefer wicked and ungodly children to godly and gracious ones. Isaac failed greatly in this, for “he loved Esau”799 (a800 profane wretch) because “he ate of his game.”

2. Other parents set themselves so to raise their house that all their care is to advance their eldest son, by education, by liberal allowance, and by leaving everything they have to him, and in the meantime they neglect their younger children. Though (as was noted801 before) the main inheritance may justly, without any show of partiality, be left to the heir, yet to care only for him and to neglect the others smacks strongly of partiality. It is most agreeable to natural reason that, as life is given to all802 children, so the means of maintaining life should be given to all.

3. Among partial parents may be counted those who unjustly disinherit their firstborn. For since the inheritance belongs to the firstborn by right, and they do not deserve to be disinherited, it is certainly some ulterior motive or other which makes parents prefer the younger to the elder; and this is plain partiality. This kind of partiality is common in parents who have had children by different wives. Sometimes dislike of a former wife makes a father dislike the children he has by her, and through that dislike disinherit his heir by her. God gave the Jews an express law against this kind of803 partiality.

Sometimes again a grasping pursuit of advantage for themselves makes parents disinherit the rightful heir. For example, a man who has buried the mother of his firstborn hears of another woman of great wealth and courts her. She refuses because he has an heir by a former wife. To remove that obstacle, he binds himself by agreement to make the son he has by her (if he has any) his heir. On this the marriage is completed; his second wife bears a son; and for his agreement’s sake he disinherits the first heir. An unjust and unlawful practice.

§. 70. Of the causes for which the firstborn may be disinherited.

Question. May a firstborn son, then, ever be disinherited?

Answer. Yes. Scripture notes two causes for which the firstborn may be put out of the inheritance.

1. If he is illegitimate, for such a one has no good title. “The slave woman’s son will never share in the inheritance with my son,”804 says Sarah, and justly. To the same purpose the sons of Gilead’s wife say to Jephthah, “You shall have no inheritance in our father’s house,805 because you are the son of another woman.” Jotham justly blamed the men of Shechem for making Abimelech,806 the illegitimate son of Jerubbaal, king; and God’s vengeance on them for that wrong done to Jerubbaal’s legitimate children was just.

2. If he is notoriously wicked. So Reuben807 lost his birthright for committing abominable incest.

Many particular crimes are listed by the808 civil lawyers, which would take too long to recite here.

Parents Being Faithful to All under Their Care

The Sixth Treatise: Of Parents · §§. 71–79

§. 71. Of the duty of stepparents and parents-in-law.

The extent of this title (fathers) is the last thing to be809 considered. Not only natural parents themselves, but also all who are in their place, are included under it. Those who are in the place of parents are so

  1. By the bond of marriage.
  2. By nearness of blood.
  3. By voluntary appointment.

The first sort are stepparents and parents-in-law, who are counted so either by the marriage of the parents themselves or by the marriage of their children.

The man or woman who is married to a parent who had children before their marriage is in the place of a natural parent. Thus Joseph was a810 father to Jesus, and Keturah811 a mother to Isaac. So again the natural parents of a son who has married a wife, or of a daughter who is married to a husband, are in the place of parents to their son’s wife and to their daughter’s husband. Thus Jethro812 was a father to Moses, and Naomi813 a mother to Ruth.

All these are to regard their stepchildren and children-in-law (that is, the814 children of their husband or wife, or the wives of their sons and the husbands of their daughters) as their own natural children. They are to perform the duties named above according to the age and place of these children, and to seek their good in every way (except in such duties as belong in a distinctive way to natural parents, as nursing to a natural mother, and leaving the inheritance to a natural parent).

For a pattern of this, take the examples of Joseph and Naomi named above. What could natural parents do more for their own children than Joseph did for Jesus, and Naomi for Ruth? The history notes how Joseph took care to have his wife’s child815 circumcised and presented in the temple; how he816 fled from place to place to preserve the child’s life; how817 distressed he was when he thought the child was lost; how he818 brought him up in his own house. The history also notes how Naomi819 brought Ruth, her son’s wife, into her own country and kept her with herself, and820 directed her where to go, and821 what husband to take, and822 became a nurse to her child.

1. Marriage makes man and wife one flesh. In this respect823 they ought to have one mind and the same feelings, as toward each other, so jointly toward each other’s children. On the same ground the husband or wife of a child, being one flesh with the child, ought to be respected as the child is. On this ground God counts the saints his824 “beloved children,” because they are825 betrothed to his natural Son.

2. To respect the children of a husband or wife as one’s own is great evidence of entire love to that husband or wife. And to respect the husband or wife of a child is great evidence of love to the child itself. If the world’s proverb holds true (love me and love my dog), how much more true is this Christian rule: love me and love my child, or love me and love my husband, or love me and love my wife.

3. This is also a special means of kindling and preserving mutual love between a man and wife who have children by former husbands and wives, and also between parents and children.

§. 72. Of the perverse conduct of stepparents and parents-in-law toward their children.

Contrary to this is the conduct of most stepparents and parents-in-law, especially of those who are married to husbands or wives who had children before the marriage. They are so far from performing the duty named above that they rather envy the prosperity of their husbands’ and wives’ children, secretly try to hinder it all they can, and cunningly seek to turn the natural parent’s affection away from them. From this826 fearful tragedies have been made, and lamentable harms have followed. What other reason can be given for this827 than a plain instigation of the devil, who labors in this way to divide those whom God has joined together? To avoid this snare, note the harms that follow from it.

1. Such parents sin against God’s ordinance and, like Eve, lean more to Satan’s suggestion than to God’s direction.

2. They estrange hearts and affections from one another: not only from their children, but from themselves.

3. They provoke their stepchildren and children-in-law to scorn and despise them, and to do no duty to them.

From this, note into what a hell unkind stepparents and parents-in-law cast themselves. If this were duly weighed, I think they would be of another mind. But the god of this world so blinds their eyes with self-love and envy that they cannot see the harms into which they plunge themselves.

This point is all the more to be weighed because the fault rebuked here is so common, and has been all too common in every age.828 What grievous complaints have been made in former times, and are still made, by children against stepparents! From this, dreadful curses have also followed. Let widowers and widows who have children think of it seriously beforehand, and be all the more careful in taking a second or third husband or wife. And after they are married, let them beware of Satan’s snares, and let conscience of duty prevail with them more than the corruption of nature.

§. 73. Of the faults of parents toward their children’s husbands and wives.

Many parents also greatly transgress and swerve from their duty toward the husbands and wives of their children. For

1. They will show much more respect to their own children than to their children’s husbands or wives: as by coming to their daughters when their husbands are away from home, and never except then, and by sending for their sons to their house, but not for their sons’ wives.

2. In all disagreements they will take their own children’s side, even when their children are in the wrong, and show great partiality.

3. They will often give very bad advice: advising their sons to keep their wives on a short allowance, and advising their daughters not to be too subject to their husbands, and even to steal secretly from their husbands.

4. If they live with their children, they will pry so into everything their child’s husband or wife does, and show such suspicion and distrust in everything, that they cannot help causing much discord. So it often comes about that either parent and child, or husband and wife, must be parted: they cannot all live together in peace.

I note these faults in this way so that they may be avoided the more carefully.

§. 74. Of the duty of those who are in place of parents to orphans.

The next sort of those who are in place of parents are those who are next to the parents in blood and kindred, such as grandfathers, grandmothers, uncles, aunts, elder brothers or sisters, their husbands or wives, and other kinsmen.

These are commonly counted to be in the place of parents829 when God takes away natural and immediate parents from their children, so that they are parents to orphans.

The duties which were prescribed to natural parents belong to them (except those830 excepted before). Their duty is to see these orphans well educated, well placed in some good calling, well married, and (if the orphans are left without means) well provided for.

Mordecai is a worthy precedent and pattern for this kind of parent. “He had brought up … Esther, the daughter of his uncle, because she did not have a father or mother,”831 and he took her in as his own daughter. When she was taken from him, he went “to learn about Esther’s welfare and what was happening to her,”832 and833 he gave her advice from time to time on how to conduct herself. Let those who are parents to orphans take this example as a direction, and as a motive to perform the other duties prescribed to natural parents as need requires and occasion is offered.

When God by his providence takes away natural parents, he commits their orphans as a charge to the next of kin, so that as their natural parents brought them into the world, these should bring them up. Therefore let them look to God for their recompense (who takes it on himself to be834 “a father of the fatherless”), and for their encouragement let them remember the reward which Mordecai received from the Lord. Indeed, let them also remember the blessing that God bestowed on Esther. God often so blesses the means used for the education of orphans that those who take the care of it have no cause to regret their pains and cost, but rather have much cause for comfort, joy and thanksgiving.

§. 75. Of the common neglect of orphans.

All too common is the contrary disposition of most kinsmen and kinswomen. They think they are bound to none but their own children, and if they have no children, to none at all. Many are of the mind of Ruth’s kinsman: they fear they would “jeopardize”835 their own inheritance. Though they are themselves exceedingly rich, and spend much on clothing, pastimes and their households, yet they can allow the orphans of their poor kindred to go without, and to beg out of need.

This is what makes the loss of natural parents so much the greater. And in this many Christians are more inhuman than the heathen. The apostle implies as much where he says that they are “worse than an unbeliever”;836 for orphans who are next of kin are to be counted among those whom the apostle calls a man’s837 OWN.

§. 76. Of the duty of guardians.

The last sort of those who are in place of parents are those who have the charge of children committed to them by the voluntary appointment of parents, or who are chosen by the children themselves, or by the magistrate when the parents are dead, or lunatic, or in any other way incapable and unable to train up their own children.

From these, care and conscience are required rather than cost and expense; for commonly their expenses are allowed them and their pains are repaid.

Those who have the charge of children committed to them because of the death or incapacity of the natural parents are commonly called guardians, and two general duties are required of them.

  1. That they see to their wards’ good education.
  2. That they preserve their patrimony and inheritance.

As for their education, they are to observe the directions given before to natural parents.

As for preserving their patrimony, they must do for their wards what they would do for their own children, and so conduct themselves that they may with a good conscience give their wards, or anyone else, the account which the law requires.

These two duties are the main ends for which guardians are chosen. If they are faithful in performing them, great amends will be made for the untimely death of parents. Though parents die before their children are old enough to manage their estate, yet their houses and families will be maintained, and young heirs kept from swindlers and cheats.

It is noted of John, who had the mother of Jesus entrusted838 to him, that he “took her into his home.” This implies his provident care for her good.

§. 77. Of the fraud of guardians.

Contrary to this is the practice of most guardians, who take wards839 for their own advantage and make a prey of them. The heathen could say that guardianship is to be carried out for the benefit of the ward, not of the guardian. Yet among Christians this fault of guardians is found.

1. There are few children (who do not have natural parents to see to their good education) who are not greatly neglected in it, and brought up very untaught and unrestrained. Indeed, many times they are kept too sparingly and stingily in food, clothing and other needful things, though they have enough to pay for all that will be spent on them.

2. The main estate and patrimony of many wards is much diminished. If they have lands, as much waste is made of them as possibly can be. And when an account is to be given, it will be an inflated, unjust and most unconscionable account. So long as the guardian can get a general release, that is all he cares about.

3. Marriages are in a way forced on many wards, and such matches put on them as they cannot like; indeed, such as are in no way fit for them, neither in standing, nor years, nor build of body, nor qualities of mind.

Little do these guardians think of the account to which they will be brought one day before the Lord, who calls himself the “helper of the fatherless,”840 and who sees the wrong done, to repay it. Fearful is the judgment which the Lord has841 threatened against those who oppress the fatherless. Therefore let unjust guardians not think that the gain they get wrongfully from their wards will prosper; rather let them expect God’s curse on their own children and goods.

If those to whom parents themselves have committed their children on their deathbeds, trusting in their faithfulness, deal deceitfully with their wards, their sin is doubled and tripled. For

  1. They violate the bond of friendship, faithfulness and the trust placed in them.
  2. They sin directly against justice.
  3. They most monstrously transgress the rules of love.

§. 78. Of the duty of schoolmasters and tutors.

Among those who are set in the place of parents by voluntary appointment, schoolmasters and tutors are to be counted. The authority and charge of a parent is committed to them for a time; therefore for that time they ought to perform a parent’s duty.

Their duty is confined to education. It does not belong to them to maintain the children committed to them; rather, they themselves are maintained by their pains in that work.

All the duties which were included before under nurture belong to schoolmasters and tutors. More particularly, they are to instruct children in three things.

  1. In learning.
  2. In civility and good manners.
  3. In true piety and religion.

I need not speak of these points more than has842 been delivered before. Only, to stir them up to be diligent in nurturing children well in those three points, let the benefit of good schoolmasters and tutors be well noted.

Schoolmasters commonly cast the first seed into the hearts of843 children; they are the first to season them. As the seed is, so will the crop be; as the first seasoning is, so will the savor continue to be. If they sow no good seed at all, what harvest can be expected? If they sow a corrupt seed of rudeness, license, profaneness, superstition, or any wickedness, the crop must of necessity correspond to it. But if they sow the good seed of learning, civility and piety, there is great hope of a good crop.

From this it follows that they are of great use, and may bring much good, not only to the children themselves and their parents,844 but also to the church and commonwealth. Julian the Apostate was not ignorant of this. Therefore, in his endeavor to root Christianity out of the world, he allowed no man who professed himself a Christian to teach a school, but in place of Christian schoolmasters he set up heathen schoolmasters in every part of his dominions.

Tutors, to whose government young students sent to the universities are committed, have to deal with children in their riper years, at the very time when they are to be settled in a course of life: the very time in which much good may be done to children, or else in which they may be utterly corrupted. There will be little hope of bending them and drawing them into another course after they are freed from a tutor’s government. Tutors therefore, as they need great wisdom, so they need a good conscience, so that they may take the greater care of their pupils and the greater pains in teaching them the three points named above: learning, civility, and piety. A good tutor may do much to repair the negligence and amend the defects of a schoolmaster; but there is no one left to redress the failings of a tutor. Children are for the most part past remedy when they cease to have a tutor.

§. 79. Of the negligence of schoolmasters and tutors.

The vices contrary to the duty of schoolmasters named above are these.

1. Unskillfulness. Many who are fitter to be taught than to teach take this weighty calling on themselves. Some lack sufficient learning; some again are rude and do not themselves know good manners; and some do not know the first principles of the oracles of God. No good can be expected from these.

2. Covetousness. All that many seek is to multiply the number of their pupils and to get as much as they can for boarding and teaching. They aim more at their own gain than at their pupils’ profit. Children are not likely to thrive well under them.

3. Negligence. Many are unwilling to take the pains of a schoolmaster, and so they come into the school as little as they can, take every small occasion to be gone again, and do not care how much their children play. If they can hire a poor assistant teacher, all the burden is thrown on him. Little fruit can be expected from them.

4. Lack of piety. Many skillful and painstaking schoolmasters, under whose teaching children come on exceedingly well in learning, think that it does not belong to them at all to teach the grounds of religion, so that they wholly neglect piety. Surely they lack it themselves; for if their own hearts were seasoned with true piety, their consciences would move them to teach it to their children. The things of the kingdom of God are like leaven, which seasons the whole batch of dough with the seasoning and savor it has itself. When children spend almost all their time with their schoolmasters, from whom should they learn it, if not from them? What blessing can be hoped for from the pains of such schoolmasters?

To these I might add the excessive laxness of some (by which children grow too headstrong) and the too great severity of others, either in correcting too often, as if they delighted in it, or in the measure of it, as if they were dealing with beasts; by this they frighten children and make them dull, and impudent too. But these extremes were845 handled before.

The common fault of tutors is to neglect their pupils altogether. Many think that being a tutor is a matter of mere title: that no more is required of them than to bear the name, and to guarantee that the college is paid for their pupils’ board. This notion, and the practice that goes with it, is the blemish and bane of the universities. Many children well trained up in schools utterly lose the benefit of all their former education when they are sent to the university, because their tutors leave them wholly to themselves, and so they are made a prey to idle and wicked companions. Because of this many parents are utterly discouraged from sending their children to the university.
